script_body: Take the 4 or 5 train to Bowling Green, or the N/R to Whitehall Street. Begin from inside Bowling Green Park, standing at the bottom of Broadway and facing north — toward the bull. From here, it is remarkable to imagine that over the next twelve miles lies the longest avenue in America. But until the second quarter of the nineteenth century, New York City went no farther than City Hall, a fifteen-minute walk to the north.

script_body: At Broadway's base lies Bowling Green Park, New York City's first official park, established in 1733. Its history runs to the business and leisure of the Dutch and English: it has been pasture for cows, parade ground for soldiers, and, true to its name, a bowling field for colonists. "Taxation and recreation," one might say, illustrates the park's varied history.

script_body: By 1770, King George III was rewarded by the colonists with a gilded statue in the center of the park for his alleged efforts in repealing the Stamp Act; a year later the fence was added. In 1776, hours after the Declaration of Independence was read in what is now City Hall Park, enraged colonists and members of the Sons of Liberty beheaded the statue. Supposedly George's molten lead was then cast into musket balls later used to shoot Tory soldiers. The fence around Bowling Green is one of the oldest in the city; iron crowns adorned the gateposts until American revolutionaries sheared them off. Touch history — you can actually feel where this happened.

poi_name: National Museum of the American Indian
script_body: Now home to the Museum of the American Indian and the U.S. Bankruptcy Court, this building was once the primary point for revenue collection in the United States. Before the income tax arrived in 1913, this was where the government made its money — and since New York was by far the leading port city in America, there was a huge amount of money to be made. As historian Henry Hope Reed once noted, if City Hall was run by the Democratic machine, the Custom House was certainly Republican. In fact it was Republican Chester Arthur who, as collector of customs of the Port of New York before becoming president on the death of James Garfield, set the wheels in motion for the building's construction.

script_body: The 1907 Cass Gilbert masterpiece is a great example of New York City's beaux arts heritage. Beaux arts translates literally as "fine arts" and derives from the great French school, the École des Beaux Arts. But in the New York context the term takes on a larger meaning: it refers to buildings that evince civic pride, that express a grandeur and stateliness to match their civic function — whether that function be to house trains, books, or tax collectors.

script_body: In front of the Custom House stand Daniel Chester French's limestone statues representing Asia, America, Europe, and Africa, from left to right — by the sculptor of the Lincoln Memorial. On the facade, Gilbert illustrates commerce: atop the cornice are twelve marble statues of history's most successful commercial states. Although you can't see it, the name Germany was effaced during World War I and replaced with Belgium. And gazing ahead from within every capital is Mercury, Roman god of commerce. Step into the museum to view the oval rotunda, decorated with a series of 1930s Works Progress Administration murals by Reginald Marsh.

script_body: Look up Broadway at No. 26, on the corner of Broadway and Beaver, at the building topped with a cast-iron oil burner. The lantern expresses the building's function: it housed Standard Oil, John D. Rockefeller's monopolistic firm. But by the time this tower was built in 1924, the flame had long been extinguished — in 1911 the U.S. Supreme Court required the Standard Oil Holding Company to be dissolved and its directors to relinquish control of its subsidiaries. Standard Oil's offices remained here until the 1930s, when Rockefeller Center was constructed. And in 1796, the town residence of another financial giant, Alexander Hamilton, stood on this very site.

script_body: Across the way, on the west side, 25 Broadway was the former central ticket office of the Cunard Shipping Line. Cunard, leader of the pack among the era's many steamship companies, put up this building in 1921 to house the firm that ran the fastest and most luxurious liners in the world. In the age of expensive cruises and mass immigration, this was big business — so much so that in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, this bottom stretch of Broadway was known as Steamship Row. Step inside (but not on Sunday) to see spectacular wall frescoes and maps outlining the old Cunard routes.

script_body: On the corner of Pearl and Whitehall, 33 Whitehall houses the National Association of Securities Dealers — NASDAQ — though unlike the Stock Exchange, its visitor center sits in Times Square, not here. Across the street to the south stood the Whitehall Induction Center, immortalized in Arlo Guthrie's classic "Alice's Restaurant" as the place where Guthrie was "injected, inspected, detected, infected, neglected, and selected." It was here that Benjamin Spock, the famed baby specialist turned antiwar leader, and the poet Allen Ginsberg were arrested in 1967 as part of Stop the Draft Week.

script_body: Goldman Sachs, the notoriously secretive investment-banking concern, is housed in this creatively built octagonal structure at 85 Broad Street, which slices through Stone Street. The building was designed to conform to the irregular street pattern, and paving stones representing Stone Street actually cut right through Goldman Sachs's lobby. The partnership between Marcus Goldman and Samuel Sachs dates from 1882, when they joined forces to further the commercial-paper business Goldman had begun thirteen years earlier.

script_body: Before its revolutionary history, the building was the mansion of Stephen Delancey — as in Delancey Street — a French immigrant who received it as a wedding present from his father-in-law, Colonel Stephanus Van Cortlandt, New York City's tenth mayor. The tavern itself was run by an immigrant from the West Indies, Samuel Fraunces, who would soon become Washington's steward, and it was a popular watering hole of the day. It was also the site where the Committee of Correspondence — later the Continental Congress — held its first meeting.

script_body: The building is a conjectural reproduction — no original bits survive save a few bricks — financed by the Sons of the Revolution in 1907. Its style is Georgian, named for those British kings and soon renamed "colonial" or "federal" in keeping with the antiroyalist mood of the new states. The block of Pearl Street just east represents one of the city's few remaining block-long groups of late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century shipping offices and warehouses; they were among the few that survived the Great Fire of 1835 unscathed. Thanks to the New York Landmarks Conservancy for saving them, the area is now the Fraunces Tavern Block Historic District.

script_body: Here in Hanover Square sits lonely Abraham DePeyster — former mayor of New York City, colonial chief justice in the late seventeenth century, and prominent merchant — who once had a more princely view up Broadway when he stood in Bowling Green Park. The square was once the center of the city's publishing industry: William Bradford's New York Gazette, the city's first newspaper of 1725, had its printing offices here. It was also the home base of Captain Kidd, the privateer turned pirate. Tellingly, Hanover Square keeps the family name of the English kings — in sharp contrast to much of New York that changed its nomenclature after the Revolution.

script_body: On the west side of the square is India House at One Hanover Square, built in the early 1850s. It was originally the Hanover Bank and later the New York Cotton Exchange, when cotton was king. Brownstone was once seen as unseemly for a proper home, but this building — like Trinity Church — helped change that, and in the later nineteenth century brownstone became a mark of dignity for New York's landed gentry. Today India House is one of Lower Manhattan's most exclusive business clubs; it takes its name from nautical trips to, and Orientalist fantasies of, the East, its original members more concerned with maritime issues than with banking.

script_body: Look eastward toward Old Slip by the river, which until 1973 housed the First Precinct Police. script_body: At 22 William, between Beaver and Exchange Place, is the City Bank Farmers' Trust Company Building of 1931. It has always been a curiosity in the canyons of Wall Street: it departs from the rectilinear and pivots as if ready to blast off, the irregular site pushing its architects to experiment. The bronze doors are its pièces de résistance, filled with trains, boats, and airplanes, and the interior uses over forty kinds of marble laced with nickel and copper.

script_body: The "Wall" in the name comes from an actual wall built by the Dutch. Governor Peter Stuyvesant had it erected in 1653, and it lasted until the latter seventeenth century, when colonists under British rule finally undermined it. Known in Dutch as De Wal, it was made of wooden planks stacked roughly nine feet high and was manned to keep both the British (until 1664) and the Indians away from New Amsterdam.

script_body: At the eastern end of Wall Street stood a number of slave markets. On the eve of the American Revolution, New York City was an ignominious second to Charleston, South Carolina, among urban slaveholding cities. It was not until July 4, 1827 — with the approval of Governor Daniel D. Tompkins and the state legislature — that slavery was officially laid to rest in New York.

script_body: At 55 Wall Street stands a building designed by Isaiah Rogers in 1842 to replace the Merchants Exchange, which had burned with seven hundred other buildings in the Great Fire of 1835. It served as the U.S. Custom House from 1863 to 1899 and later as a branch of Citibank. It's notable for a seamless arrangement of structure: the lower Ionic colonnade of 1842 — each column a single block of stone — works hand in glove with an upper Corinthian colonnade added seventy years later. The mammoth lobby measures 198 feet long and 132 feet high, and houses the largest display of Wedgewood china in the world around its central chandelier.

script_body: Across from 55 Wall stands the J. P. Morgan Building at 60 Wall, Kevin Roche's rich postmodern monolith — praised even by critic Ada Louise Huxtable, no friend of recent New York architecture. By the 1970s the modern movement had grown so moribund, producing a surfeit of flat-topped knockoffs, that it seemed the grace of earlier eras was lost. Roche's tower holds its own among Wall Street's pantheon and, unusually for a tall building, blends in rather than dominates — its faux colonnade answering 55 Wall's real one across the street. In a quirk, it was 55 Wall that sold its air rights to allow the J. P. Morgan Building's fifty-five stories.

script_body: At 40 Wall Street — originally the Bank of Manhattan — sits one of the great stories in American skyscraper construction. In the summer of 1929, longtime professional rivals and former partners William Van Alen and Craig Severance were hard at work trying to outdo each other in the battle for dominant skyscraper height. The Woolworth Tower still held sway as the city's tallest, but Severance was convinced to the last moment that his Bank of Manhattan would outdo Van Alen's automotive giant, the Chrysler Building, and dethrone Frank Woolworth. Hidden from view, and unveiled only at the final moment of the competition, was Chrysler's razor-sharp spire — its additional 125 feet outdid 40 Wall and brought the Chrysler Building the fame of being the tallest. Severance's consolation prize? 40 Wall broke all records for speed, finished in eleven months with over a million square feet of floor space. For Van Alen, success was short-lived: the Empire State unseated the Chrysler after only eighteen months. As for the Bank of Manhattan, in five years it dropped to fifth-tallest in the country — today it's at number 30 and counting.

script_body: Finished in 1960, David Rockefeller's Chase Manhattan Bank Building is a shining example of sleek postwar modernism. It helped usher in a new "democratic" era of bank building, where banks became transparent structures that could be "seen through" rather than maintaining the impenetrable fortress facades of tradition. For the sharpest contrast, look through the Chase building at the Federal Reserve behind it — an impenetrable fortress, as well it should be, to hold all the gold inside.

poi_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
script_body: Built like a fortress in 1924, the Federal Reserve Bank was made to resist the elements. It is not New York snobbery to call it the most significant of the thirteen Federal Reserve sites. Its limestone facade is noted for weathering in different tones — notice how they change from light to dark — and the magnificent wrought-iron lanterns were designed by the Philadelphian Samuel Yellin. The Federal Reserve itself was set up in 1914 to have a central bank, rather than one person, make policy: in 1907, for example, J. P. Morgan personally mobilized enough banking support to stave off a collapse that could have rivaled the Great Depression.

script_body: Westward at 14 Wall stands the Bankers Trust Building. Bankers Trust is no more, but Trowbridge and Livingston's pyramidal top — modeled on antiquity's mausoleum at Halicarnassus — remains one of the great pinnacles in a city bathed in sumptuous finishing touches. J. P. Morgan even shacked up beneath the pyramid to have a bird's-eye view of the construction of his own building across the street. The pyramid became the logo of Bankers Trust for years, though, in a testimony to the downtown canyons, you cannot see it from Wall Street itself. Inside, peek at the bronze lobby gates representing the enterprises of capitalism — metallurgy, shipping, mining, agriculture, and power.

script_body: On the northeast corner of Nassau and Wall stands Federal Hall National Memorial, dubbed the "Parthenon of Wall Street." The site has a vigorous past as the city's second city hall, later the Custom House and subtreasury, and now a federal museum. The current Greek-revival structure dates from 1842; the earlier building on the site, where Washington took his oath and the new government operated for its first eighteen months, was designed by Pierre L'Enfant — the master planner of Washington, D.C. — and was demolished in 1790 when the capital moved to Philadelphia. The Greek-revival style suited an age when Athenian democracy and the Greek independence movement produced a bumper crop of Doric-templed civic buildings; later, as abolitionism gained steam, Greece became associated with slavery rather than the demos, and those classical buildings lost their place in the sun.

The current structure dates from 1842... script_body: Before its federal function, the building on this site teemed with the birth pangs of the republic. The famed Stamp Act Congress met here in 1765 to draft the Declaration of Grievances against "taxation without representation." The Declaration of Independence was read here on July 9 — it took some days to travel from Philadelphia to New York. And the site even served as the British headquarters during the Revolutionary War.

script_body: On the southeast corner of Broad and Wall stands a plain, unornamented, unsigned building — J. P. Morgan's bank. As Morgan wanted all to realize, if you didn't know what this building was, you had no business being there. The only decoration on the facade are the pockmarks that dot the Wall Street side: remnants of a bomb, blamed on anarchists, that killed thirty-eight people and wounded hundreds in 1920. The scars remain because Morgan felt they were a testament to his invincibility.

script_body: The forlorn little tree out front on Broad Street isn't any old tree but a buttonwood, or sycamore. In 1792, twenty-four brokers met under a buttonwood — in actuality further east on Wall Street — and began trading the massive debt from the Revolutionary War. The so-called Buttonwood Agreement, as Edwin Burrows and Michael Wallace tell us in Gotham, "laid the foundations for a structured securities market." Early the next year the traders moved into the Tontine Coffee House on the northwest corner of Water and Wall — a site that had been the locale for the infamous Royal African Trading Company, where the English bought and sold enslaved Africans.

script_body: Directly across Broad Street from Morgan's building is the sine qua non of capitalist institutions, the New York Stock Exchange — even if its address is on Broad Street, it's the best known of Wall Street's buildings. In contrast to Federal Hall's severe Grecian temple across the way, the NYSE's Roman trappings are all pomp and circumstance. The market has seen a multitude of changes since the crash of 1929: it took a full twenty-five years before the Dow surpassed that summer's highs, and not until 1968 did daily volume surpass the 16 million shares traded on Black Thursday. Today the NYSE trades 16 million in each day's first few minutes.

script_body: New York City was no stranger to slavery: it was the largest slaveholding city in all the colonies until 1750, and the number-one place for slave importation and auctions. Slaves arrived as early as 1626 from the Dutch West Indies, but on September 15, 1655, the Witte Paert docked with three hundred African slaves, signaling the city's beginning as a large-scale port for the transatlantic slave trade. By 1664 the city was 20 to 25 percent black. Under the Dutch, some were given "half freedom" — a degree of freedom in housing and employment, though even half-free blacks had to work for the Dutch West India Company when needed, and their children were company property. When the British conquered in 1664 they recognized all slave property, eliminated half-free status, and made freedom harder each year; in 1706 a law decreed that conversion to Christianity did not affect a slave's status. New York City held 3,137 slaves by 1771. The institution was dismantled only gradually: the Manumission Society began work in 1785, the Gradual Manumission Act of 1799 freed males born after that year at twenty-eight and females at twenty-five, and full emancipation finally took effect in 1827.

script_body: New York saw several significant slave uprisings in the eighteenth century, most notably the 1712 uprising on Maiden Lane and Nassau Street — the present site of the Home Insurance Company. There more than fifty armed slaves gathered for an uprising that killed nine white settlers before the slaves dispersed to the north. Ultimately nineteen participants were captured and executed in gruesome fashion — by hanging, burning, and goring — to intimidate the remaining slave population.

script_body: The building at 1 Wall Street now houses the Bank of New York, which absorbed the original owners, Irving Trust, in 1988 — at the time the building carried the highest real-estate price tag of any site in New York City. Inside, the three-story reception hall is one of the most glorious interiors in Manhattan: this is Art Deco at its most majestic, soaring and emboldened. Lewis Mumford called 1 Wall Street a building of "untrammeled imagination." At the very top of the fluted skyscraper sits a gilded mosaic boardroom, testament to the extravagance of a different age — before the golden age of Deco came to a screeching halt with the Great Depression.

script_body: There was a time when churches were all one could see on the skyline, and Trinity, at 280 feet, was the highest point in New York City until surpassed by the towers of the Brooklyn Bridge — which says a lot about commerce. Trinity began as a land grant from King William III to the colonists in the late seventeenth century; the church originally controlled all the land from Fulton up to Christopher Street. Many early belfrymen, pastors, and rectors now have city streets named after them — Chambers, Murray, and Reade, for example. Trinity has gone through three incarnations: the first (1698-1776) burned in the fire of 1776, the second saw its roof implode in 1839, and the present building by Richard Upjohn has withstood the ravages of time.

script_body: Walk the churchyard and you'll meet an illustrious gathering of the city's financial elite and early purveyors of freedom. Alexander Hamilton was buried here after his fateful duel with Vice President Aaron Burr in Weehawken; Robert Fulton, inventor of the steamship, is memorialized; William Bradford, publisher of New York's first newspaper, rests here; and so does Francis Lewis, the only signer of the Declaration of Independence buried in Manhattan. Opposite Pine Street stands the Soldiers/Martyrs monument, erected in 1852 to soldiers who died imprisoned in the Rhinelander Sugar House during the Revolution — of the war's 18,500 who died in captivity, more than half perished in New York.

script_body: Take a detour through the graveyard and down the stairs to Trinity Place to peek at the American Stock Exchange. The AMEX has its roots at the curbstone of Broad Street and Exchange Place, where "curb brokers" would literally stop at nothing to buy and sell. Only in 1921 — after fifty-six years — did the New York curb market find a home, and in 1953 it was officially designated the American Stock Exchange.

script_body: Standing on Thames Street opposite 120 Broadway gives a crash course in New York City's first zoning ordinance. The Equitable Building's extreme mass — floor area thirty times the site's area, shafts going straight up forty floors, forty-five acres of floor space on a site just over an acre — was discouraging enough that light and air became the most desired commodities on the block. The new ordinance called for a "zoning envelope" that forced what became known as the "setback": the stepped-back, stairlike recesses you see as buildings grow taller. Spurred on by Hugh Ferris's exquisite drawings, setbacks became a design challenge, each architect trying to outdo the next in geometry and flair.

Forty-five acres of floor space all on a site that was just over an acre in size!... the new ordinance called for a "zoning envelope" that restricted pure shafts darting straight into the sky and forced what became known as the "setback"—the stepped-back, stairlike recesses one sees as buildings grow taller. script_body: You may wonder how, in this dense and overoccupied district, an open-air plaza with benches managed to emerge here at Liberty Plaza. It was the great Seagram Building on Park Avenue, with its pristine plaza and open space, that convinced the city to find incentives for developers to allow more public use. Thus was born the 1961 zoning ordinance, which rewarded builders who provided public space integrated with private buildings.

Thus was born the 1961 zoning ordinance, which encouraged and rewarded builders who provided public space integrated with private buildings.

script_body: Directly west of Liberty Plaza once stood the seven-building complex of the World Trade Center, spotlighted by the twin towers — Towers 1 and 2 — the third-tallest buildings in the world. In the greatest act of terror to occur on American soil, almost three thousand persons lost their lives on September 11, 2001, when two hijacked planes were crashed into the towers, resulting in horrible fires and the buildings' implosion. As the authors wrote, it was too early to know what would become of this tragic space — but in New York's unceasing effort to rebuild that which is torn down, it was unlikely the area would remain fallow far into the future. The question of how to memorialize echoed the long-debated African burial ground just north near City Hall.

script_body: Across Broadway, the Marine Midland Bank Building at 140 Broadway shows what an ambitious developer could do. It was uncommon — impossible, really — in the late 1960s and 1970s for a developer to think about quality as a way of attracting tenants, but Harry Helmsley was ahead of his time. He hired one of the great international-style architects, Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore Owings and Merrill, who also designed the Chase building behind it, as well as the sculptor Isamu Noguchi. The result is a sleek, refined glass exterior, and Noguchi's contribution is an orange cube — to be exact, a six-sided rhombohedron — with a cut-out hole.

script_body: On the site of today's U.S. Steel Building at 1 Liberty Plaza once stood one of the great downtown buildings, the Singer Building. Perhaps the mourning wasn't as great as when Pennsylvania Station was slaughtered in 1963, but the Singer Building's demolition brought tears of rage consistent with its long-standing place in the skyline. Its tragic epitaph: it is the tallest building ever to be demolished.

script_body: The tallest building in the world from 1913 to 1929, the Woolworth at 233 Broadway is symbolized by its trademarked name, the "Cathedral of Commerce." It was Frank Woolworth's revolutionary genius to open stores where the buyer could touch, feel, and examine every item — and it made him a mint. The exterior is dressed in late Gothic style, its terra-cotta facade and clear base-shaft-tower form making it, for many enthusiasts, the archetype of a skyscraper. Inside, look for the magnificent gargoyles, including Cass Gilbert the architect and Woolworth himself counting the nickels and dimes with which he literally paid for the building — in full, with $13 million in cash, so it never had a mortgage.

The exterior of the building is dressed up in late Gothic style. specifically the terra cotta used throughout the facade; the clear and articulated form of the base, shaft, and tower. script_body: The Lower East Side is probably the single most significant multiethnic neighborhood in America. For two hundred years it has been the first area of settlement for migrant and immigrant communities, and it still is. New Yorkers continue to argue about where it begins and ends; the contemporary neighborhood is bordered to the north by Houston Street, to the west by Lafayette, and to the south and east by the East River. But it is better understood as a living multiethnic neighborhood, not one fixed by geographic boundaries.

script_body: Early eighteenth-century maps show this area as the country estates of established Dutch and English settlers — the Stuyvesant, Delancey, Rutgers, DePeyster, and Roosevelt families. After the American Revolution the estates gave way to suburban settlements, and by the mid-nineteenth century the first great influx of immigrants arrived. By the 1840s the largest groups were Irish, Germans, and free blacks. A half century later these had moved northward, replaced by southern and eastern Europeans from Italy, Russia, and Poland. Most of today's immigrant residents are Latino and Asian.

A half century later these groups had largely moved northward and were replaced by southern and eastern Europeans from Italy, Russia, Poland, and elsewhere. Most of today's immigrant residents are Latino and Asian immigrants.

script_body: In 1900 the Lower East Side was the most densely populated spot on earth, with 850 residents per block and nearly 1,000 per acre. A single square block beside Sara Delano Roosevelt Park — bounded by Canal, Hester, Eldridge, and Forsythe Streets — housed 2,628 people in 1890. That same block today houses no residents at all; it holds only a school and a few manufacturers. Other blocks were destroyed to build the approaches to the Manhattan and Williamsburg Bridges in 1903 and 1909, forcing tens of thousands from their homes.

script_body: This green space exists because seven blocks of tenement houses were destroyed between 1932 and 1936. The demolition was part of a Depression-era plan to employ thousands of laborers with federal relief funds: the city proclaimed eminent domain over the tenements, removed the tenants, and tore the buildings down. Like most public spaces in New York, the park is named for a significant New Yorker — Franklin Delano Roosevelt's mother, Sara, who was raised in a manor house, now long gone, on nearby Chrystie Street.

script_body: In 1637 the Bowery was created by New Amsterdam governor Willem Kieft to connect the distant Dutch farms of what we now call the East Village with the city, then south of Wall Street. Some historians claim the name derives from bowerij, the Dutch word for farm; others say it comes from de bowerie, the road to the farms. Either way, it linked the city to the countryside, and by 1776 the Bowery connected New York City all the way to Boston, Massachusetts.

script_body: In the early twentieth century the Bowery was a geographical divider — Little Italy to the west, the Jewish Lower East Side to the east. Between 1878 and 1955 an elevated train ran the length of the street. Before electrification, soot and burning embers falling from the engines made crossing under the tracks dangerous and unpleasant, and the El shrouded the Bowery in darkness, deepening its seedy, dingy atmosphere.

script_body: The Hotel Providence on the southeast corner of Bowery and Grand, at 125 Bowery, is one of eight surviving Bowery flophouses. These private hotels emerged in the early 1870s; the largest, the Mills Hotel, had five hundred rooms and slept over a thousand men. For eight to fifteen dollars a night a male resident gets a four-by-eight-foot cubicle with a cot and a hanging light, sharing toilets and baths on each floor. The rooms are nicknamed cages because the walls do not reach the ceiling — just above the door jamb, the wall is replaced with a wire screen.

script_body: Across the Bowery from the Hotel Providence stood Steve Brodie's Saloon, at 114 Bowery. Brodie, a national champion racewalker, jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge in July 1886, collected a two-hundred-dollar bet for surviving the leap, and used the money to open his saloon here. On the wall behind the bar he painted a large image of himself falling between the bridge and the water. While a regular saloon, Brodie's quickly became a prime tourist spot: for a small consideration he would retell his story to visitors. Should anyone doubt his tale, he would point to the signed affidavit from the nearly dozen witnesses who saw his leap. A cloud of suspicion does remain — those who signed were members of Brodie's gang. For years after his death an old man would pretend to be Brodie and recount the tale, much to the delight of the tourists.

script_body: Wrapped around the old Bowery Bank is the Bowery Savings Bank, built 1894 to 1895 and designed by Stanford White. The L-shaped building's street address is 130 Bowery, and it is one of the few landmarked buildings on the Lower East Side. The Bowery Savings Bank was created in 1834 by three prominent New York businessmen: Hamilton Fish, Peter C. Stuyvesant, and Anson Phelps. The original 1834 safe box is displayed in a small historical exhibit in the restored main banking room.

script_body: Di Palo's Fine Foods, on the northeast corner of Mott and Grand, is one of the few Italian stores left in the midst of New Chinatown. It was opened by Savino Di Palo in 1910 and moved to this corner in 1925, where it has remained ever since. The family comes from Puglia, a rural region known for its dairy farmers and cheese-makers, and the shop still makes its own mozzarella and other cheeses. The low marble counters are reminiscent of the Italian kitchen table — designed for conversation as well as commerce — and the entire front of the store is kept at cheese-curing temperature.

script_body: At 203 Grand Street, on June 22, 1905, Dr. Vincent Sellaro founded the Order of the Sons of Italy in America. Sellaro wanted an organization with a dual mission: to encourage Italian immigrants to work together despite their provincial origins, and to preserve Italian languages and customs in America. The Sons of Italy grew into a national umbrella organization bringing together more than 750 Italian social clubs, family societies, and fraternal orders — much like the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association and the Irish Ancient Order of Hibernians.

script_body: Between 1880 and 1920, nearly 4.1 million Italian immigrants came to the United States — no other ethnic group in American history has sent so many in such a short period. Manhattan had fewer than twenty thousand Italian residents in 1880, but by 1930 more than a million New Yorkers were of Italian descent. Most came from the rural south, driven out by extreme poverty, heavy taxation, a population surge, and recurring agricultural crises. Today more than eighty percent of the residents of what used to be Little Italy are Asian; the Italians, like the Irish and Germans before them, have migrated away.

script_body: Banca Stabile, at 189 Grand Street on the southwest corner of Grand and Mulberry, is an 1865 Neapolitan family bank that served the varied needs of Italian immigrants. The tin ceilings, terrazzo floors, large vault, and brass tellers' cages have all been preserved. Beyond banking, Stabile provided currency exchange, translation services, and steamship-ticket sales. Look inside at the cashiers' cages, still labeled tickets, money exchange, and foreign transfers.

script_body: The oldest building in this area now houses Paolucci's Restaurant at 149 Mulberry. Built in 1816 as the Van Rensselaer residence, it is a perfect early-nineteenth-century merchant house: shop on the first floor, storage in the basement, family on the upper floors, and servants or slaves in the attic. In the 1880s it became the Italian Free Library.

script_body: The Franciscan Fathers who care for the Shrine of San Gennaro, Saint Januarius, keep a rectory at 109 Mulberry Street, with the Church of the Most Precious Blood entered from 113 Baxter Street behind it. San Gennaro, the patron saint of Naples, was martyred by the Romans at Pozzuoli in A.D. 305; the legend says an old couple gathered his blood after his beheading and preserved it in a vial. That blood is said to liquify twice a year — the miracle of San Gennaro — on the first Sunday in May and on September 19. Two thousand years later, in 1917, four Neapolitan businessmen on Mulberry Street decided to celebrate Gennaro's martyrdom, and a great New York tradition was born. Every year for ten days in mid-September, Mulberry Street from Canal up to Houston is closed for the Feast of San Gennaro. Although most of the feast today is sausage and zeppole stands, a bust of the saint is paraded through the streets by the faithful; between parades it sits in the window of the Mulberry Street Cigar Company at 140 Mulberry.

script_body: Columbus Park sits atop the former Five Points district and the old Collect Pond. Before 1790 this was a beautiful freshwater pond ringed by low hills and the cottages of wealthy New Yorkers. In 1790 the chief landowner, Sarah Delancey, daughter of colonial governor James Delancey, leased much of it to a consortium of forty-six butchers, who set up a slaughter yard along the shore. Bone-boiling and leather-tanning shops followed, rapidly polluting the pond. The city drained it by way of Canal Street in 1805, leveled the surrounding hills, filled the pond, and renamed the area Paradise Square. But the Collect had been fed by underground springs, and with the constant dampness the ground decayed. The upper-middle-class residents moved out to Greenwich Village and St. John's Park, replaced by poor Irish Catholic immigrants. Paradise Square became Five Points — named for the five-pointed intersection where Park (now Mosco), Worth, and Orange (now Baxter) Streets met, at the southwestern tip of today's Columbus Park.

script_body: Built between 1892 and 1894, Columbus Park was the first open space designed and built for this neighborhood. The person most responsible was Jacob Riis, the Danish American photographer and writer who chronicled the lives of poor New Yorkers. To create it, the city destroyed an entire block of tenements by right of eminent domain. First called Mulberry Bend Park, it was rechristened Columbus Park by Italian residents in 1911. Note how Mulberry Street curves here — this sharp crook is the infamous Mulberry Bend, which residents and newspapers called Ragpickers' Row, Bandits' Roost, and Thieves' Alley.

script_body: On the south corner of Mosco and Mulberry, at 28 Mulberry, a building with marble pillars and a terra-cotta eagle was Antonio Cuneo's 1881 bank. Cuneo, a Piedmontese immigrant who arrived in 1855, began selling nuts and fruit from a pushcart and slowly built a real estate and banking empire. In 1887 a U.S. congressional investigation found the bank operated under the padrone system — a labor arrangement in which the bank, for a fee, ran an agency in Naples coordinating prepaid steamer tickets and requests for underpaid labor. The system, outlawed in 1885 by the Contract Labor Law, brought immigrants in to undercut American wages.

script_body: At the southern end of the block, where Mulberry meets Worth, was the Cow Bay section of Five Points — the largest free-black neighborhood in Manhattan in the early nineteenth century. In 1805, nearly 1,200 of the 1,960 free blacks in Manhattan lived in this general area, and by 1825 the community had built seven churches. Historians debate whether the free blacks and Irish immigrants coexisted peacefully; newer research finds they not only shared the street but even shared houses, and historian Graham Hodges reports a dozen intermarried couples living here in the late 1860s.

script_body: The Church of the Transfiguration at 29 Mott Street was originally built in 1801 as the English Lutheran First Church of Zion, a Georgian-style church serving the farmers of the area. In 1827, as the neighborhood became Irish, the Lutheran congregation leased the building to the Catholic Church, which bought it outright in 1853. Look carefully at the facade and you'll notice different stone was used for the church and the steeple — the steeple was added after 1853.

script_body: The parish was founded in 1827 by Padre Félix Varela, New York's first Spanish-speaking priest. Born in Havana in 1788, Varela was an outspoken voice for Cuban independence; after his expulsion from Cuba he became a leader of this church and its Irish parishioners. The plaque calls him Father to needy Irish immigrants. By the early 1880s the Irish began migrating out and Italians used the basement for services — the two congregations worshiped the same God but in styles different enough that they didn't worship together. In 1902 an Italian priest, Father Cappo, moved the Italian community upstairs to sit with the Irish, and this became the church of Enrico Caruso, Jimmy Durante, and Mother Cabrini, the first naturalized American saint. By the 1960s the congregation had become increasingly Chinese; today it is almost exclusively so, with Mass given in Cantonese, Mandarin, and English.

script_body: Of all the immigrant groups that passed through the Lower East Side, the Chinese have had the longest continuous presence — a small group of sailors lived here as early as 1850, and by 1859 the New York Times estimated some 150 Chinese in the district. After the transcontinental railroad's completion in 1869 and rising anti-Chinese nativism, Chinese immigrants moved to cities, and Mott, Pell, and Doyers Streets became home to two thousand Chinese within a decade. America's anti-Chinese bigotry culminated in the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 — the Chinese became the first and only ethnic group excluded from admission and denied citizenship. Because the laborers already here could not bring their wives, the result was a bachelor society: in 1910 the New York ratio of Chinese young men to young women aged fifteen to twenty-one was 3,961 to 100. The act was finally revoked in 1943, and after the Immigration Act of 1965 the neighborhood's Chinese population exploded from 11,000 in 1960 to nearly 150,000 by 1995.

script_body: On the third floor of 12 Mott Street, south of the Church of the Transfiguration, was the former New York headquarters of the Kaoshen — High Mountain — Club, a secret political organization founded by Dr. Sun Yat Sen in 1895. This was the local chapter of Sun's secret revolutionary party, the Hsing Chung Hui, which helped overthrow the Chinese emperor in 1911. After a life as a revolutionary, Sun became the first president of the Republic of China — but only for a month. A junior high school on Hester Street is named for him.

script_body: For Chinatown, the umbrella organization overseeing many of the social groups is the Zhonghua Gong Suo — the New York Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, or CCBA — at 62 Mott Street, with the Taiwanese flag flying from the roof. Founded in 1883 in response to the Chinese Exclusion Act, it served as spokesperson and advocate for the community, settled disputes among Chinese organizations, hired lawyers to defend Chinese in court, and ran social-welfare programs. For a long time it was seen as the informal government of the Chinese community, binding together more than sixty family and fraternal associations.

script_body: At No. 24 Pell Street stands the former Sun Wui Association, the last wooden pagoda building in Chinatown and a great example of symbolism in Chinatown architecture. The roof is a pagoda topped with two fish — symbols of good luck and abundance, since the word for fish in many Chinese languages sounds like the one for profit or surplus. Its colors are red, gold, and green: red for good luck, gold for money or wealth, green for growth and flowering. Many signs in Chinatown combine these three traditional colors.

script_body: The Hip Sing Tong, the most powerful individual fraternal organization in Chinatown, is at 16 Pell Street, in the building labeled Pell Street Social Club. Tong means association, like wui, but it is a charged word carrying insinuations of criminal activity. These secret societies began arriving in New York in the early 1880s to protect their members' business interests. Over the years numerous tongs have been investigated and indicted for extortion, prostitution, and gambling — yet they also serve community functions. The Hip Sing Tong, for example, runs a federally insured credit union and offers business loans and student scholarships.

script_body: As you walk these narrow, curved streets, notice that they predate urban development and the automobile. Pell Street, which appeared on maps beginning in 1776, is named for John Pell, a prosperous butcher. Mott Street is named for Joseph Mott, also a butcher. The street names are our last link to those very early residents of the neighborhood.

script_body: In the nineteenth century scores of seedy saloons lined Doyers Street. Where the Chinatown Post Office now stands, at 4-6 Doyers, was one of the most famous: Callahan's. Neighborhood saloons hired singing men and scantily clad women to draw customers, and Callahan's hired two of the most popular young Jewish singers — Asa Yoelson and Israel Baline. When the pair were able to move out of the neighborhood, they changed their names to the more familiar, more American Al Jolson and Irving Berlin.

script_body: On an island slightly south of Doyers stands the 1962 Benjamin Ralph Kimlau Memorial Arch, dedicated to all Chinatown residents who died serving in the American armed forces during World War II. The war was a crucial turning point in Chinatown. Before the 1940s, books, plays, and reporters described the Chinese as opium addicts, gangsters, and the Yellow Peril. For Chinese Americans the war began not in December 1941 with Pearl Harbor but in 1932, with the Japanese invasion of Manchuria. When America entered the war, propaganda films presented the Chinese as patriotic and loyal, and other Americans slowly began to see them in an entirely different light.

script_body: At 55-57 St. James Place is the First Cemetery of the Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue, Shearith Israel — both a National Historic and a New York City Landmark, and the oldest Jewish cemetery in the United States. Buried here are Jewish American soldiers who fought in the American Revolution and Benjamin Mendes-Seixas, one of the founders of the New York Stock Exchange. When the cemetery was established it lay over a mile north of the city limits; Dutch governor Peter Stuyvesant, New York's first prominent anti-Semite, ordered it built outside New Amsterdam proper. The congregation still exists, meeting at Seventieth Street and Central Park West.

script_body: The Irish are one of the oldest immigrant groups in New York; the first St. Patrick's Day parade was held in 1766, and in 1784 the Society of the Friendly Sons of St. Patrick became the city's first specifically ethnic self-help organization. Mass Irish immigration began in the 1820s and peaked in the famine years of 1845 to 1855; by 1860 roughly one in six city residents claimed Irish heritage. The Irish helped found the police and fire departments and, through Tammany Hall, came to dominate Democratic politics by the 1870s. Tammany was a rampantly corrupt machine, but to immigrant Irish it was a crucial institution offering social welfare in exchange for a vote — and it was behind the 1880 election of William Grace, New York's first Irish Catholic mayor.

script_body: The 1976 elementary school P.S. 124 on Division Street, opposite Market Street, is named for Yung Wing — both school and man serving as role models for the area's Chinese immigrant children. Yung Wing, born near Macao in 1828, came to the United States as a student in 1847, entered Yale, and in 1854 became the first Chinese person to graduate from an American college. He devoted his life to the modernization of China and served as a Chinese diplomat in the United States, remaining in America until his death.

script_body: The Manhattan Bridge, the third bridge connecting Lower Manhattan with Brooklyn, was designed by engineer Gustav Lindenthal in 1905 and was the divider between Chinatown and the old Jewish East Side. The structure is greatly enhanced by its restored 1916 colonnade at the Canal Street entrance. Built by the architects Carrère & Hastings, this triumphal arch is a wonderful example of the City Beautiful movement, which from 1890 to World War I saw New York invest in beautifying its neighborhoods — planting trees, clearing slums for parks, and adding architectural enhancements.

script_body: The East European Jews began arriving in large numbers in the early 1880s and settled almost exclusively in the Lower East Side, regrouping not as Jews but by country and region — Russians, Poles, and Hungarians forming distinct enclaves. Because American law forbids asking an immigrant's religion, estimates of how many Jews came range widely, from three to five million. Unlike most Italians, most Jews were fleeing political or religious oppression and came to stay: for every thousand Jews who arrived through Ellis Island, only three chose to return to Europe. The population of the Lower East Side climaxed at some 542,000 residents in 1910, then declined as subways opened newer neighborhoods uptown and in the outer boroughs.

script_body: At 12-16 Eldridge Street stands the Congregation Khal Adath Jeshurun and Anshe Lubz Synagogue, popularly the Eldridge Street Synagogue. Built in 1886-87 by the Herter brothers, German architects, in a Moorish revival and Romanesque style, it was named a National Historic Landmark in 1996. The exterior rose window resembles those of Christian churches but is distinctly Jewish: it contains twelve rondels, smaller windows representing the twelve tribes of Israel. Note too the recurring patterns — two tablets for the Ten Commandments, five windows for the five books of the Torah, and three sets of stairs leading to four sets of doors for the Jewish biblical matriarchs and patriarchs. The interior is a beautiful Orthodox synagogue with women's balconies, designed in Moorish and Sephardic style.

script_body: The wide Allen Street thoroughfare is very different today than in the heyday of the Jewish Lower East Side. Before 1932 the street was only thirty-two feet wide and completely covered by an elevated train; that year the buildings on the east side were torn down and the street widened to 138 feet for the automobile. The city removed the El in 1942, planning a Second Avenue subway to connect the northern Bronx with Wall Street. Construction finally began in 1972 but was soon discontinued for lack of money — New York, like so many American cities, became beholden to the automobile at the expense of public transit.

script_body: On the southwest corner of Canal and Orchard stands the tall former Jarmulovsky Bank, a story of how one could make it and lose it on the Lower East Side. Sender Jarmulovsky began his banking career with savings from his peddler days and built this building in homage to himself in 1912. The bank catered to poor immigrants, especially those sending money back to family in the Old World. Jarmulovsky died a few months after the building was finished, and his sons continued the business. Then came World War I: Jewish depositors rushed to withdraw their money to help family in Europe, and, distrusting paper money, demanded silver and gold coins. The runs forced the state to close the bank on August 4, 1914. The New York Times reported that two thousand people demonstrated in front of the bank, a mob of fifteen hundred enraged depositors required a hundred policemen to restrain, and five hundred people gathered outside Jarmulovsky's apartment, forcing the family to flee.

script_body: Four buildings at 27-33 Orchard Street are excellent examples of pre-law tenements — multifamily dwellings built before 1879, among the oldest and least desirable housing in New York City. Each building holds sixteen apartments, four to a floor. Each apartment averages three rooms totaling 270 square feet: a kitchen, bedroom, and living room, each only nine by ten feet. The only windows are two in the living room; there is no elevator, and before 1901 no indoor plumbing — residents shared backyard outhouses, cleaned out twice a year, and hand pumps. Compare these with the more ornate tenements nearby: a few doors back, at 14-16 Orchard, the terra-cotta details show two rows of Jewish stars surrounded by twelve pomegranates. Contrary to popular lore these were never Jewish buildings — the decoration was meant to entice Jews to live here.

script_body: Hester Street between Orchard and Essex was the site of the Khazzer Mark — Pig Market in Yiddish — where Jewish and Italian peddlers set up pushcarts to sell an incredible array of goods. Why Pig Market? Jacob Riis described turn-of-the-century Hester Street as a place where scarcely anything other than pork could not be hawked from a wagon, at ridiculously low prices, amid crowds pushing, struggling, babbling, and shouting in foreign tongues — a veritable Babel of confusion. Pushcart peddling was finally abolished by Mayor Fiorello La Guardia in 1935, who built enclosed markets and offered peddlers heated, policed buildings in exchange for a license and taxes.

script_body: The small three-acre Seward Park, built in 1901 and named for Lincoln's secretary of state William Seward, was the first park built in this part of the neighborhood. The city tore down three blocks of tenement houses and displaced nearly three thousand people to create it — like Columbus Park, less a philanthropic gift than an early attempt at slum clearance and population control. The park is best known as a gathering point for striking garment workers: in 1909, 1912, and 1916, thousands of workers gathered here and gazed south toward the Jewish Daily Forward Building, waiting for reports on their demands for a living wage and an eight-hour day.

script_body: Straus Square is the small traffic triangle with the marble pillar before you. Its namesake is Nathan Straus, financier, philanthropist, and a leader of the New York Jewish community, best remembered for sponsoring the 1919 program to bring free sterilized-milk stations to children across the country. The marble column itself is a tribute to the neighborhood's Jewish men and women who died in both world wars and the Korean War, presented by the Morris Dickstein Post of the Veterans of Foreign Wars in May 1953.

script_body: Look southeast across the square at the old Forverts Building at 173 East Broadway. Built in 1912 and designed by George A. Boehm, the twelve-story Jewish Daily Forward Building was a towering presence over the neighborhood, with the name Forverts inscribed across the top beneath a huge clock. From 1901 until 1951 the Forward was edited by Abraham Cahan, a Russian Jewish immigrant who made it the most widely read Yiddish paper in the world and used it as an Americanizing tool to introduce East European Jews to American life. The most popular section was the Bintel Brief, the Bundle of Letters, where readers presented their problems and received answers from the editors. The Forward moved out in 1975; the building became an evangelical Protestant church, and in 1999 it was sold to a developer transforming it into luxury condominiums — the first luxury doorman condo in the Lower East Side, a clear sign of the gentrification to come.

script_body: At the southeast corner of East Broadway and Jefferson is the Educational Alliance, known as the Edgies. Built in 1889 by uptown German Jews to Americanize the East European immigrants, it offered day and evening classes in English, citizenship, and hygiene, coordinated the immigration process for Jews arriving at Ellis Island, and became the center for American relief to Jews in Nazi-occupied Europe. The main building was renamed for David Sarnoff after a 1960s renovation. Sarnoff's life is a veritable Horatio Alger story: born in Russia in 1891, he arrived in America at age nine, and the family's first home was a fourth-floor walk-up on Monroe Street at ten dollars a month. Within days he was earning money selling the Yiddish paper Tageblatt at four a.m. At night he took English classes here at the Educational Alliance. From newsboy to messenger at the Commercial Cable Company, his career took off — he eventually became president and CEO of RCA and was instrumental in RCA's creation of NBC television in 1926.

script_body: The converted double tenement at 229 East Broadway was the first home of the Hebrew Sheltering and Immigrant Aid Society, now known as HIAS. Founded in 1892 to provide burial services for Jews who had died on Ellis Island, by 1897 it offered job training, legal aid, temporary housing, and interpreter services. This block of East Broadway is known as Shteebel Row — a shteeblach is a Jewish synagogue based in a house, and most of these tenement buildings contain synagogues, each with a Hebrew and English sign. Note how the communities are organized by landslayt, or homeland, rather than by religious denomination.

script_body: At 263, 265, and 267 Henry Street stand three 1827 Federalist buildings, now National Historical and New York City Landmarks. Here in 1893 Lillian Wald began the Henry Street Settlement, and with the help of philanthropist Jacob Schiff she launched the Visiting Nurse Service — nurses who brought care to people in their homes rather than requiring a visit to a medical office. The settlement house is still a strong anchor of nonsectarian assistance for the neighborhood. Before being added to the settlement, no. 267 had been the Hebrew Technical School for Girls, a trade school for immigrants.

script_body: St. Mary's Church, on the corner of Grand and Ridge Streets, is the oldest Catholic church building in all of New York City and its third parish, founded in 1827. Originally built in 1833, its brick facade and double spires were added in 1871 by architect Patrick C. Keely. Unlike other Lower East Side houses of worship, this building has served the Catholic community without interruption since it was erected — no other house of worship has served one religion for so long in this neighborhood. When the Catholic Church abolished the mandatory Latin Mass in 1965, churches like this became more diverse; St. Mary's now offers Mass in English and Spanish.

script_body: On the north side of Grand between Clinton and Suffolk, no. 402 is a wonderful 1830s merchant house, shop at street level and family above. Next to it stands a fine example of a dumbbell tenement. The tenement law changed in 1887, and the crucial addition was the airshaft, along with a required window in every room. But the airshafts failed in their mission to provide fresh air — they mostly cost residents usable square footage. An 1888 journal described them as great prison-like structures of brick, with a narrow court-yard that was a damp, foul-smelling place supposed to do duty as an airshaft, and that in case of fire would be perfect death-traps.

script_body: At 60 Norfolk is the Beth Hamedrash Hagadol, the Great House of Study. Built in 1850 as the Norfolk Baptist Church and purchased by a Jewish congregation in 1885, it is the oldest Russian Ashkenazic Orthodox congregation in the United States, formed in 1852. In 1888 it became the pulpit of Rabbi Jacob Joseph, the first and only chief rabbi of New York's Orthodox community — but the neighborhood's diverse Jewish communities proved unable to sustain a single chief rabbi. Once the largest Russian synagogue in the country, the congregation is now small; the building is worth visiting for its beautiful Gothic interior and was made a New York Historical Landmark in January 1967.

script_body: Broome Street is worth pondering for a moment. In 1946 Robert Moses, the great builder and destroyer of New York, wanted to run the Lower Manhattan Expressway across it, connecting the Holland Tunnel with the Williamsburg and Manhattan Bridges. It would have stood about a hundred feet above the ground and devastated this neighborhood. Luckily, Moses was foiled.

script_body: Note the very small plaque on the wall at what would be 60 Essex Street. This was the site of Sinsheimer's Cafe, where on October 13, 1843, the B'nai Brith — Sons of the Covenant — was organized by immigrant German Jews. Like the other immigrant groups' organizations, it was founded as a self-help and defensive society to protect American Jews against anti-immigrant sentiment, and it is the oldest Jewish fraternal organization in America.

script_body: For many years, Greenwich Village was the center of New York City's lesbian and gay community, and it remains the focus of legend and history. A walk through its streets passes landmarks from more than one hundred years of the lesbian and gay past. The Village is also home to the movement's most sacred site: the building that once housed the Stonewall Inn, where three days of unrest in June 1969 are widely considered the spark that launched the modern lesbian-and-gay liberation movement.

source_passage: While the geographic center of gay and lesbian life in the city has been shifting in recent years (for men, up to Chelsea, and for women, out to Brooklyn), Greenwich Village remains the focus of legend and history, and a walk through the streets of the Village will take you past landmarks from more than one hundred years of the lesbian and gay past. Greenwich Village is also home to the gay-and-lesbian rights movement's most sacred site: the building that once housed the Stonewall Inn, site of the legendary Stonewall riots. The three days of unrest that took place there in June 1969 are widely considered the spark that launched the modern lesbian-and-gay liberation movement.

script_body: With its mix of immigrant, elite, and artistic populations, the Village was a refuge for lesbians and gay men for nearly a century before the Stonewall riots. They prized the anonymity and freedom of its streets, tenements, and boarding houses, and the relative openness of its bohemian society. Once the subway was extended down Seventh Avenue South, the Village became accessible from all parts of the city and gained a reputation as 'the place where the Bronx meets Brooklyn' for a taste of wild nightlife.

They prized the anonymity and freedom of its streets, tenements, and boarding houses and the relative openness of its bohemian society. Once the subway was extended down Seventh Avenue South, the Village was accessible from all parts of the city and became known as "the place where the Bronx meets Brooklyn" for a taste of wild nightlife.

script_body: The earliest evidence of gay life in New York is also the most macabre: criminal statutes against 'sodomy,' which in New York and New Amsterdam was narrowly defined as sex between men. In 1613, under Dutch rule, such activity was punishable by death, and it remained among New York's eleven capital crimes after the English duke of York established his laws in 1665. The executions were gruesome. On June 25, 1646, a black man named Jan Creoli was sentenced to be 'choked to death and then burnt to ashes,' and on June 17, 1660, Jan Quisthout pleaded guilty to the same charge and was condemned to be 'tied in a sack and cast into the river and drowned until dead.'

It remained among New York's eleven capital crimes after 1665

Jan Quisthout on June 17, 1660 was condemned to be sacked and drowned
source_passage: In New York and New Amsterdam, sodomy was narrowly defined to cover only sex between men. In 1613, when the Dutch established their rule over New Amsterdam, sexual activity between men was punishable by death. In 1665, when the English duke of York established his laws for the colony, sodomy remained among New York's eleven capital crimes. Executions for sodomy in New York City were gruesome: on June 25, 1646, a black man named Jan Creoli was sentenced to be "choked to death and then burnt to ashes" for having sex with another man, and on June 17, 1660, Jan Quisthout pleaded guilty to the same charge and was condemned to be "tied in a sack and cast into the river and drowned until dead."

script_body: By the late 1800s, New Yorkers were well aware of gay men and lesbians in their midst. In 1889 the American Observer wrote that 'there is in every community of any size a colony of male sexual perverts who are usually known to each other and are likely to congregate together.' In Greenwich Village at the time, clubs featuring waiters in drag had become a top tourist attraction.

script_body: Lesbian lives were far less visible on the streets, but awareness of women's relationships grew in certain circles. Temperance leader Frances Willard, who herself had several romances with other women, observed in the late nineteenth century: 'The loves of women for each other grow more numerous each day. That so little is said about them surprises me, for they are everywhere.'

script_body: Café Society, an integrated club known as 'the wrong place for the right people,' filled the basement of the two buildings — one is 1 Sheridan Square — that meet where Barrow Street and Washington Place cross. From 1938 to 1950 the owner ran a club where, he said, 'black and white worked together behind the footlights and sat together out front.' New York Confidential called it one of the most famed cabarets in the Village, New York's neighborhood for 'long-haired men, short-haired women, and those not sure exactly what they are' — and noted with alarm that the club's patrons 'hopped across the race fence.'

script_body: In the late 1930s a young man named Bayard Rustin frequented Café Society as both patron and performer — an aspiring singer attending City College who would become a key figure in the Civil Rights movement. A committed disciple of nonviolence, Rustin went to prison as a conscientious objector during World War II and served as an important lieutenant of A. Philip Randolph in the 1940s, until an arrest in California for soliciting another man for sex forced him to take a lower profile. During the Montgomery bus boycott he went south and worked with King behind the scenes, helping make nonviolence King's strategic focus, and remained one of King's closest advisers until the early 1960s — when a rival civil rights leader threatened to spread the false rumor that King and Rustin were having an affair, and King distanced himself to avert a scandal. In 1963 Randolph brought Rustin back as his deputy for planning the March on Washington. Despite Strom Thurmond denouncing him from the Senate floor as a pervert and a Communist, the march was a triumph. Those in the know called Rustin 'Mr. March,' but he never received the public credit he deserved before his death in 1987.

Rustin was one of King's closest advisers until the early 1960s, when a rival civil rights leader threatened to spread the false rumor that King and Rustin were having an affair. To avert a scandal, King distanced himself from Rustin. In 1963, A. Philip Randolph brought Rustin back into the fold, making him his deputy for the planning of the March on Washington. Despite attacks by Strom Thurmond, who denounced Rustin from the floor of the Senate as a pervert and a Communist, the march was a success. Those in the know called Rustin "Mr. March," but he never received the public credit he deserved before his death in 1987.

script_body: No. 337 Bleecker Street was the former home of Lorraine Hansberry, the African American playwright whose A Raisin in the Sun brought a groundbreaking portrayal of black family life to Broadway when it opened in 1959. The play ran for two years, and Hansberry became the first black playwright to win the New York Drama Critics Circle Award for Best Play of the Year. Married to Robert Nemiroff, she wrote anonymous letters during the 1950s to One magazine and The Ladder, early gay-rights publications; Nemiroff was aware of her lesbianism, and the couple divorced in 1964 but remained close.

script_body: Bleecker Street was notorious in the mid- to late nineteenth century, second only to the Bowery for its rough and racy reputation, and Greene and Mercer Streets were among the busiest red-light districts in the city. In the early 1890s, in the building that now houses Kenny's Castaways at 157 Bleecker Street, an entrepreneur opened a drag club called the Slide. Such clubs — the most famous being Columbia Hall, a.k.a. 'Paresis Hall,' at 392 Bowery — were places where straight patrons came to gape, but also centers of gay male social life and relatively safe gathering places. The Slide quickly became infamous: in 1892 the New York Herald reported that out-of-towners seeking 'the low life' were directed there first by detectives. A vice cop described the waiters as 'men of degenerate type,' some 'rouging their necks,' who in falsetto voices 'sang filthy ditties' and dropped into a chair at any visitor's table. The police closed the Slide in 1892. Down the block at 183 Bleecker Street, a sex club called the Black Rabbit featuring gay-themed acts managed to stay open until a police raid in 1900.

script_body: Across the street from the Slide is an apartment building now called the Atrium. Above the modern lettering you can still see the shadow of its old name, 'Mills House No. 1.' The Mills Houses were male residence halls created by philanthropist Darius O. Mills to provide sanitary and moral accommodation for unmarried working men; this one was built in 1896. As historian George Chauncey notes, these inexpensive rooms were home to a number of working-class gay men, including a few who ended up in court for homosexual activity.

script_body: By the late 1800s, the streets of the Village south of West Fourth Street and Washington Square Park had become the city's second most important Little Italy. Greenwich House at 27 Barrow Street, a settlement house founded by Mary Simkovitch in 1904, is a reminder of that past. It offered English classes, cooking lessons for immigrant women coping with unfamiliar American ingredients, and activities for neighborhood children. Further evidence of the former Italian presence survives along Bleecker and Cornelia Streets, where Italian businesses and restaurants remain.

script_body: Until the Civil War, the southeastern section of Greenwich Village was home to one of New York's largest African American communities, an area known as 'Little Africa,' and many buildings along Minetta Lane and Minetta Street survive from that period. Among Little Africa's residents in the 1860s was Addie Brown, a young black woman from Connecticut who worked as a domestic servant. From her room in the Sullivan Street house of her employer, a prosperous African American man named John H. Jackson, Brown wrote letters to her dearest love, Rebecca Primus, a black woman from Hartford with whom she had an intimate 'romantic friendship.' Their correspondence is one of the most remarkable surviving documents of romantic friendship between women from the nineteenth century — and one of the few examples of black women's writing from the mid-1800s. The record is uneven: 120 of Brown's letters survive, but none of Primus's replies. In 1859 Brown wrote, 'How did I miss you last night. I did not have anyone to hug me up and to kiss. No kisses is like yours.' Primus's family knew of the bond; in 1866, after a gentleman caller disparaged their affection, Mrs. Primus said that if either woman were a gentleman they would marry. Both women eventually married men, though their letters reveal ambivalence and tension about those decisions.

script_body: MacDougal Street was the main drag of New Bohemia — the Village's first Christopher Street, the center of lesbian and gay life and the place where the city's first gay and lesbian businesses outside the seediest neighborhoods were established in the 1910s and 1920s. By the 1930s, the west side of Washington Square Park had become a major cruising area known as the 'meat rack' or the 'auction block.'

script_body: Eve Addams's Tea Room at 129 MacDougal Street was New York City's first lesbian bar. 'Eve Addams' was Eva Kochever, a Polish Jewish immigrant who opened her business here in 1925, hanging a sign outside the door that read 'Men admitted but not welcome.' In 1926 police raided the bar and charged Kochever with writing an obscene book and with disorderly conduct. After serving a one-year sentence in a New York prison, she was deported to Paris in December 1927.

script_body: At 146 MacDougal stood the Calypso Restaurant, where James Baldwin worked as a waiter in the early 1940s. The gay African American writer befriended many locals who came to see him there, including Henry Miller, Paul Robeson, Marlon Brando, and Eartha Kitt. Baldwin met Brando — who lived nearby on Patchin Place and never tried to hide his own homosexual impulses — when the two were students at the New School. In 1956 Baldwin would publish Giovanni's Room, his second novel and one of the first to deal openly and centrally with homosexuality.

script_body: New Bohemia's artists even witnessed periods of 'lesbian chic.' In a famous tale from the 1920s, poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, seeking relief from persistent headaches, asked an analyst's advice at a party. The analyst, not wanting to shock her, gently suggested she might have 'an occasional impulse towards a person of your own sex.' Millay shot back: 'Oh, you mean I'm a homosexual! Of course I am, and heterosexual too, but what's that got to do with my headache?'

script_body: From about 1908 to 1913, 82 Washington Place was home to novelist Willa Cather and her partner Edith Lewis. Cather — author of My Ántonia and Death Comes for the Archbishop — had two central relationships with other women and referred to herself as 'William' in letters to a woman she admired as an undergraduate at the University of Nebraska. Cather and Lewis lived together at various Greenwich Village addresses for nearly forty years, until Cather's death in 1947. She took great care to destroy most of her personal correspondence before she died, and in one surviving college letter she laments her 'unnatural' attraction to another woman.

script_body: As you walk through Washington Square Park, you're passing over the remains of probably thousands of bodies interred here during its years as a potter's field in the eighteenth century. A yellow fever epidemic in 1822 forced many to flee downtown for the 'village,' and many stayed as the area developed; luxury townhouses appeared on the park's northern edge in the 1830s. The Arch itself was designed by Stanford White in 1892 to replace a papier-mâché antecedent erected in 1889 to celebrate the centennial of George Washington's return to the city after the Revolutionary War.

script_body: In her apartment at 23 Fifth Avenue, Mabel Dodge ran a weekly salon that became a center for Village artists and intellectuals. Openly bisexual, Dodge opened her doors to many unconventional women, including Emma Goldman, Margaret Sanger, and Gertrude Stein — whose work A Portrait of Mabel Dodge was named in the hostess's honor. Dodge was also one of the people who made possible the Armory Art Show, which opened in February 1913, bringing Marcel Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase and works by Picasso and Cézanne to the protesting masses.

script_body: 86 University Place was the former site of the Bagatelle, one of the few lesbian bars in the city in the 1950s, alongside the more working-class Sea Colony and the Swing Rendezvous. Black poet and essayist Audre Lorde wrote about the Bagatelle in her autobiography Zami: A New Spelling of My Name. There was a tiny dance floor in back, and the front room 'smelled like plastic and blue glass and beer and lots of good-looking young women.' Lorde recalled that she and the other 'out' black lesbians rarely acknowledged one another, and that 'the Bag was always The Club.'

script_body: From 1913 through the 1930s, Webster Hall at 125 East Eleventh Street hosted the annual Greenwich Village Ball — masquerade balls patronized by the Village's bohemian society, including many gay men in drag. By the early 1920s, gay men and lesbians held events of their own there. In 1934 the New York Herald Tribune described the scene: 'Men danced with women in men's clothes. Women danced with men in women's clothes. And strange androgynous couples careened about the floor, oblivious to the workings of society and nature.' Today Webster Hall is a popular, mostly straight nightclub.

script_body: The drag balls gave rise to one of gay life's most familiar terms: coming out. Today it suggests emerging from the closet, but its earlier ball-scene origins were lighter — participants used 'coming out' with a wink toward straight debutantes. As the Baltimore Afro-American put it in 1931, the 'coming out of new debutantes into homosexual society' was the outstanding feature of Baltimore's eighth annual 'pansy' ball.

Today, coming out is generally thought of as "coming out of the closet," emerging from terrified secrecy. Earlier origins of the phrase in the ball scene, however, were much less dark and sad. Participants in the balls used the term coming out with a wink and a nod to straight debutantes. As the Baltimore Afro-American put it in 1931: "Debutantes Bow at Local 'Pansy' Ball: The coming out of new debutantes into homosexual society was the outstanding feature of Baltimore's eighth annual frolic of the pansies..."

script_body: The house at 457 Sixth Avenue was the former home of Murray Hall, a 'ward heeler' for Tammany Hall who organized the vote in this district. Married twice and known as a heavy drinker, a brawler, and 'sweet on women,' Hall died in 1901 leaving a wife and an adopted daughter — and the revelation that Hall had died of breast cancer and had been a woman who passed as a man for all of her adult life. The New York Times covered the story for days. One lawyer friend insisted, 'I saw him play poker like a veteran... I just can't believe he was a woman, that's all,' still referring to Hall as 'he.'

script_body: From the 1920s through the 1950s, 171 West Twelfth Street was home to a network of lesbian couples and comrades-in-arms: artist Nancy Cook and educator Marion Dickerman; activist Polly Porter and Democratic official Molly Dewson; and Grace Hutchins and Anna Rochester, both Communist Party leaders. Many — especially Dickerman and Cook — were good friends with Eleanor Roosevelt, who kept her own apartments at 20 East Eleventh Street and later at 29 Washington Square West. When Franklin D. Roosevelt became president, Eleanor became a fierce champion for women in government, and many of her friends gained New Deal posts: Molly Dewson directed the Women's Division of the Democratic National Committee, and among the president's appointees were Frances Perkins, the first woman cabinet member, and Grace Abbott of the Children's Bureau. Roosevelt herself had an intimate relationship with Associated Press reporter Lorena Hickok, assigned in 1932 to cover the new first lady; their letters reveal a passionate intimacy, though many biographers strenuously insist Roosevelt was not a lesbian.

source_passage: From the 1920s through the 1950s, the building at 171 West Twelfth Street was home to a number of lesbian couples. Many of these women, particularly Dickerman and Cook, were good friends with Eleanor Roosevelt, who had apartments of her own at 20 East Eleventh Street from 1933 to 1942 and at 29 Washington Square West from 1942 to 1949.. Molly Dewson served as director of the Women's Division of the Democratic National Committee. Among President Roosevelt's other appointees were Frances Perkins, the secretary of labor. In 1932, an Associated Press reporter named Lorena Hickok was assigned to file stories on the new first lady. Despite such effusive letters, many biographers strenuously insist that Roosevelt herself was not a lesbian.

script_body: Since 1984, 208 West Thirteenth Street has been the home base for New York's gay and lesbian community. The Lesbian and Gay Community Services Center hosts dozens of meetings and events on any given day, with rooms for numerous LGBT organizations. On March 14, 1987, novelist and activist Larry Kramer — scheduled to read from one of his novels — instead rose and delivered an impassioned plea for action on AIDS. Within a week, the AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power, or ACT UP, was founded, rejuvenating gay and lesbian activism in the Reagan era and forcing action on AIDS by pharmaceutical companies and governments.

script_body: Julius', at 159 West Tenth Street, dates back to before Prohibition and is one of the oldest bars still open in the Village — and the site of an important early gay rights victory in New York State. In 1966 the Mattachine Society of New York staged what it called a 'sip-in,' consciously borrowing from the civil rights movement. At the time, if a bartender knowingly served alcohol to a homosexual, the State Liquor Authority could rescind the bar's license, and bars around the Village posted signs reading 'If you're gay, go away.' Members went from bar to bar, sat down, announced they were homosexual, and ordered drinks. In most places they were served — but at Julius' they were refused. Working with the City Human Rights Commission, the Mattachine Society sued, and in 1967 the New York State Supreme Court ruled that the liquor authority needed substantial evidence of indecent behavior — not just same-sex kissing or touching — to close a bar. That precedent would matter just two years later and two blocks away.
