script_body: This stretch of Christopher Street is widely considered the birthplace of the modern lesbian and gay rights movement. The bar that once stood here at No. 53, the Stonewall Inn, was an unprepossessing place — crowded and popular on weekends but nothing fancy. Like most bars serving a gay clientele, it was owned by the Mob, which paid off the local police; raids and shakedowns were the norm, and many such bars had a light over the door that flashed when the police were coming. In the early morning hours of June 28, 1969, the patrons fought back. When the cops singled out several drag queens for arrest and pushed the rest into the street, refusing to disperse, one butch lesbian struck the officer who had hit her, and the crowd unleashed a hail of coins and invective. The police were forced back into the bar; the crowd attacked the building and tried to set it on fire, leading the cops to draw their guns. Riot police averted a possible shooting, but the crowd would not back down. Those actions sparked several nights of unrest and launched a new phase of activism — 'gay liberation.'

script_body: On the first anniversary of the riots, New York witnessed its first Gay Pride march, up Sixth Avenue from Christopher Street to Central Park; every year since, the riots have been remembered worldwide with June parades. As one activist quipped, 'I am probably one of six people who lived in the Village at the time who does not claim to have been at the Stonewall riots.' The riots spurred two organizations: the Gay Liberation Front, launched immediately after, and the Gay Activists Alliance, which split off in December 1969 after infighting over the scope of the work. The GLF saw itself as part of the New Left and pushed coalition politics; the GAA had a constitution barring alliance with any organization not directly related to the homosexual cause. Together they answered homophobia with 'zap' actions and created new visibility. The first GLF meetings were held at an organization called Alternate U at 534 Sixth Avenue, and from 1971 to 1974 the GAA was headquartered in a renovated firehouse at 99 Wooster Street — the GAA Firehouse, a center of gay life until it was firebombed in October 1974 amid a rash of arson attacks on gay bars, homes, and offices.

script_body: The 'love that dare not speak its name' has in fact had many names. In the 1860s a gay German writer and activist, Karl Heinrich Ulrichs, coined 'Uranians' — people physically male or female but with the spirit of the opposite sex — drawing the term from Plato's Symposium to create a respectable label, rejecting 'pervert' and 'sodomite.' The word homosexual first appeared in an 1868 letter to Ulrichs. On the New York streets, 'fairy' was the common word for an effeminate gay man, with 'queer' as the more universal term; black gay men and lesbians spoke of being 'in the life.' The word gay itself first meant prostitutes — 'gay women' — and was adopted as a code word that police did not crack until the late 1940s.

script_body: The Daughters of Bilitis, founded in San Francisco in 1955, was part of the first wave of the organized gay rights movement and published a magazine called The Ladder from 1956 to 1970. Its first New York chapter was organized in 1958 by activist Barbara Gittings and from 1963 ran out of a basement office at 26-32 Charlton Street. The chapter was at the forefront of public actions, including the 'Annual Reminder' marches at Independence Hall in Philadelphia from 1963 to 1969 and a 1965 picket at the White House protesting the ban on gay federal employees. The DOB was one of the 'homophile' organizations of the 1950s — alongside the Mattachine Society (1950) and ONE (1954) — which took a conservative approach, asking members to 'dress appropriately,' men in suits and women in skirts.

script_body: In 1777 a man wrote to another man: 'I wish, my dear Laurens, it might be in my power, by action rather than words, to convince you that I love you.' The writer was Alexander Hamilton, addressing a fellow soldier in the Continental Army. Historians have long debated such effusive correspondence between people of the same sex from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — what they call 'romantic friendships' in an intensely homosocial age. Among those whose letters reveal such attachments are Ralph Waldo Emerson, Margaret Fuller, and Susan B. Anthony. By the late 1800s, women's long-term partnerships came to be known as 'Boston marriages,' a term drawn from Henry James's novel The Bostonians.

script_body: The man most responsible for founding these squares in the 1830s was a lawyer and visionary real estate investor named Samuel Ruggles. Correctly anticipating New York's growth uptown, Ruggles bought up undeveloped plots in the area that would become Union Square and Gramercy Park, hoping to entice the wealthy to settle around exclusive, fenced parks at each square's center. The value of his property climbed after the Great Fire of 1835 pushed Manhattanites uptown in large numbers. Union Square opened in 1839 with an oval-shaped iron fence around its central park. Ruggles built himself a four-story home here — though his true masterpiece, where he never actually lived, was Gramercy Park.

source_passage: The man most responsible for the founding of these squares in the 1830s was the lawyer and visionary real estate investor, Samuel Ruggles. At that time, the area between Fourteenth and Twenty-eighth Streets had begun to take shape as a genteel suburb on the northern outskirts of the city. Correctly anticipating New York's impending growth uptown, Ruggles purchased numerous undeveloped plots of land in the area that would become Union Square and Gramercy Park. Ruggles saw an opportunity to beautify these suburban communities and turn them into neighborhoods for the city's elite. By designing an exclusive, fenced park in the center of each square, Ruggles hoped to entice the wealthy to settle around them. The value of Ruggles's property grew after the Great Fire of 1835 prompted Manhattanites to migrate uptown in large numbers. In 1839, Union Square opened with an oval-shaped iron fence surrounding the park at its center. Ruggles built a four-story home for himself at Union Square, but his masterpiece, although he never lived there himself, was Gramercy Park, which opened in 1844.

script_body: Although Union Square was New York's most fashionable shopping and theater district in the late nineteenth century, it fell into a long decline beginning in the 1920s. The department stores and boutiques of 'Ladies' Mile' moved further uptown, and the square, caught between the midtown and downtown business districts, was left to deteriorate. By the 1960s and 1970s it was known as a haunt for drug dealers and the homeless. A $3.6 million reconstruction project launched in 1985 dramatically refurbished the park's neglected landscape and addressed its safety problems. Crowning that restoration, Union Square Park was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1997.

script_body: The nickname 'Ladies' Mile' took on a far different meaning after dark. Above the department stores along Broadway lay lavishly furnished brothels catering to upper-class men. These high-priced 'Temples of Love' advertised themselves in publications such as the Gentleman's Directory, promising women who were beautiful, charming, and refined conversationalists. Outside the elite brothels, throngs of streetwalkers worked Ladies' Mile after dark. By the 1890s, reformers complained that both Union and Stuyvesant Square Parks had become a place where, in their words, 'tramps both male and female haggle and dispute over their price.'

script_body: The proliferation of department stores along Broadway from Ninth to Twenty-third Street earned this stretch the nickname 'Ladies' Mile' in the 1870s. It began when A. T. Stewart built a massive cast-iron emporium filling an entire block at Broadway and East Ninth Street, selling expensive furnishings, antiques, fabrics, and women's wear. His triumph drew a succession of upscale stores: Tiffany and Company demolished James Renwick Jr.'s Church of the Puritans at Union Square to build its store in 1869, while Lord & Taylor's, Arnold Constable's, and W. & J. Sloane's filled out the avenue. Macy's and B. Altman's opened two blocks west on Sixth Avenue.

In a cast-iron building that filled the entire block, A. T. Stewart's sold expensive furnishings, antiques, fabrics, and women's wear. The triumphant success of A. T. script_body: While Broadway brought department stores, Union Square's other tributary — the Bowery — brought theaters. New York Sun reporter Ted McAlpin dubbed the district 'the Rialto,' and by the 1870s Union Square had replaced the Bowery as the hub of theater activity in the city. In 1854 the Academy of Music, one of the largest theaters in the world, opened on Fourteenth Street near the square. As the city's primary opera house it hosted the American premieres of Aida, Lohengrin, Die Walküre, and Carmen. All of New York society pined for the prestige of an opera box; despite a cost of as much as $30,000, the waiting list was long and included names like Vanderbilt, Astor, and Gould.

script_body: At the south side of the park stands Henry Kirke Brown's George Washington, dedicated on July 4, 1856, and considered by some the finest equestrian statue in the country. It depicts Washington's triumphant return to New York City on November 25, 1783, as British troops ended their seven-year occupation at the close of the Revolutionary War. Washington came personally to repossess the city he had lost to the British in 1776, and at this very spot he and his officers were greeted by a crowd of jubilant citizens. The site was then known as Union Place, a grassy clearing north of the city named for the juncture of the Boston Post Road — later the Bowery — and the Albany Post Road, later Broadway. As the statue depicts, Washington then headed southward down the path of the Albany Post Road toward the city, accompanied by the cheering crowd, while New Yorkers thronged the streets to catch a glimpse of him. For years afterward, the anniversary of that day was celebrated in New York as 'Evacuation Day.'

source_passage: At the south side of the park is Henry Kirke Brown's George Washington, dedicated on July 4, 1856. Considered by some to be the finest equestrian statue in the country, it depicts Washington's triumphant return to New York City on November 25, 1783. As British troops ended their seven-year occupation of the city at the close of the Revolutionary War, Washington came personally to repossess the city he had lost to the British in 1776. At this spot, Washington and his officers were greeted by a crowd of jubilant citizens. Known then as Union Place, this grassy clearing north of the city was named for the juncture of Boston Post Road (later to become the Bowery) and Albany Post Road (later Broadway). As the statue depicts, Washington then headed southward, accompanied by the cheering crowd, down the path of Albany Post Road toward the city, where New Yorkers thronged the streets to catch a glimpse of him. For years afterward, the anniversary of this day would be celebrated in New York as "Evacuation Day."

script_body: On September 5, 1882, the nation's first Labor Day parade ended at Union Square after marching up Broadway from City Hall. From then on, the square became the preferred site of labor rallies and mass political protests. Soapbox orators regularly drew crowds, and thousands turned out for every May Day and Labor Day. The anarchist Isadore Wisotsky later recalled the atmosphere of the 1910s: 'We gathered to make revolution and stayed to talk. And how we talked — anarchism, atheism, against the military, for birth control, against injustice, for socialism and for the rights of workers to organize. The right to speak at Union Square was more precious than the bread we sweated to earn.'

Square became preferred site of labor rallies and protests
Anarchist Isadore Wisotsky recalled the 1910s atmosphere

script_body: One of the most tension-filled protests at Union Square came on the night of August 22, 1927, when five thousand people gathered for a candlelight vigil for the anarchists Sacco and Vanzetti, about to be executed in Boston. The police were so afraid of violence that they stationed machine guns on the roof of Klein's department store nearby — but no incidents occurred. A few years later, though, police and protestors battled in a bloody riot here on March 6, 1930. Demonstrators had come, six months after the 1929 stock market crash, to mark International Unemployment Day, an event sponsored by the American Communist Party. When thousands tried to march down Broadway without a permit, the police met them with force, igniting a violent conflict that left hundreds injured.

script_body: Directly in front of the band shell stands Henry Kirke Brown's Abraham Lincoln, dedicated at Union Square in 1868 and believed to be the first public statue of Lincoln erected in the country. Unlike Brown's masterful Washington at the opposite end of the park, this statue was not well received. With his rumpled clothes and plain demeanor, Brown's Lincoln may have accurately captured the historical man, but it was deemed uninspiring — the outpouring of emotion after Lincoln's assassination on Good Friday 1865 had raised the fallen president to an almost Christlike stature in the popular mind. In Brown's rendering, the solemn Lincoln holds a rolled speech — or perhaps the Emancipation Proclamation — in his left hand, hanging calmly and unheroically at his side.

script_body: Union Square is a fitting place to honor Lincoln, for it was during the Civil War that the square became the central gathering place in the city — the Times Square of the nineteenth century. After the fall of Fort Sumter, Lincoln's call for volunteers was answered by thousands of young men who flocked to enlist at recruiting tents that dotted the interior of the park. Nearly a quarter-million people gathered here on Saturday, April 20, 1861, to hear speakers denounce the Southern rebellion, while the tattered American flag rescued from Fort Sumter waved from the George Washington statue, where it had been patriotically placed.

script_body: On the south side of Fourteenth Street, an apartment complex completed in 1998 carries on its facade an elaborate $3 million artwork titled Metronome. Unveiled in September 1999, it is a jumble of symbols its creators, Andrew Ginzel and Kristin Jones, called 'an ode to the impossibility of knowing time.' It features fifteen digital numbers counting the time elapsing from midnight, a black-and-gold sphere that rotates with the phases of the moon, and a five-foot opening that periodically belches blasts of steam. In a whimsical nod to the neighborhood, the artists cast the disembodied hand reaching out from the top of Metronome from Henry Kirke Brown's statue of George Washington across the street.

script_body: To the southeast of the square lies an infamous intersection once known as 'Dead Man's Curve,' where speeding trolley cars and horse-drawn carriages often mowed down careless pedestrians thronging the shopping and theater district. Looming over it today are the four massive red towers of the Zeckendorf Towers, built in 1987, a mixed residential and business complex. They stand on the former site of S. Klein's discount department store, which left its building abandoned in 1975 — thus betraying its nickname, 'S. Klein-on-the-Square.' Residents protested the enormous complex, which partly blocks the view of the striking Con Edison clock tower behind it, but its luxury apartments helped regentrify Union Square.

script_body: On the east side of the square stands the statue of the French general Marquis de Lafayette, done in 1873 by Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi — the same man who designed the Statue of Liberty. Lafayette served as a major general on George Washington's staff, and an inscription on the pedestal quotes his words: 'As soon as I heard of American Independence my heart was enlisted.' In 1824, at the invitation of Congress, Lafayette returned to America and was warmly embraced as the toast of New York society. He was the first foreigner ever granted honorary American citizenship — the second being Winston Churchill.

trigger_address: Seventeenth Street and Park Avenue, Union Square
script_body: At the corner of Seventeenth Street and Park Avenue, the New York Film Academy is housed in the last of the Tammany Hall headquarters, built in 1929 during the administration of Mayor Jimmy Walker. Walker, the last mayor elevated to power by Tammany Hall, embodied the flashy style of the affluent 1920s. The construction of this federal-style building was financed by Wall Street investments — but the stock market crash that ruined those investors later that year also helped bring about the downfall of Tammany Hall itself. In 1933, New Yorkers elected a Republican mayor, Fiorello La Guardia, who promised to destroy Tammany forever.

script_body: The Society of St. Tammany, or Columbian Order, was formed in 1788, taking its name from the legendary Delaware Indian chief Tamanend, adopted as the club's patron saint. The organization loved pseudo–American Indian titles: 'sachems' for council members, 'braves' for the rank and file, 'wigwam' for headquarters. Under Aaron Burr it became a Jeffersonian club, and later, under Martin Van Buren, a Jacksonian Democratic one. Its real power came from a grassroots alliance with immigrant voters, built on graft: local 'bosses' dispensed financial aid and protection in exchange for votes. In the 1860s, Tammany's 'Grand Sachem' William M. 'Boss' Tweed used the machine autocratically to control patronage while embezzling millions; the exposure of the Tweed ring in 1871 scandalized the nation. Yet Tammany endured as a defender of the working man and a patronage engine well into the 1930s, facilitating the careers of Governor Alfred E. Smith and Mayor Jimmy Walker — both sons of Irish immigrants. Perhaps its ethic was best summed up by sachem George Washington Plunkitt, who explained his vast wealth by saying: 'I seen my opportunities and I took 'em.'

script_body: At 109–111 East Fifteenth Street stands the oldest surviving clubhouse in the city — the Century Association Building, now the Century Center for Performing Arts, designed by Charles Gambrill and Henry Hobson Richardson in 1869. The Century Association, formed in 1847, brought together men 'of all guilds' to cultivate 'a taste for Letters and the Arts and social enjoyment,' aspiring to become the American equivalent of the French Academy — though in reality it remained more about socializing than serious discussion. In the 1880s, William Watson Gilder, the first editor of Century magazine, borrowed his journal's name without permission from the Century Club, of which he was a member.

script_body: The headquarters of the Consolidated Edison power company towers above the southeast corner of Fourteenth Street and Irving Place, on the site of its predecessor, the Manhattan Gas Light Company, which stood here from 1885 to 1910. Construction began in 1911, and the main section was designed by Henry J. Hardenbergh, the same architect responsible for the Dakota on Seventy-second Street and Central Park West. The building's most majestic feature is the Tower of Light, a massive clock tower added in 1926, most impressive when brilliantly illuminated at night.

script_body: Arriving at Stuyvesant Square from Fifteenth Street, the first landmarks to grab your attention are the red-brick Friends Meeting House and Seminary to your left, dating from 1860. Part of a five-building complex that also includes the original schoolhouse, an elegant nineteenth-century townhouse across Fifteenth Street, and a modern school building, the Friends Seminary dominates the southwest corner of the square. A doctrinal split in the Quaker community prompted the construction of this meetinghouse, when one group seceded from another congregation a few blocks away at Gramercy Park. When the two groups reconciled in 1958, the Gramercy Park congregation abandoned their building to join this one.

script_body: Across Sixteenth Street from the Friends Meeting House stands St. George's Episcopal Church, completed in 1856 — one of the earliest examples of Romanesque revival architecture in America. The brownstone exterior, by Otto Blesch, had to be restored after the church was badly damaged in an 1865 fire; Leopold Eidlitz, who designed the original interior, rebuilt it according to Blesch's original plans. The two spires were never properly restored and were finally torn down in 1888. Next door, on the north side, is St. George's Chapel of 1911, a fine Gothic revival companion to the older building.

script_body: The four-acre twin parks of Stuyvesant Square are bisected by Second Avenue, whose traffic makes a noisy invasion of an otherwise pastoral setting. The extension of Second Avenue through the park was part of the original plan when Peter Gerard Stuyvesant deeded the land to the city in 1836 — for just five dollars — though no one could have foreseen the volume of traffic that would later speed down the avenue. The cast-iron fence that surrounds each section of the park dates from 1850. Stuyvesant Square, and all the land from Twentieth to Fifth Street, lay within the farm of Peter Stuyvesant back in the 1650s.

script_body: In the far northeast corner of the square's east wing stands a life-size bronze of the celebrated Czech composer Antonín Dvořák, done by the Yugoslavian sculptor Ivan Meštrović. For nearly three decades the statue was tucked away in obscurity on the roof of Avery Fisher Hall at Lincoln Center, where a planned roof garden was never built; the New York Philharmonic finally placed it here in 1997. Dvořák lived on East Seventeenth Street, within sight of this spot, while serving as director of the National Conservatory of Music from 1892 to 1895. During that time he composed the acclaimed symphony From the New World — his tribute to the music of America.

script_body: By the 1890s, Stuyvesant Square had become a small, wealthy enclave of American-born residents amid a growing immigrant population of Jews and Catholics moving up from the Lower East Side. St. George's Parish was dominated for decades by its senior warden, the banker J. P. Morgan — one of the most powerful men in the world. When the neighborhood's dwindling Episcopalian population left its pews increasingly empty in the 1890s, St. George's, with Morgan's approval, became a leader in the Social Gospel movement. It survived by de-emphasizing doctrine and offering secular educational and recreational programs, enlisting thousands of young people from the nearby tenements.

script_body: On Sunday, April 18, 1920, a neighborhood anarchist named Thomas W. Simpkin tried to assassinate J. P. Morgan Jr. outside St. George's. Incensed by the younger Morgan's anti-Communist remarks, Simpkin attempted to ambush him as he left Sunday Mass. In a case of mistaken identity, Simpkin instead tragically shot and killed Dr. James Markee, the Morgan family doctor. Five months later, the bombing of the Morgan Bank on Wall Street was widely assumed to be another anarchist attack aimed at Morgan.

script_body: On the northwest corner of Seventeenth Street and Second Avenue stands the former Manhattan General Hospital Building, the most impressive of the hospital buildings bordering Stuyvesant Square. Completed in 1902 with money donated by J. P. Morgan and designed by Robert H. Richardson, it originally housed the New York Lying-In Hospital — once the largest maternity hospital in the United States, serving the impoverished Lower East Side and often letting its bills go uncollected. Viewed in philanthropic circles as Morgan's personal charity, it struggled to find other benefactors and turned to Morgan each year to cover its deficit, becoming one of his most expensive ventures. Today the building houses luxury apartments and medical offices.

script_body: The New York City Draft Riots of July 1863 were the largest and most destructive urban riots in American history, killing at least 105 people, and the greatest uprising of Americans against their government short of the Confederacy's secession. They sprang from the resentment of New York's working classes — especially Irish immigrants — toward the Civil War draft, made worse by a clause allowing the rich to buy a $300 substitute, condemned as 'a rich man's war, but a poor man's fight.' On Monday, July 13, protestors smashed the lottery wheel at the Third Avenue draft house, and by midmorning a full-scale riot had erupted. The rioters targeted symbols of the war, Republican leaders, and African Americans: at least eleven black men were lynched, and the Colored Orphan Asylum on Fifth Avenue was torched, its 237 children left to flee. A mob of thousands besieged the Union Steam Works, a former wire factory converted to arms production; twice they seized thousands of weapons before the Metropolitan Police and the Twelfth New York Infantry, firing howitzers down Second Avenue, fought them out. Rather than surrender, the rioters burned the five-story building to the ground, killing ten of their own trapped inside. The next day, five regiments diverted from Gettysburg arrived; the 152nd New York Volunteers camped in Stuyvesant Square while the Eighth Regiment Artillery encamped in Gramercy Park, and by Thursday order was restored.

source_passage: The New York City Draft Riots were the largest and most destructive urban riots in American history, resulting in at least 105 deaths. ... A clause that allowed draft substitutes to be purchased for $300 was deemed particularly obnoxious by Peace Democrats, who perceived the law as promoting "a rich man's war, but a poor man's fight." ... On Monday, July 13, working-class protestors marched on the draft house at Third Avenue and smashed the lottery wheel. ... At least eleven black men were lynched and mutilated. Rioters also torched the Colored Orphan Asylum on Fifth Avenue, leaving its 237 children to flee for their lives. ... A mob of thousands besieged the Union Steam Works, a former wire factory that had been converted for wartime arms production. ... Twice the mob took control of the building and seized thousands of weapons. The Metropolitan Police were joined by the Twelfth New York Infantry in the bloody effort to dislodge rioters from the building. Howitzers were used by policemen to clear Second Avenue. In the end, rather than surrender the factory, the rioters burned the five-story brick building to the ground, killing ten of their own who remained trapped inside. The next day, July 15, five regiments of the Union Army, diverted directly from the battle of Gettysburg, began to arrive in the city. The 152 New York Volunteers established their camp in Stuyvesant Square, while the Eighth Regiment Artillery Troop encamped in Gramercy Park. By Thursday, July 16, order was restored.

script_body: At 146 East Nineteenth Street, an oval plaque marks the former home of George Bellows, who lived here from 1910 until his early death in 1925. A great realist painter, Bellows belonged to the 'Ashcan' school for his gritty scenes of everyday life, drawn like William Dean Howells's from the tenement districts. An avid socialist, he often entertained leading radicals including Emma Goldman, Eugene O'Neill, Max Eastman, and John Reed.

script_body: Directly across the street from Bellows lived Carl Van Vechten, in a home that used to stand at 151 East Nineteenth Street. His parties brought figures like the poet Langston Hughes and jazz singer Bessie Smith into contact with the artists and wealthy patrons of the Gramercy Park neighborhood.

script_body: To a remarkable degree, the Gramercy Park neighborhood has stayed true to the vision of its founder, Samuel Ruggles, providing a striking contrast to the noisy commercial districts around it. When Ruggles took possession of Gramercy Seat in 1831, it was a mixture of swampland and small hills. The name 'Gramercy,' some believe, is a corruption of an old Dutch phrase, krom moerasje, meaning 'little crooked swamp;' others say it comes from crommessie vly, meaning 'knife-shaped swamp.' Whatever the case, Ruggles filled in the swamp in the 1830s with soil from the leveling of the nearby Bowery Hill. When he drew up the deed to the park in 1831, he provided for five trustees, regularly elected by the neighborhood, to maintain the grounds to his precise specifications; he laid out the pathways himself and had fifty different trees and shrubs planted. The eight-foot iron fence has stood around it since it officially opened in 1844. Gramercy Park was also one of the first New York developments to impose building restrictions: Ruggles's deed permitted only 'brick or stone dwellings' and barred any 'slaughter house, smith shop,' 'brewery, distillery, public museum,' or 'circus.' Today it is the only private park left in New York City.

script_body: From the 1850s until the 1870s, Gramercy Park ranked among the city's most fashionable neighborhoods. It lost status after the Third Avenue Elevated Railroad was built close by in 1878. Though many residents left, those who stayed were influential enough to persuade Governor David Hill to veto a measure that would have run a cable-car line on Lexington Avenue through the park in 1890, and several later proposals to cut a road through the park were defeated. Since the 1940s most of the townhouses have been converted into apartments, and by the 1980s Gramercy Park had once again become a fashionable neighborhood, home to many celebrities.

script_body: Both 15 and 16 Gramercy Park South, completed in 1845, were among the original townhouses on the square. No. 15 today houses the National Arts Club, but in the 1870s and 1880s it was the home of Samuel J. Tilden — 1874 New York governor and 1876 presidential candidate, whose career was built on bringing down the Tweed ring. Fearing disgruntled Tammany henchmen, Tilden built an underground tunnel from his house to Nineteenth Street as an escape route. When he died in 1886, he left a vast book collection and an estate exceeding $5 million to New York City specifically for a new public library — and when the New York Public Library's headquarters opened in 1911, his books were combined with the Astor and Lenox collections to form its original holdings.

source_passage: Both 15 and 16 Gramercy Park South, completed in 1845, were among the original townhouses on the square. Today, No. 15 houses the National Arts Club. In the 1870s and 1880s, however, it was the home of 1874 New York governor and 1876 presidential candidate Samuel J. Tilden. Tilden's political success was built upon his role in bringing down the Tweed ring. Fearing for his life from disgruntled Tammany henchmen, Tilden built an underground tunnel from his house to Nineteenth Street as an escape route in case of an emergency. When Tilden died in 1886, he left behind a vast book collection and an estate exceeding $5 million, which he left to New York City specifically to be used for the building of a new public library and reading room. The New York Public Library's new headquarters opened in 1911, and his book collection was combined with the Astor and Lenox library collections to make up its original holdings.

script_body: The National Arts Club, founded in 1898, moved into Samuel Tilden's former home in 1906. The building's face had been redesigned in 1884 by Calvert Vaux, who added the bow fronts and arched windows in Victorian Gothic style; the faces of Goethe, Dante, Franklin, and Milton appear in decorative medallions adorning its facade. Founding club members included J. P. Morgan, Frederic Remington, Theodore Roosevelt, and Woodrow Wilson.

script_body: At 16 Gramercy Park South is the Players Club, founded by Edwin Booth in 1888. Widely considered the greatest actor of his generation, Booth came from a family of distinguished actors that included his unstable brother, John Wilkes Booth. Devastated by Lincoln's assassination at his brother's hand, Booth vowed never to appear in public again and resigned from his starring role in Hamlet; friends and admirers persuaded him to return nine months later, where New York society greeted him with an outpouring of sympathy. The acting profession was not highly regarded in nineteenth-century America, and perhaps because of his own family history, Booth felt the stigma deeply and endeavored to raise actors to 'a higher social grade than the Bohemian level.' He conceived the Players Club as a genteel society where actors could mix with the more cultivated, and in 1887 enlisted his friend Stanford White to remodel the facade with a portico and balcony. Founding members included Mark Twain and General William T. Sherman. At the center of Gramercy Park stands a statue of Edwin Booth as Hamlet, erected by the Players Club in 1918.

source_passage: At 16 Gramercy Park South is the Players Club, founded by Edwin Booth in 1888. Widely considered to be the greatest actor of his generation, Booth came from a family of distinguished actors that included his unstable brother John Wilkes Booth. Devastated by Lincoln's assassination at his brother's hand, Booth vowed never to appear in public again and resigned from his starring role in a popular production of Hamlet. Friends and admirers, however, persuaded him to return to the stage nine months later, where he was greeted with an outpouring of sympathy and approval by New York society. The acting profession was not highly regarded in nineteenth-century America. Perhaps because of his own family history, Edwin Booth felt this stigma most deeply and endeavored to raise the social standing of actors to "a higher social grade than the Bohemian level." He conceived of the Players Club as a genteel private society where actors could mix with those who were more cultivated. In 1887, Booth enlisted his friend Stanford White to remodel the facade of this building by adding the portico and balcony. Founding members included Mark Twain and General William T. Sherman. At the center of Gramercy Park stands a statue of Edwin Booth performing in the role of Hamlet (Edmond T. Quinn, 1917), erected by the Players Club in 1918.

script_body: At 19–20 Gramercy Park South is the former Sonnenberg mansion, a brick townhouse built in 1845 but altered many times since. When the Sonnenberg estate put it up for sale in 1979, the New Yorker's Brendan Gill called it 'unquestionably the greatest house remaining in private hands in New York.' Originally four stories, it gained a fifth floor and mansard roof in the 1850s, and in 1887 it was remodeled inside by McKim, Mead and White. In 1931, publicity man Benjamin Sonnenberg bought the house along with the apartment complex next door at No. 20, installed connecting doors, and turned No. 20's studio apartments into guest rooms — bringing his mansion to thirty-seven rooms. It remains a private home today.

script_body: At 144 East Twentieth Street, off the southeast corner of the square, is the Brotherhood Synagogue, formerly the Friends Meeting House, built in 1859. Its Italianate architecture is almost identical to Henry Ward Beecher's 1849 Plymouth Church in Brooklyn Heights. Rescued from demolition by the Landmarks Commission in the 1960s, it was bought in 1975 by the Brotherhood Synagogue for $425,000. A Holocaust memorial stands on the east side of the building.

script_body: The first cooperative apartment in New York City, 34 Gramercy Park East, was designed by architect George da Cunha. Opened in 1883, this gorgeous brick building with red terra-cotta ornamentation originally held twenty-seven apartments, three per floor, of seven to twelve rooms each. Abundant amenities were offered to attract a 'better' class of residents, including a gourmet restaurant owned by Louis Sherry on the eighth floor. The original gaslights flank the entrance, and the hydraulic elevators inside, the first in the city, still function. Next door at No. 36, another early cooperative designed by James Riley Gordon in 1910 carries whimsical medieval ornament in white terra-cotta, with monks, gargoyles, and cherubs, its front entrance guarded by two cast-stone knights in armor.

script_body: Near the northern entrance to the park, a number of prominent New Yorkers made their homes. At 1 Lexington Avenue lived the daring entrepreneur Cyrus West Field, who conceived and organized the laying of the first undersea transatlantic cable, establishing telegraph communication between London and New York. After several disappointments, the cable finally became operable in 1865, making Field a national hero; he also built much of Manhattan's elevated railroads in the 1870s. Next door, at 9 Lexington Avenue, lived his friend and supporter Peter Cooper, one of New York's most beloved citizens and an inventor of extraordinary talents. Cooper created America's first steam locomotive, the 'Tom Thumb,' produced the first steel rails, and invented household products including glue and gelatin. Never having had a higher education himself, he founded Cooper Union, a free university for the working classes, which still runs tuition-free thanks chiefly to his endowment of nearly $1 million.

script_body: Architect Stanford White lived along Gramercy Park North from 1901 to 1906. One of the greatest and most prolific architects of his time, White designed lavish mansions, churches, clubhouses, and monuments all over New York, and was a serious collector who imported antiques to furnish his home. Yet he is best remembered today not for his architecture but for the scandalous circumstances of his death, the site of which the tour visits later.

script_body: At the corner of East Twenty-first Street and Park Avenue stands Calvary Church, once the prestigious parish of the Roosevelt, Vanderbilt, and Astor families, now assimilated into St. George's Parish of Stuyvesant Square. When this impressive brownstone church was completed in 1848, it heightened the appeal of the Gramercy Park area and prompted the sale of several of Samuel Ruggles's still-vacant lots. Its architect, James Renwick Jr., also designed Grace Church and St. Patrick's Cathedral. Both Edith Wharton and Eleanor Roosevelt were baptized at Calvary. The church is best viewed from across the street, where the empty base of one of its two original wooden steeples can be seen; the steeples were taken down after repeated lightning strikes.

script_body: This walk begins at what was the city hall of the City of Brooklyn until 1898, and ends at what has been the City Hall of New York City since 1812. Confused? Brooklyn and New York were separate cities until 1898, when they were consolidated into Greater New York, the current five boroughs. In that year, Brooklyn's 1849 City Hall was renamed Borough Hall, and a cupola was added to make it appear more like New York's City Hall. The building was originally designed in the spirit of common-man Jeffersonian democracy by Brooklyn carpenter and grocer Gamaliel King.

script_body: The idea of Brooklyn joining New York was contentious, much as Staten Island's threat to secede was in the mid-1990s. The consolidation referendum passed by only a few hundred votes in 1894. Many prominent Brooklyn citizens didn't want to merge what they saw as corrupt New York with pristine Brooklyn. After the referendum passed, a group of businessmen, including A. A. Low and Henry Pierrepont, two of the city's wealthiest landowners, along with cultural and religious leaders, formed the League of Loyal Citizens to oppose consolidation. Their vision of Brooklyn was of a white, prosperous, Protestant borough that wasn't teeming with Manhattan's immigrants. The League's spokesperson was St. Clair McKelway, editor of the Brooklyn Eagle, which sponsored an anticonsolidation song contest. "Up with the Flag of Brooklyn" won the three-hundred-dollar prize. McKelway wrote an editorial against consolidation in 1894, warning that "Brooklyn is a city of homes and churches. New York is a city of Tammany Hall and crime government," and that if tied to New York, Brooklyn would become "a Tammany suburb, to be kicked, looted and bossed as such." In spite of the League's opposition, Brooklyn and New York were joined.

script_body: The "park" stretching into the distance is Cadman Plaza, the eastern border of Brooklyn Heights. The Heights was the city's first historic district, though you wouldn't know it from the unattractive high-rises that surround Cadman Plaza; if not for historic preservation, all of Brooklyn Heights might look like them. Before the 1965 historic district law, property owners and the city could and did destroy homes at will. In 1953, construction for Robert Moses's Brooklyn-Queens Expressway razed parts of Columbia Heights, Middagh Street, and Poplar Street. Cadman Plaza itself destroyed much of the eastern Heights, including the building in which Walt Whitman set the type for the first edition of Leaves of Grass. In the face of all this destruction, a group of neighborhood residents formed the Community Conservation and Improvement Council, pronounced "kick," in 1958. CCIC joined with the Brooklyn Heights Association in 1959 and proposed a historic zoning designation modeled on Boston's Beacon Hill. In January 1965 the U.S. Department of the Interior declared the Heights a historic district, and in April the New York City Landmarks Preservation Law passed. Brooklyn Heights was the first such neighborhood in New York, predating Greenwich Village. The reason the Heights still looks as it does is that a band of citizens fought to make it so.

script_body: Spencer Memorial Church, from 1853, stands on the southeast corner of Remsen and Clinton. Built as the First Presbyterian Church of Brooklyn, its first minister was Ichabod Spencer, hence the name. Because the Heights was developed as an idyllic suburban enclave whose promoters emphasized its respectable character, they saw to it that churches were erected wherever possible. Brooklyn was sometimes called the "borough of churches." The church is now a group of co-op apartments.

script_body: Montague Street is the major shopping street in the Heights. During the late nineteenth century it was also called "Bank Row" because of the number of banks here. A cable car ran along its center beginning in 1887, becoming an electrified trolley from 1909 to 1924. True Brooklyn trivia lovers know that the Brooklyn Dodgers baseball team was named after borough residents who had to dodge trolleys like this one while crossing streets.

script_body: In addition to banks, Montague was the original site of three of Brooklyn's greatest cultural institutions, all now demolished but rebuilt elsewhere in the borough. The 1864 Mercantile Library sat on the north side of the block; it eventually merged with the Brooklyn Public Library, which moved to Grand Army Plaza in 1941. To the south was the 1872 Brooklyn Art Association, a forerunner to the Brooklyn Museum now on Eastern Parkway. And the Brooklyn Academy of Music had its opening night here in 1861, before relocating east to the neighborhood of Fort Greene.

script_body: On the northwest corner of Montague and Clinton stands the 1847 Church of St. Ann and the Holy Trinity, whose stained-glass windows were made by William Jay Bolton. Supposedly Bolton left America for England after finishing these windows, never to work in stained glass again. Many years later one of his elderly surviving daughters, nearing the end of her life, discovered her father's past and journeyed to Brooklyn Heights to see the work. Seeing the windows inspired her to live another ten years.

trigger_address: Pierrepont and Clinton Streets, Brooklyn Heights
script_body: The 1880 Brooklyn Historical Society stands on the southwest corner of Pierrepont and Clinton. Its architect was George Post, who also designed the New York Stock Exchange Building. The society began in 1863 as the Long Island Historical Society and today houses one of the most extensive regional collections in the country. On the building's facade are busts of Christopher Columbus and Benjamin Franklin, and flanking the entranceway are the heads of an Indian and a Viking. On the east side are numerous other heads and an inscription from Cicero translated as "History, the Witness of Time."

script_body: 5 Montague Terrace is where Thomas Wolfe lived from 1933 to 1934 and finished Of Time and the River. A friend described his rooms: the chief piece of furniture was an old table, work-worn and ancient, marked by cigarette burns, its surface dented like a shield after a hard battle. Opposite the windows stood a gas range and an electric refrigerator that bumped and hummed; Wolfe claimed the rhythm of that sound stimulated him, and on the old table and on the refrigerator he did most of his writing.

script_body: Two of three original mansions designed by Richard Upjohn in 1857 still stand near the playground. Farthest south, at 3 Pierrepont Place, was the former home of Abiel Abbott Low, a merchant who got rich trading with China and moved to the Heights in the mid-nineteenth century. His son Seth Low was the only person to be mayor of both Brooklyn, in 1884, and New York City, in 1901, and later became president of Columbia University. The next mansion, at No. 2, was the home of Alfred Tredway White, a wealthy merchant and philanthropist whose charitable motto was "Philanthropy plus 5 percent"; White funded model tenements for the poor in Brooklyn. The playground next door is all that remains of the third Upjohn mansion, demolished in 1946, which had been the home of Henry Pierrepont, whose family owned much of the surrounding land early in the nineteenth century.

script_body: Standing on the Promenade looking out over the harbor to downtown Manhattan, you have a modern version of the view that merchants like A. A. Low had 150 years ago, when they wanted to look upon their business on South Street in New York. From here you can also see why the neighborhood is called the Heights; many streets that end at the Promenade once sloped down to the shoreline. And from here, in 1776, George Washington evacuated Long Island, fleeing with his troops across to Manhattan under cover of fog and then northward to Harlem and out of New York, which was occupied by the British for the entire course of the Revolutionary War.

script_body: The three Federal-style townhouses set back from the street at 155, 157, and 159 Willow are among the earliest in the Heights, built in the 1820s. Note the arched dormered windows on top of two of them. A plaque on the middle house says it hid an underground storage space used to conceal runaway slaves as they escaped northward to Canada from the South. You can see the glass brick that forms the roof of this space if you look down at the sidewalk near the stairs of 157 Willow. Whether the spot was actually used as such is a matter of debate.

script_body: Willow Street shows off most of the architectural styles in the Heights. On your left are Gothic revival townhouses of the 1830s and 1840s, given away by the large blocks of their outer walls and Tudor arched windows. Further along on the right, 109 Willow is a Colonial revival building with exposed outside shutters, while across the street 108-112 Willow is a Queen Anne building from the 1880s, mixing terra-cotta, shingles, bay windows, gables, and a small tower into a bizarre style that somehow works. At the southeast corner of Clark stands 101 Willow, an excellent 1838 Greek revival home with a Greek Ionic portico over the front door and a high basement; its current owner had bricks from the back of the house moved to the front, where they would make it look appropriately aged.

script_body: Look east down Clark to the St. George Hotel, which takes up most of the block between Hicks and Henry. The St. George defined residence-hotel elegance in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Built in stages from 1885 to 1929, it had between twenty-six hundred and twenty-eight hundred rooms, making it the largest hotel in the United States for many years. Many New Yorkers held coming-out parties, weddings, and anniversaries in its giant ballroom, and it was a favored hangout of the Brooklyn Dodgers. Today the St. George has been divided into apartments; its saltwater swimming pool with the mirrored ceiling is gone, replaced by racquetball courts.

script_body: The St. George was also the site of the largest fire ever in Brooklyn. Early on the Sunday morning of August 27, 1995, a man using a blowtorch to remove copper pipes to sell for scrap started a fire in the 51 Clark Street part of the hotel. It spread to several attached buildings and grew to eighteen alarms, bringing five hundred firefighters to the neighborhood.

script_body: Why is there a Cranberry, an Orange, and a Pineapple Street in Brooklyn Heights? The myth is that Mabel Middagh Hicks, a descendant of two wealthy Brooklyn families, was upset at all the family names on the streets, so she put up her own, more colorful ones, and the Board of Aldermen eventually let them remain. Is it true? We don't know. Another great Heights story, this one not true, concerns Mabel's relatives, the Hicks brothers, "Milk" and "Spitter" Hicks. The family did have a farm here and likely sold produce in Manhattan; supposedly the word hick for a country bumpkin comes from the cry "Here come the Hicks" when the family came to sell vegetables. It's a great story, but "Hick" is actually a seventeenth-century British abbreviation for "Richard."

script_body: The building at 124 Columbia Heights, on the river side of the street, sits atop what was 110 Columbia Heights. Washington Roebling, the chief engineer of the Brooklyn Bridge, lived in this house for a few years after suffering a nervous breakdown, or a severe case of the bends depending on whom you ask, and watched his bridge go up through a telescope for months at a time. The writer Hart Crane later rented what he was convinced was Roebling's room, from 1924 to 1929. He wrote of the bridge: "And up at the right the Brooklyn Bridge, the most superb piece of construction in the modern world, I'm sure, with strings of light crossing it like glowing worms as the Ls and surface cars pass each other coming and going."

script_body: Across the grass courtyard from the 1849 Italianate Plymouth Church of the Pilgrims, designed by Joseph Wells, stands a statue of the Reverend Henry Ward Beecher. Beecher was America's leading abolitionist, using Christianity to condemn slavery and speaking so widely that extra ferries, called "Beecher's Boats," ran on Sundays to bring listeners from Manhattan to hear him preach. By 1859 he was making thousands yearly as a minister, and both Abraham Lincoln and Mark Twain came to hear him speak. His fame at the time was exceeded only by that of his sister Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, which outsold all books except the Bible in the 1850s. It is hard to impress on the modern reader the national stature of a preacher like Beecher, the authors note: think Billy Graham, Jesse Jackson, and Norman Vincent Peale all rolled into one.

script_body: Henry Ward Beecher was the subject of the "trial of the century" of the 1800s. In 1874 the preacher who advocated high moral standards in others was accused of "alienation of affection": he had had an affair with a married parishioner, Elizabeth Tilton. Beecher hushed the affair up until it was brought into the open by Victoria Woodhull and her sister Tennessee Claflin, both noted equal-rights advocates, spiritualists, investors, and feminists. Woodhull held the radical idea that a woman's sexual needs were equal to a man's and that love should not be controlled by anyone but the parties involved; she called it "free love." Her newspaper, Woodhull and Claflin's Weekly, declared Beecher a closet "free lover" and cleverly linked her struggle for "social freedom" to Beecher's fight against slavery, vowing the article would "burst like a bombshell into the ranks of this moralistic social camp." Woodhull, Claflin, and their publisher were almost immediately jailed for obscenity, though other papers reprinted the charges and no one else was arrested. Beecher's six-month civil trial, brought by Elizabeth's husband Theodore Tilton, became a fascinating entrée into sex, infidelity, and free love in Victorian America. It ended with a hung jury, and two church inquiries exonerated Beecher, though historical evidence has long since shown that he was clearly guilty. A contemporary paper had the last word: "The trial was a fine illustration of the power of money and the tricks that can be played with the law."

trigger_address: Cranberry Street and Cadman Plaza West, Brooklyn Heights
script_body: About where Cranberry used to meet Fulton Street, now Cadman Plaza West, stood the greatest landmark of all in Brooklyn Heights, now gone: here Walt Whitman set the first edition of Leaves of Grass. On Cranberry behind Plymouth Church is the site of one of Whitman's many Brooklyn homes. As he remembered it: "From 1824 to 1828 our family lived in Brooklyn in Front, Cranberry, and Johnson Streets. In the latter my father built a nice house for a home, and afterwards another in Tillary St. We occupied them one after the other, but they were mortgaged, and we lost them." And we have lost them all too, the authors add, including Whitman's printer's and the building where he edited the Brooklyn Daily Eagle.

script_body: The bridge is pregnant with aesthetic symbolism. You're looking at the most ancient material, stone, girded with what was in its time the most modern, steel. A suspension bridge brings together the two great forces in engineering, tension and compression. The steel cables are under nothing but tension as they strain to hold up the bridge; the granite towers are under nothing but compression as they strain to support the massive cables. In a suspension bridge the roadway is hung from cables, which take the load and transmit it to the towers and then to the ground. Anchorages underground on the Brooklyn and Manhattan shorelines hold down the ends of the four cables, each composed of thousands of strands. The deck is hung by yet more steel cables called "suspenders," and diagonal cables called "stays" hold the bridge rigid.

script_body: Suspension bridges of rope, vine, leather, and wood have existed for thousands of years. But it wasn't until the early 1800s that wrought iron could be produced cheaply enough to replace wood, stone, and cast iron, making the modern suspension bridge possible. Even then the iron was first made into a chain and lifted all at once, a feat limited by the chain's weight. It was the idea of "spinning" a cable one strand at a time, making the cables in place, that made possible the suspension bridges we have today.

Spinning cables one strand at a time, in place, was the key innovation

Even then, the iron was first made into a chain and lifted up all at once, a feat that was limited by the weight of the chain. script_body: Pause to think about the anchorages hidden beneath you. Inside these massive stone structures, the cables are connected to a series of eyebars attached to metal plates that sit beneath tons of cement and rock. The lower ends of the eyebars are bolted to the plates and the upper ends to the cables. The sheer weight of material on top, including your own body right now, holds down the cables and resists their pull, just as if you stood on a string while a cat tried to pull it out from under your foot.

script_body: Stop when the walkway turns from cement to wood and consider the men who designed the bridge. John Augustus Roebling, born in 1806, grew up in Germany and finished his engineering degree at the Royal Polytechnic Institute in Berlin in 1826; his senior thesis was on suspension bridges, and he also studied with the philosopher Hegel. Like many young men of his generation he left Germany for the United States, where, as he later said, the "hindrances, restrictions, and obstacles" of timid governments "are not to be found." He settled in the Pennsylvania community of Saxonburg and started farming, but soon tired of the fields. Roebling got the idea for wire rope while on an engineering job, noting that the thick hemp ropes used to tow canal boats up inclined railways were expensive and dangerous; metal rope, he believed, would be stronger and cheaper. He was right, and soon had most of the townsfolk making wire rope. In 1848 he moved his family to Trenton and founded a wire-rope company that ran as John A. Roebling's Sons until it was sold in 1953. He went on to build aqueducts, suspension-bridge canals, and a railroad bridge across Niagara Falls, becoming the most famous bridge builder in the United States when the New York Bridge Company chose him as chief engineer in 1867. Roebling, unfortunately, believed in the curative powers of water. While surveying for the anchorages on a Brooklyn dock on June 28, 1869, his foot was crushed against a piling by a docking ferry. He treated the wound by pouring cold water over it and died a month later of tetanus, leaving his thirty-two-year-old son Washington to take over.

script_body: Washington Roebling, born in 1837, earned a civil engineering degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York. script_body: At the Brooklyn tower, look at the plaques illustrating the bridge-building process. From August 1876 to October 1878, after the towers were finished, Roebling's workers spun the cables back and forth across the river. The first strand crossed on August 11, 1876. Two weeks later Master Mechanic E. F. Farrington made the first crossing of the East River by the great bridge, sitting in a boatswain's chair, nothing more than a flat board with a rope loop holding it to a pulley wheel; it took him twenty-two minutes to go from the Brooklyn to the New York side. The Brooklyn Bridge was the first bridge to use steel cables rather than iron. Under ideal conditions the cables traveled at five and a half feet a second, but wind, ice, snow, and breakdowns slowed the work; ten wires a day in each cable was considered good, and the entire cable spinning took eighteen months.

script_body: Read the anachronistic plaque to Emily Warren Roebling on the Manhattan-facing side of the Brooklyn tower. Emily Roebling, born in 1843, was Washington's tireless go-between for communicating instructions to E. F. Farrington and the other engineers on the bridge. When Washington became too ill in 1872 to keep supervising the work personally, Emily became his private secretary. He dictated specifications to her, and she carried the information to the assistant engineers. By 1879 she had spent seven years absorbed with the bridge.

script_body: You're now near the midpoint, 135 feet above the high-water mark by order of the War Department, which had to ensure ships built at the Brooklyn Navy Yard upriver could pass beneath. A bridge is a constant invitation to the reckless. The first person to jump from the bridge was Robert Odlum, a Washington, D.C., swimming instructor, who leaped on May 19, 1885, hoping to survive; unfortunately he didn't. The most famous jumper was Steve Brodie, who at age twenty-seven took bets that he could jump and live. He did, or at least said he did. Witnesses claimed he succeeded, and Brodie took his two-hundred-dollar winnings and opened a saloon on the Bowery, where he hung an oil painting of himself jumping and sat beneath it for years telling his story to all comers.

script_body: Remember that the bridge was built before automobiles clogged the streets. It was used by horse carts, pedestrians, and a cable railway running on the two inside lanes. A steam engine on the Brooklyn side powered the cable car on its five-minute, five-cent trip; from one to five in the morning the steam was shut off and locomotives did the work. The cable car was gradually electrified but didn't stop running until 1944, when an electric trolley took over the middle lanes, leaving only the outside lane to horses.

script_body: The Manhattan tower is not standing on bedrock, and how it got here is another story. Excavating the foundations was the most innovative, difficult, and uncertain part of building the bridge. The problem was how to get a foundation onto an area 100 by 170 feet, 44.5 feet beneath the water on the Brooklyn side and 75 feet on the Manhattan side. The solution was caissons, huge bottomless wooden boxes, fifteen feet thick at the top and tapering at the sides. The Brooklyn caisson was 168 by 102 feet, the Manhattan one 172 by 102 feet. They were built in shipyards north of the site, launched like giant barges, floated into place, and anchored with pilings. Compressed air was pumped in to keep the water out except for a foot or so at the bottom. Shafts driven through the roof allowed things in and out: dirt and rocks went out through a water shaft fitted with a giant clamshell-shaped dredging claw, and men entered and left through an airshaft. As the men dug and dynamited downward, masonry was laid on top, sinking the caisson further into the earth. The caissons were lit by sperm-whale-oil candles, the temperature inside eighty degrees and humid. Master mechanic E. F. Farrington said the scene gave one, if of a poetic temperament, "a realizing sense of Dante's inferno." When the workers reached bedrock on the Brooklyn side and hardpan on the Manhattan side, they were pulled out and the caissons filled with concrete.

script_body: Inside the caisson, workers labored in conditions that broke their bodies. Frank Harris, author of My Life and Loves, claimed that as a sixteen-year-old boy he worked there: in a bare shed the men warned him no one could do the work for long without getting the "bends." In the air-lock, as compressed air was turned on, the pain in their ears was so acute the men clapped their hands over them. Below, six of them worked naked to the waist in a small iron chamber at about eighty degrees, sweat pouring within five minutes while they stood in icy water held down only by the terrific pressure; the headaches were blinding, and most men didn't work more than ten minutes at a stretch. Harris said he plugged on, resolved to prove himself, though some historians believe he never actually worked in the caissons at all.

script_body: Take one final look at the bridge. When it opened on May 24, 1883, it was the biggest celebration since the opening of the Erie Canal at the beginning of the century. Tickets for seven thousand guests were issued; fifty thousand more attended; and the celebration began with an hour of fireworks and bands on steamers beneath the bridge. President Chester Arthur and the mayors of both Brooklyn and New York attended, and Emily Roebling led them across. It was a glorious day for New York. One week later, on Memorial Day, twelve pedestrians were trampled to death on a narrow stairway like the one you climbed at the Brooklyn end; the crowd thought the bridge was falling and panicked trying to get off. They were wrong, but it was a tragic end to a masterful building process.

script_body: If you can get close to City Hall when you read this, it means New York City has relaxed restrictions on people getting near the government. Finished in 1811, the building is only the third city hall New York has ever had, and its construction costs came in under the $250,000 budgeted. Originally most of the building was marble, with the north face and basement covered in less-expensive brownstone, because the planners assumed few would view it from the north. But between 1954 and 1956 the top four inches of the entire facade were stripped off and replaced with Alabama veined limestone, the basement redone with red granite, and all the columns, capitals, balustrades, and trim recut in new limestone. The entire facade you see is thus a replica of the original.

script_body: You are about to enter what many call the largest work of art in New York City. Central Park looks like a natural landscape, but almost everything inside it was designed, planted, landscaped, and laid out by human hands. As its designer Frederick Law Olmsted put it, "Every foot of the Park's surface, every tree and bush, as well as every arch, roadway and walk, has been placed where it is with a purpose." It is a nineteenth-century space — a natural environment, a recreational place, a commercial space, and a civic center all at once.

script_body: The park was the work of two men. The American Frederick Law Olmsted, who was not a park designer before Central Park made him one, took charge of the landscaping. The English immigrant Calvert Vaux — pronounced "vawx" — probably the first person to call himself a "landscape architect" rather than a "landscape artist," handled many of the park's structures, helped by architect Jacob Wrey Mould. Olmsted's earlier life was improbable: a small farmer on Staten Island, an agricultural writer, a founder of the Nation magazine, and supervisor of a California gold mine, but best known for his writing on slavery in the South. Vaux had come to America to join landscape designer Andrew Jackson Downing, who would have been the most likely candidate to design the park had he not drowned tragically before it began. In 1857, Olmsted landed a job as supervisor of land clearance through influential friends, then teamed up with Vaux to design the winning Greensward Plan. The city's request for proposals had strict requirements, and the pair met them masterfully — a parade ground became the Sheep Meadow, a fire lookout tower became Belvedere Tower, "the castle," a skating area became the Lake, and four cross-streets became the sunken transverse roads hidden below ground level.

source_passage: The two men most responsible for the park's design are the American Frederick Law Olmsted (1822–1903) and the English immigrant Calvert Vaux (1824–1895). Olmsted, who was decidedly not a park designer before Central Park made him one, was responsible for the park's landscaping. Vaux (pronounced "vawx"), who was probably the first person to call himself a "landscape architect" as opposed to a "landscape artist," was responsible for many of the park's structures, helped by architect Jacob Wrey Mould. Olmsted's pre-park experience included being a small farmer on Staten Island, an agricultural writer, a founder of the Nation magazine, and supervisor of a California gold mine. But he was best known for his writing on slavery in the South. Vaux had come to the United States to join a partnership with landscape designer Andrew Jackson Downing, who would have been the most likely candidate for park designer had he not drowned tragically before the project began. Olmsted landed a job in 1857 as the supervisor of land clearance for the park through influential friends. He then teamed up with Vaux to design the winning Greensward Plan for the park. The city's request for proposal had specific design requirements, which Olmsted and Vaux met masterfully. A parade ground became the Sheep Meadow; a fire lookout tower became Belvedere Tower—"the castle"; a skating area became the Lake; and four cross-streets became the four sunken transverse roads that are hidden from view below ground level.

script_body: After Central Park, Olmsted became one of the country's best-known park designers, shaping in whole or in part Prospect and Riverside Parks, Boston's Back Bay Fens, Philadelphia's Fairmont Park, Detroit's Belle Isle, Montreal's Mount Royal, Stanford's campus, and much more. Vaux designed Prospect and Fort Greene Parks with him, plus the Metropolitan Museum, the American Museum of Natural History, and Frederic Church's Olana home, but their partnership ended in 1872. Never as celebrated as Olmsted, Vaux grew bitter in later life. He drowned off the current site of the Brooklyn Navy Yard in 1895, and it is entirely possible he committed suicide.

source_passage: After designing the park, Olmsted went on to become one of the best-known park designers in the country, designing in whole or in part New York's Prospect and Riverside Parks, Boston's Back Bay Fens, Philadelphia's Fairmont Park, Louisville's park system, Detroit's Belle Isle, Montreal's Mount Royal, Buffalo's parks and parkways, Chicago's Riverside suburb, Oakland's Mountain View Cemetery, Washington, D.C.'s Capitol grounds, Stanford University's campus, and more. Though Vaux designed Prospect and Fort Greene Parks in Brooklyn with Olmsted, their partnership ended in 1872. Vaux went on to design the Metropolitan Museum, the American Museum of Natural History, Frederic Church's Olana home along the Hudson River, and buildings for the Children's Aid Society. He was never as celebrated as Olmsted and became bitter in later life. He drowned off the current site of the Brooklyn Navy Yard in 1895, and it is entirely possible that he committed suicide.

script_body: The desire for a great city park grew among wealthy New Yorkers in the mid-nineteenth century. Park boosters ranged from writers like William Cullen Bryant and Horace Greeley to real estate speculators like James Beekman and Mayor Fernando Wood. They compared New York unfavorably to European cities with parks, and the wealthy wanted somewhere to ride their carriages away from the hoi polloi of the city streets. There were many competing arguments: that a park would establish New York as the nation's cultural capital, provide a retreat for the rich, and serve as a social safety valve for the poor crammed into tenements with no green space. But the idea of a truly democratic park for all people frightened the middle classes. An 1858 editorial in the New York Herald sneered that when a public park opened, "Sam will air himself in it," knock down any better-dressed man who remonstrated, and turn the park into "nothing but a great beer garden for the lowest denizens of the city." Standing here, you can still ask the questions the park has always provoked: Is a picnic acceptable? Music? Volleyball? Barbecuing? Dancing? What is "respectable," and what is "unacceptable," today?

source_passage: New Yorkers, especially wealthy ones, gradually developed a desire for a city park in the mid–nineteenth century. Park boosters included writers such as William Cullen Bryant and Horace Greeley, real estate speculators such as James Beekman, and Mayor Fernando Wood. They compared New York unfavorably to European cities that had parks. Further, the wealthy wanted a place to ride their carriages away from the hoi polloi of the city streets. There were many competing arguments for the park: for example, that it would establish New York as the nation's cultural capital, provide a retreat for the wealthy, and be a social safety valve for the city's poor, who were crammed into tenement housing with no parks to the south. Interestingly, the desire for a democratic park for all people was frightening to the middle classes and precipitated a debate over the use of public space by "respectable" and "disorderly" classes, as this editorial in the New York Herald of 1858 illustrates: It is folly to expect in this country to have parks like those in old aristocratic countries. When we open a public park, Sam will air himself in it.

script_body: A democratic park did not mean treating those who already lived on the land democratically. Boosters demonized the pre-park inhabitants to make it easier for the city to seize their property. The New York Times, voicing the anti-Irish Catholic bigotry typical of the era, described park residents as "principally Irish families [in] rickety little one storie shanties inhabited by four or five persons, not including the pig and the goats." Other papers played up the "vagabonds" and "scoundrels" supposedly living in the park. Yet more than 90 percent of those living on the future parkland were immigrants — largely Irish and German — or African Americans, and a careful look at the records shows a far higher share of them owned their land than did city dwellers at large. Landowner, renter, and squatter alike were evicted in 1857 and 1858 to make way for construction.

source_passage: Furthermore, a democratic park did not mean treating those who currently lived in what would become parkland democratically. A lot of propaganda and boosterism demonized the pre-park inhabitants of the land to make it easier for the city to take their property. The New York Times, expressing anti–Irish Catholic bigotry typical of the nineteenth century, described park residents as "principally Irish families [in] rickety . . . little one storie shanties . . . inhabited by four or five persons, not including the pig and the goats," and other newspapers made much of the "vagabonds" and "scoundrels" living in the park. More than 90 percent of those living on what would be parkland were either immigrants, largely Irish and German, or African Americans. In the latter case, Seneca Village, whose principal street was in the park across from West Eighty-fifth Street, was a well-established town with a school, three churches, and 250 residents. Indeed, a careful search of records shows that a far higher percentage of people living in the park actually owned their own land than did people in the city at large. Nonetheless, landowner, renter, and squatter alike were evicted in 1857 and 1858 to make way for construction.

script_body: We begin at the giant monument to the Maine, regilded now and shining in the sun. It memorializes the American battleship that blew up — or was blown up — in Havana harbor in 1898, killing over 250 sailors and precipitating the Spanish-American War. William Randolph Hearst, whose New York Journal fervently supported the war, helped raise money for the monument. It was meant to stand in Times Square but never made it there. Look up and you'll see "Columbia Triumphant," the statue at the top, surrounded below by Victory, Peace, Courage, and Fortitude; on the back stand Justice, Warrior, and History; and on the sides the Pacific Ocean as an old man and the Atlantic Ocean as a young man.

script_body: Greyshot Arch is one of over forty bridges Vaux designed with Jacob Wrey Mould. Walk under its sandstone balustrade and through the vaulted, red-brick archway — a passage just over thirty feet wide, ten feet high, and eighty feet long. Continue along the path and take the left fork to reach Pine Bank Arch, two hundred feet beyond. Walk over this cast-iron beauty, whose entire structure was rebuilt with a new wooden floor in 1984. In Central Park, every single arch and every bridge is different.

script_body: Alongside the path rises Umpire Rock, the giant piece of Manhattan schist that supervises the Heckscher Ballfields and the Ballplayers House just to the north. Schist is the bedrock under Manhattan — geologically a combination of mica, quartz, feldspar, and hornblende. Look carefully at the outcroppings here and you'll notice they are smoother on the north side, where glaciers first scraped them, and rougher and more irregular to the south. You can impress friends by telling them that major outcroppings are called roche moutonnée, or "laying sheep," because the glacial cuttings supposedly make them look like sleeping sheep.

script_body: The ball fields seem a perfectly natural part of the park, but recreation had almost nothing to do with the original design. The first park had no playground at all, only three meadows for children's field sports — and to play on them, kids needed a certificate of good attendance and character from their teachers, a hard thing for the many nineteenth-century children who were working rather than in school. Concrete and asphalt playgrounds arrived around the turn of the twentieth century, championed by social reformers who believed playgrounds would save children from gangs and, later, from unemployment. Adult baseball diamonds weren't a serious feature until the 1920s. Olmsted and Vaux had wanted "a ground to which people may easily go after their day's work is done" — a place that completely shut out the city.

script_body: How big is the park, and what did it cost? It runs north-south from 110th Street down to Fifty-ninth Street, and east-west from Fifth Avenue to Central Park West — just over 840 acres, about twice the size of feudal-relic Monaco and several times bigger than Governors Island. In the late 1850s the city paid the landowners of this rocky, swampy farmland almost $7.5 million, only a few hundred thousand dollars more than the United States would soon pay Russia for all of Alaska. Construction began in 1858, and much of the landscaping south of Seventy-ninth Street was finished by December 1860; it took another five years to reach 110th Street, though the park is never truly finished. As far as historians can tell, Irish workers did almost all the labor, there were no black workers, and the only women employed cleaned offices. Crews swelled from about two thousand workers in early spring to thirty-five hundred by late summer. For a ten-hour day, unskilled laborers earning a dollar brought in millions of cubic yards of soil, planted hundreds of non-native trees, laid six and a half miles of road, dug out a 106-acre reservoir, and built mile upon mile of trails.

source_passage: The park runs north-south from 110th Street (Central Park North) to Fifty-ninth Street (Central Park South) and east-west from Fifth Avenue to Central Park West (Eighth Avenue). It is just over 840 acres, which is about twice as large as feudal-relic Monaco and several times bigger than Governors Island in New York Harbor. The city paid the landowners of this rocky, swampy farmland almost $7.5 million for their land in the late 1850s. By contrast, the United States paid a few hundred thousand dollars less to Russia to buy Alaska only a few years later. Construction began in 1858, and much of the landscaping south of Seventy-ninth Street was finished by December 1860. It took another five years to complete things up to 110th Street, but the park is never truly finished; it is a continuous work in progress. As far as historians can tell, Irish workers did almost all the labor and there were no black workers. The only women employed cleaned offices. The general rhythm of construction was, to begin with, about two thousand workers in early spring, expanding to thirty-five hundred by late summer and then cut back in the fall. A ten-hour day paid $1 for unskilled laborers who brought in millions of cubic yards of soil, planted hundreds of non-native trees, laid out six and a half miles of road, dug out a 106-acre reservoir, and built mile upon mile of trails and walkways.

script_body: The Carousel before you was built in 1908 in Coney Island and moved here in 1951, replacing the park's original 1871 carousel, which burned down. That original was supposedly powered by a blind horse and a blind mule walking a treadmill underneath it. The Carousel runs on a contract from the city. For years Sal Napolitano ran it, until he was outbid by the Makkos Organization — formerly the M & T Pretzel Company — an immigrant success story run by Greek immigrant Themis Makkos and his sons.
