script_body: The Sheep Meadow, the large grass field before you, was originally landscaped as a parade ground but began hosting sheep in 1864. Olmsted required a particular breed of Southdown sheep whose gray-and-white coloring offset the grass — he was following William Gilpin, whose book Forest Scenery he loved. Gilpin wrote: "Sheep particularly are very ornamental in a park. Their color is just that dingy hue, which contrasts with the verdure of the ground; and the flakiness of their wool is rich and picturesque." The meadow stayed green until a series of concerts in the 1960s and 1970s killed much of the grass. Replanted in 1979, it stays green today by banning organized sports, concerts, and any activity when the grass is wet.

Gilpin wrote: "Sheep particularly are very ornamental in a park. Their color is just that dingy hue, which contrasts with the verdure of the ground; and the flakiness of their wool is rich and picturesque." The Sheep Meadow was fairly green until a series of concerts in the 1960s and 1970s killed much of the grass. It was replanted in 1979 and remains green by banning organized sports, concerts, and any activity when the grass is wet.

script_body: A huge inlaid-marble plaque on the ground calls this the Literary Walk, though New Yorkers call it the Mall — the formal promenade at the center of the naturalistic park. A wide, straight pathway bordered by double rows of overhanging elms runs northwest up to Bethesda Terrace. Surprisingly, Olmsted and Vaux did not intend statues anywhere but at Bethesda Terrace; all the rest were forced on them by the city, pressured by civic, ethnic, and religious groups who wanted figures of their great men in the park. At the southern end you'll find Shakespeare from 1870, Sir Walter Scott from 1871, and Robert Burns from 1880.

New Yorkers call it the Mall. The Mall is the formal promenade at the center of the naturalistic park. A wide, straight pathway bordered on both sides by double rows of overhanging elms runs northwest right up to Bethesda Terrace, the formal center of the park. Note the statues at the southern end. You will see Shakespeare (1870) toward the Mall's eastern entrance, Sir Walter Scott (1871) on your immediate right, and Robert Burns (1880) on your immediate left.

script_body: Further north along the Mall stands the statue of Fitz-Greene Halleck, on your right. Halleck, who died in 1867, was one of the most famous poets in the country in the nineteenth century — though his poems are now almost completely forgotten. That makes it astonishing to learn that when this statue was unveiled in 1876, President Rutherford B. Hayes, his entire cabinet, and ten thousand others came for the ceremony. That no one knows who he is today says volumes about representing people in statues, an idea well past its heyday.

script_body: Can you name the most famous statue of a woman in the park? It's Alice in Wonderland. In fact there are no statues in the park of women who were living, historical figures — all are allegorical figures or characters from nursery rhymes. Across all of Manhattan's public spaces, statues of actual women number only four: Gertrude Stein, Golda Meir, Joan of Arc, and Eleanor Roosevelt.

All the statues of women are allegorical figures or characters from nursery rhymes. In all of the public spaces in Manhattan there are many statues of women, but again, these are invariably not of actual people. We can count, at present time, only four: Gertrude Stein, Golda Meir, Joan of Arc, and Eleanor Roosevelt.

script_body: Olmsted and Vaux installed a cast-iron bandstand to the west in 1859, but this band shell on your right is a later anachronism: retired banker Elkan Naumburg donated money to build it in 1923. Over the years it has hosted Leonard Bernstein, Duke Ellington, Benny Goodman, Martin Luther King Jr., Fidel Castro, and Mayor Fiorello La Guardia selling war bonds during World War II. It was a wildly popular spot for ballroom dancing in the 1940s and 1950s, when the Goldman Band played live. When the city later wanted to tear it down, Naumburg's great-grandson and others sued — and the courts ruled the city had to maintain a gift it had willingly accepted.

source_passage: Olmsted and Vaux installed a cast-iron bandstand to the west in 1859, but the current one is a historical anachronism. In 1923, retired banker Elkan Naumberg donated money to build it. This band shell has hosted Leonard Bernstein, Duke Ellington, Benny Goodman, Martin Luther King Jr, Fidel Castro, and Mayor Fiorello La Guardia selling war bonds during World War II. It was a very popular spot for ballroom dancing in the 1940s and 1950s, when the Goldman Band played here live. But as the popularity of ballroom dancing waned, so did the use of the band shell. The city wanted to tear it down in accordance with plans by the Central Park Conservancy (the nonprofit agency that actually runs the park), but Naumberg's great-grandson and others sued the city. The courts ruled that the city had to maintain it as a gift it had willingly accepted, whether or not it fit with the old-style benches that have been built around it.

script_body: Above the band shell on the hill is Rumsey Playfield, a once-desolate asphalt lot with a storied past, now home to SummerStage and its free concerts. The hill was originally the site of the Ladies Refreshment Pavilion, but in the late 1920s Mayor "Gentleman" Jimmy Walker asked his friend Sidney Solomon to take over the space. Solomon hired Joseph Urban to redesign the interior, which included a black-glass ballroom. Walker and his mistress Betty Compton reviewed the plans personally, and some of the financing even came from Arnold Rothstein — the man who had fixed the 1919 World Series. The building opened as the Central Park Casino, without gambling, in 1929, and became one of the most elegant places to eat in the city until Walker fled office under corruption charges a few years later. In 1934 Robert Moses, then parks commissioner, demolished the casino, arguing that only restaurants "within the reach of persons of average means" belonged in the park. Tellingly, Moses then converted the sheepfold west of the Sheep Meadow into Tavern on the Green — which persons of average means have always found far too expensive.

script_body: On June 22, 1901, the benches along part of the Mall were replaced with new green rocking chairs. The moment a park visitor sat down, a uniformed attendant walked up to demand five cents for a chair with arms, three cents for one without. Entrepreneur Oscar Spate had secured a rocking-chair franchise from Tammany Hall and hoped to make $250 a day here and in other city parks. Instead the angry public rioted, smashing and stealing the chairs. A chastened Parks Commission withdrew Spate's franchise and replaced his chairs with ones marked "For the Exclusive Use of Women and Children, FREE."

script_body: Bethesda Terrace was the only place Olmsted and Vaux wanted any statues, and they ended up with just one. The Moorish building you walked underneath was designed by Jacob Wrey Mould, who had studied Islamic architecture and reproduced its style here; its ceiling was originally covered with thousands of tiles, now being reinstalled by the Central Park Conservancy. Bethesda Fountain is crowned by Emma Stebbins's Angel of the Waters, from 1873 — the only sculpture in the park by a woman. Stebbins was the sister of the president of the Central Park Board of Commissioners. The fountain refers to the pool in Jerusalem named in the Gospel of John: "There is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda." In the Bible, the sick waited at the pool for an angel to stir the waters, then entered to be cured. There's even a long-running debate over whether Stebbins's angel is a man or a woman — some see a proto-feminist celebration of women, while others note that angels are sexless and the statue simply reflects the design conventions of its day.

script_body: Bow Bridge is one of seven cast-iron bridges built in the park. Seen from ground level on the side, it really is shaped roughly like a bow. Stand on it and look west along Central Park West, and you'll see the low-peaked, verdigrised roofs of the Dakota with a flagpole on top — perhaps Manhattan's most famous apartment building. When it was built in the mid-1880s there was very little this far north; today most people know it as the building where John Lennon lived, and where he was shot. To the left and right of the Dakota stand two of Central Park West's twin-towered apartment buildings, the Majestic and the San Remo.

script_body: The Ramble was designed as a small forest of meandering paths, and it's easy to get lost in here. Olmsted believed, "There can be no better place than the Ramble for the perfect realization of the wild garden." Wind your way through and you'll reach the Rustic Shelter, a rebuilt cedar-log shelter meant to mimic English ideas of a Romantic landscape.

script_body: No account of Central Park is complete without crime. For whatever reason, crimes in the park carry national resonance while crimes elsewhere in the city usually don't — likely because so many Americans imagine the park as a sanctuary, so that violence here feels like an assault on the body politic. Early arrests were mostly for driving carriages too fast. The first robbery-murder, in 1872, moved the New York Times to remark, "Murder has actually stained the turf of that green fairy land." In the 1880s the Police Gazette warned of "murderous attacks upon the chastity of pure-minded young females" — meaning flashers. Homeless men, "tramps" in the vernacular, drew the papers' ire too; the New York Tribune wrote in the 1870s that "tramps and other unpleasant people [have] quit their winter quarters for the benches in the Park," and that ladies and children hesitated to venture into the Ramble without escorts. Today the park has its own police precinct with the lowest violent-crime rate of any in the city, though the occasional horrific assault still draws enormous attention.

Ladies and children hesitate to venture into the Ramble without escorts." Today the Park has its own police precinct, and it has the lowest rate of violent crimes of any precinct in the city. script_body: Vaux designed the castle to serve as a fire watchtower. It sits atop 135-foot-high Vista Rock, through which — beneath your feet — a tunnel is blasted for the Seventy-ninth Street transverse road. If the castle is open, climb the stairs to one of the lookouts. The original castle had no glass in its windows; the structure was meant to deteriorate as the park grew around it, showing people that the work of human hands is ephemeral while nature is eternal. Since 1920, the official weather-reading station for New York City has stood atop the castle and in the fenced-in area behind it, where instruments measure wind, sunshine, temperature, precipitation, and humidity.

script_body: From the castle, look north over the redone Turtle Pond to the 1960 Delacorte Theater, home of free Shakespeare in the Park, and beyond to the giant green ball fields of the Great Lawn. The lawn sits on the site of an 1840s reservoir that was drained in 1930. Until the early 1990s it hosted the park's giant free concerts and gatherings — Elton John in 1980, Simon and Garfunkel in 1981, an antinuclear rally in 1982, Diana Ross in 1983, Paul Simon in 1991, and a Billy Graham gathering the same year, each drawing hundreds of thousands. The Central Park Conservancy then spent over $18 million renovating it with irrigation, drainage, soil, Kentucky bluegrass, and perennial rye. No more large events will take place on it.

script_body: The largest town on the land that became Central Park was Seneca Village, which stretched from Seventy-ninth to Eighty-sixth Streets west of today's Great Lawn, its main street running east-west into the parkland at what is now Eighty-fifth Street. In 1855, two years before its residents were evicted, the village had 264 residents — about three-quarters black, the rest Irish — with homes, gardens, three churches, cemeteries, a school, and a spring that still bubbles up east of Eighty-second Street. It began in 1825, when John and Elizabeth Whitehead started selling parts of their farm to black New Yorkers. The first buyer was Andrew Williams, a twenty-five-year-old bootblack, who bought three lots for $125. Members of the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, "Mother Zion," followed, and by 1829 there were nine houses. When the old Croton reservoir displaced the black community of York Hill, many moved here too. Contrary to the accounts that demonized park residents as squatters, Seneca Village's tax and housing records show several two- and three-story buildings, one even with a wraparound porch on three sides.

source_passage: The largest town in the land that would become Central Park was Seneca Village (the origins of the name are still being debated), which stretched from Seventy-ninth to Eighty-sixth Streets to the west of the Great Lawn. Its main street ran east-west into the parkland at what is today Eighty-fifth Street. In 1855, two years before all its residents were evicted, Seneca Village had 264 residents (about three-quarters black and the rest Irish), homes, gardens, three churches, cemeteries, a school, and a spring that still bubbles up in the park east of Eighty-second Street. All that is left today are the cornerstones of one of the churches. How Seneca Village came to be is one of the most interesting stories in the park. Beginning in 1825, John and Elizabeth Whitehead started selling parts of their farm to black New Yorkers. The first buyer was Andrew Williams, a twenty-five-year-old bootblack, who bought three lots for $125. Williams was followed by members of the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Zion Church, "Mother Zion," from downtown. By 1829 there were nine houses on the side. The building of the now-demolished old reservoir (not the new one that's still there), which was part of the Croton Aqueduct system at the center of the park from 1825 to 1832 displaced another black community known as York Hill, and many of its residents moved to Seneca Village. Contrary to mid-nineteenth-century accounts that demonized residents of the park as "vagabonds" or "squatters," the tax and housing records of Seneca Village tell a different story. Assessors' maps show several twoand three-story buildings, one even with a wraparound porch on three sides.

script_body: For black New Yorkers, land in Seneca Village meant more than homes and income — it meant the vote. In 1821, New York revised its constitution to grant universal white male suffrage but required free blacks to own $250 worth of property to vote. By 1855 there were twelve thousand black residents in New York but only one hundred black voters — and ten of them lived in Seneca Village. Black residents there were far more likely to own property than whites elsewhere in the city. About three-quarters of the villagers regularly attended one of its three churches, among them All Angels' Church, built in 1849 by the white Reverend Thomas Peters for a black and German congregation.

source_passage: Land ownership provided not only homes and income for black New Yorkers but voting rights. In 1821, New York revised its state constitution to allow universal white male suffrage but required free blacks to own $250 worth of property to vote. In 1855 there were twelve thousand black residents in New York but only one hundred black voters, and ten of these lived in Seneca Village. Indeed, black Seneca Village residents were far more likely to own property than whites elsewhere in the city. About three-quarters of Seneca Village residents regularly attended one of its three churches. The African Methodist Union Church was established by black migrants from York Hill. All Angels' Church was built in 1849 by the white Reverend Thomas Peters, with money he raised and other funds he donated. It held a black and German congregation, including members of AME Zion Church from downtown, until AME Zion moved into Seneca Village in 1853.

script_body: Seneca Village's All Angels' Church housed Colored School No. 3, whose black teacher struck a blow for equality a full century before Rosa Parks. In July 1854, the teacher, twenty-four-year-old Elizabeth Jennings, boarded a Third Avenue streetcar downtown on her way to church. The car carried no sign reading "Colored People Allowed in This Car," as others did, and when Jennings refused to get off, she was forcibly removed by the conductor and a policeman. She sued the Third Avenue Railway Company and was represented at her 1855 trial by another twenty-four-year-old: the future president Chester A. Arthur. The jury ruled that under state law the railway was a common carrier "bound to carry all respectable people," and that colored persons, if sober, well-behaved, and free from disease, had the same rights as others. The third Seneca Village church, AME Zion — the oldest black church in New York, founded in 1796 — counted among its members Sojourner Truth, Harriet Tubman, Frederick Douglass, and Thomas Fortune.

script_body: Not even the churches could save the community when the park came. A city commission surveyed and assessed every lot, and those inside the future park were taken by eminent domain — the government forcibly, but with pay, taking land for what it declares the common good. The city paid Andrew Williams, the first property owner, $2,335 for his two-story house and three lots; Williams argued in vain that the house alone was worth $1,400 and that he'd been offered $3,500 for house and lots. The New-York Daily Times introduced white readers to the village in jarring terms, calling it a "neat little settlement, known as 'nigger village,'" whose inhabitants made "a pleasing contrast" to the Irish elsewhere in the park's domain. By 1857 Seneca Village was gone, its residents scattered, its history unknown to most who walk the park today.

source_passage: Alas, not even churches were enough to preserve the community when it came time to build the park. A city commission surveyed and assessed the value of all lots in and around the park. Those inside the park's future limits were taken from their owners by right of eminent domain, which means the government forcibly, but with pay, takes your land for what it declares is the common good. The city paid Andrew Williams, the first property owner, $2,335 for his two-story house and three lots. Williams argued to no avail that the value of the house alone was $1,400 and that he had been offered $3,500 for house and lots. About this time, the New-York Daily Times introduced white New Yorkers to black residents of Seneca Village as a contrast to Irish residents elsewhere in the park's domain: "West of the reservoir within the limits of the Central Park, lies a neat little settlement, known as "nigger village." The Ebon inhabitants after whom the village is called, present a pleasing contrast in their habits and the appearance of their dwellings to the Celtic occupants. How gently they went is unknown, but almost every property owner protested vehemently that the city was not paying fair market value for their land. Nonetheless, by 1857, Seneca Village was gone. Its residents scattered among many neighborhoods, and their history is unknown to most who walk through the park today.

script_body: Near Turtle Pond stands the statue of King Jagiello on horseback, by Stanislaw Ostrowski. It was meant for Kraków, but instead appeared at the Polish pavilion at the 1939–40 World's Fair, and the Polish government in exile gave it to New York in 1945. Jagiello was actually a grand duke of Lithuania who married the Polish queen to unite the two lands.

script_body: This two-hundred-ton obelisk, also known as Cleopatra's Needle, was erected in the park in 1881, but it was first installed in Egypt in the fourteenth century B.C. by Thutmosis III. Over the next twenty-five hundred years it was vandalized by those who carved on, burned, and eventually buried it. The United States was offered the needle in the nineteenth century, and it sailed from Egypt to New York in 1880, with William Vanderbilt paying the hundred-thousand-dollar shipping cost. It landed at West Ninety-sixth Street and was rolled along on cannonballs and giant timbers to railroad tracks, then inched forward as workers picked up the track behind it and laid it in front, over and over — work that took 112 days to reach this spot. On January 22, 1881, the obelisk was pivoted upright into place in under five minutes. Contrary to what's often written, New York pollution has barely altered its surface: most of the blackening is fire damage from the Persians' sacking of Heliopolis thousands of years ago, and its long burial caused salt to crystallize within, making it vulnerable to freezing and thawing.

script_body: East Drive was built for elegant carriages, not cars. There was a New York tradition of a formal carriage procession that entered the park at Fifth Avenue and Central Park South, rolled up East Drive, and crossed Bethesda Terrace to the west side. Commercial wagons were banned when the park opened, and for years police refused entry to anyone not driving a "pleasure carriage." Then in 1899 Winslow E. Buzby drove in the first auto, testing the commissioner's ban with what he called an "automobile victoria-phaeton." Given a summons, Buzby went before a magistrate, who ruled that under the ordinance allowing "pleasure carriages, bicycles, or horseback" his car counted as a pleasure carriage. The park board changed the rules to ban "horseless carriages and motor wagons," but soon relented — and the drives were asphalted beginning in 1912.

source_passage: As you pass under East Drive, remember that it was built for elegant carriages, not cars. In fact, there was a New York City tradition of a formal carriage procession that entered the park at Fifth Avenue and Central Park South and proceeded up East Drive and then across Bethesda Terrace to the west side. Commercial wagons were banned from the park when it opened, and police would refuse entry to anyone not driving a "pleasure carriage" onto the drive for many years after the park opened. Alas, the first auto was driven into the park in 1899 by Winslow E. Buzby, who tested the park commissioner's ban with what he called an "automobile victoria-phaeton." Buzby was given a summons and appeared before a magistrate, who ruled that under the city ordinance that said, "The drive shall be used only by persons in pleasure carriages, on bicycles, or on horseback," Buzby's car was a pleasure carriage. In response, the park board changed the rules to ban "horseless carriages and motor wagons" but soon relented. Nonetheless, change was relentless, and the park's drives were asphalted beginning in 1912.

script_body: The Metropolitan Museum is today one of the largest art museums in the world, with almost three and a half million items ranging from prehistory to a few decades ago. In 1872, Olmsted and Vaux reluctantly allowed a museum on this spot, since the view to it was then blocked by the walls of the reservoir on the Great Lawn. The museum was built in many pieces: the first building, designed by Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould in 1871 and opened in 1880, is almost completely hidden inside the many later additions. The Met stayed closed on Sundays until 1891, when it was forced open by protests from workers who wanted to visit on their only day off and by the city, which threatened to withhold funds.

script_body: We begin at the gilded statue of General William Tecumseh Sherman, best known for his bloody march through the South in the fall of 1864, when, as the Union's commander in the West, he burned large portions of Georgia and South Carolina. Sherman showed little remorse at Georgia's fate; as he famously put it, "War is cruelty and you cannot refine it." Walking before him, waving an olive branch, is the figure of Victory. The pine branch on the granite pedestal signifies Georgia, and the horses stomping on the pines are a painful reminder of the destruction of Sherman's March.

script_body: The Pulitzer Fountain, in the plaza in front of the Plaza Hotel, was erected in 1916 with a fifty-thousand-dollar gift from Joseph Pulitzer, who hoped to outdo his newspaper-magnate rival William Randolph Hearst. The statue on top is Pomona, the Greek goddess of abundance, finished by Karl Bitter, protégé of architect Richard Morris Hunt. The day he finished the clay model in 1915, Bitter was tragically killed crossing the street as he left the Metropolitan Opera, then on Forty-seventh Street, and his apprentices were left to complete the statue.

script_body: The Plaza, dating from 1907, is one of New York's great luxury hotels. Frank Lloyd Wright, who hated New York, would stay only here when he passed through; other luminaries who made it their temporary residence included the Beatles, Mark Twain, Groucho Marx, and Eleanor Roosevelt. The very first guest to sign the Plaza's register was Alfred Gwynne Vanderbilt — who would later lose his life in the sinking of the Lusitania. The French Renaissance building was designed by Henry Hardenbergh, the same architect responsible for the Dakota.

script_body: J. Pierpont Morgan formed the Metropolitan Club here, on the northeast corner of Fifth Avenue and Sixtieth Street, in anger. Some of his close comrades and fellow captains of industry had been unable to win entrance into the other elite clubs of the time, principally the Union Club. Morgan had proposed John King, president of the Erie Railroad, whose "career and character have won him the universal respect of all who know him" — but it was said King's table manners were not up to snuff, and he was promptly denied membership. Morgan's retribution was to get New York's most famous architect, Stanford White, to build "the largest, most imposing, and most luxurious of the clubhouses of New York." Morgan, it is said, summoned White with the words "Damn the expense." In its temerity to challenge the Union Club, the Metropolitan was dressed in an all-marble facade. One lure to new members was a dining room set aside for female guests — the Ladies Restaurant, overlooking the courtyard. Joining Morgan were Cornelius Vanderbilt and Robert Goelet.

script_body: Across from the Metropolitan Club stands the Harmonie Club at 4 East Sixtieth Street. It was formed in 1852 by the German Jewish community as the Harmonie Gesellschaft — the Harmony Society — and was distinguished by having German as its official language and by hanging the kaiser's portrait in its hall. It was the first men's club in the city to admit women at dinner, and the first eventually to have women as members. The club dates from a period when the chasm between first-wave German Jews and the second-wave Eastern Europeans was massive, and many Harmonie denizens, eager to assimilate, had little desire to associate with their poorer brethren from the East.

script_body: In October 1961, New York City detectives Eddie Egan and Sonny Grosso were having drinks after work at the Copacabana when they noticed a "little man in a silk suit, with a diamond stickpin in his tie, flashing a huge bankroll." They decided to follow him. The chase would last eighteen months and turn into The French Connection: in the end there were nine arrests, and a hundred and twelve pounds of heroin were secured — thirty-two million dollars' worth in 1960s dollars. The film's famous car-chase scene was shot over five weeks under Brooklyn's Bensonhurst Elevated, at full speed, with real pedestrians and traffic.

script_body: The Copacabana was a venue for New York's stage and sports celebrities and for the average New Yorker alike — the stuff of high-school proms, college balls, and first dates. May 1957 saw one of its more notorious nights. With Sammy Davis Jr. on the stage and Yankee Billy Martin celebrating his twenty-ninth birthday alongside Mickey Mantle, Yogi Berra, and Hank Bauer, a brawl broke out between the Yankee players and a New Jersey bowling team. Police charges were ultimately dropped, but the Yankees' owner blamed Martin and traded him that July to Kansas City; he would not return until the 1970s, as the team's manager.

script_body: The Grolier Club, at 47 East Sixtieth Street, is — in contrast with the business-titan appeal of the Metropolitan down the road — a club for book lovers. It was named for the sixteenth-century bibliophile Jean Grolier de Servières and founded for "the literary study and promotion of the arts pertaining to the production of books." Bertram Goodhue, best known for St. Bartholomew's Church next to the Waldorf Astoria, designed the clubhouse in 1916. The original Grolier Club stands at 29 East Thirty-second Street.

script_body: Madison Avenue, one of New York City's narrowest avenues, is named for America's fourth president, who sadly died in 1836 — the year of the avenue's opening. It has a curious history, going from a predominantly residential thoroughfare to an outstanding commercial zone; because of zoning, many of its fashionable stores are now housed in the very townhouses and brownstones that survive from its residential days. Of the tour's three avenues, Madison emerged first, and it turned headfirst toward the commercial, becoming in the early postwar period the advertising capital of the world. No longer the center of advertising, it has reinvented itself, at least here, as "Boutique Row."

script_body: The low building on the northeast corner of Sixty-second and Madison was originally Louis Sherry's restaurant, where to take tea was to "see a certain number of Our Best People." Sherry made his money as a first-class confectioner to the rich. His restaurant was better known for its antics — including the 1903 dinner for the New York Horseback Riding Club, sponsored by Chicago millionaire Cornelius Billings, at which diners ate on horseback. The tab? A mere fifty thousand dollars.

trigger_address: west side of Madison Avenue near Sixty-second Street
script_body: Although there is no plaque, across Madison Avenue on the west side stood the home where Theodore Roosevelt lived from 1895 to 1897, during his tenure as police commissioner of New York. As commissioner, he forced the resignation of the chief of the uniformed police, who had justified amassing $300,000 from "successful stock picks." Roosevelt took to prowling the streets at night in a black cape, hunting for policemen shirking their duty. The strolls made for good public relations, but his popularity suffered when he enforced the Sunday blue laws and closed the saloons; New Yorkers were happy to see him move on in 1897 to become assistant secretary of the navy.

script_body: The fabulous beaux-arts townhouse at 11 East Sixty-second Street is the Fabbri Mansion, commissioned and built in 1900 for William Vanderbilt's eldest daughter, Margaret Louisa Vanderbilt Shepard, who presented it to her daughter Edith and her son-in-law. The name Fabbri is for Edith's husband — note the F's designed into the wrought-iron balconies. Inside survive a wholly original nineteenth-century interior, with 1890s mahogany paneling in a twenty-five-by-forty-one-foot dining room, and walk-in safes and coal bins untouched for generations. The Fabbris left after only a year, preferring the more bucolic Carnegie Hill.

script_body: A few doors from the Fabbri Mansion, at 5 East Sixty-second Street, is the Fifth Avenue Synagogue, with mid-1950s cat's-eye windows of elliptical stained glass. The architect, Percival Goodman, met the challenge of the narrow lot through the traditional Sephardic layout, which calls for a bimah and ark in a clear central area with facing sections of worshipers — a centralized plan that, unlike the more common arrangement where rabbi and cantor face the audience from the front, lets congregants better hear the service. Goodman, brother of the social critic Paul Goodman with whom he wrote Communitas, designed more than fifty synagogues in all.

script_body: The Knickerbocker Club, on the southeast corner of Fifth Avenue and Sixty-second Street, was founded in 1871 as a reaction to the eased entry requirements at other clubs. It was Washington Irving who coined the word knickerbocker for New York's most socially prominent families — those who could trace their line to the original Dutch settlers — in his 1809 comic history, A History of New York, attributed to the imaginary Dutch-American scholar "Dietrich Knickerbocker." The book became part of New York folklore. Among the club's founders were Alexander Hamilton's grandson, John Jacob Astor, and Moses Lazarus, father of Emma Lazarus.

script_body: The apartment house at 810 Fifth, greeting you with a grand iron marquee, was laid out with just one apartment per floor at an average of five thousand square feet. Its best-known resident to New Yorkers was former governor Nelson Rockefeller, who was so charmed by the building that he lived here with both his first and second wives. In 1963, Richard Nixon bought the fifth-floor apartment, shortly after Nelson and his second wife, Happy, moved in. Five years later the two men were dueling Republican candidates for the nomination — and during the battle they used different elevators to reach their respective apartments.

script_body: Just inside Central Park at Sixty-fourth Street stands the Arsenal, built 1848 to 1851 — one of only two structures in the park that predate the park itself. When built it housed the majority of New York State's ammunition during the war with Mexico, set deliberately four miles from City Hall as a safety measure. During the Civil War it served as a bunkhouse for Union troops, and later became, in turn, the city's Museum of Natural History, park headquarters, a police station, and a weather observatory; since 1934 it has housed the city's Parks headquarters. Look for the eagle over the door and the pyramids of cannonballs on the facade.

script_body: The famous Wildenstein Gallery, at 19 East Sixty-fourth Street, was founded in Paris in 1875 by Nathan Wildenstein, who left his native Alsace after the Franco-Prussian War to remain a French citizen. Raphael's Madonna and Child and Van Gogh's Entrance to the Public Garden at Arles are but two of the thousands of works sold over the years to major museums and collectors. The building itself was built in 1932 by Horace Trumbauer with Julian Abele — one of the few Black architects working in a major firm at that time, and the lead architect of the Duke University campus in North Carolina.

script_body: The Seventh Regiment Armory, built by Charles Clinton in 1877 to 1880, is the only serious holdover from when the New York Central Railroad came barreling down Fourth Avenue. The socially prominent Seventh Regiment had formed in 1806 and, in 1824, became the first regiment to adopt the term National Guard; in 1874 the city leased this site to it, and the regiment raised the money for a monumental new armory. This extravagantly turreted red brick and brownstone structure became the prototype for the medieval-inspired armories built across New York for the next fifty years. The wealth of the regiment shows in its interiors: Louis Tiffany, Stanford White, and the Herter Brothers all worked on rooms here, and all ten companies hired the foremost New York design firms for their second-floor company rooms, fitted out with Renaissance woodwork, ornamented piano alcoves, stained glass, and parquet floors. The drill room — two hundred by three hundred feet and one hundred feet high — is one of the largest unobstructed spaces in New York. And the building is still a living, breathing armory, where you'll often see National Guardsmen amid Sunday-afternoon antique enthusiasts.

script_body: Sara Roosevelt, mother of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, commissioned Charles Adams Platt to design the twin buildings at 47–49 East Sixty-fifth Street in 1907, shortly after FDR married Eleanor — a wedding present. The two homes share a single entranceway and have interconnecting doors, though Eleanor was not fond of Sara's penchant for bursting in, as she often did. Franklin and Eleanor lived here on and off for some twenty years, and it was in the fourth-floor bedroom that FDR convalesced from polio in 1921 and 1922. After Sara's death in 1941, the building was purchased for use by Hunter College.

script_body: Temple Emanu-El, at 840 Fifth Avenue on the corner of Sixty-fifth Street, is the largest Reform synagogue in the world, edging out the Dohány synagogue in Budapest. The congregation, formed in 1845, joined with Temple Beth-El in 1927. On this very site once stood Richard Morris Hunt's double-size mansion for the Mrs. Astor — Caroline Schermerhorn Astor — and, alongside it, the home of her son John Jacob Astor; both masterpieces came down to make way for the synagogue. Built in a Byzantine and Romanesque style that mixes western European and Near Eastern forms, the building is particularly expressive of the Jewish diaspora. Its main sanctuary rises to a hundred and three feet — St. Patrick's Cathedral, by contrast, is a hundred and eight — and the auditorium runs a hundred and fifty feet long. The side walls are among the largest load-bearing masonry walls anywhere, carrying huge transverse steel beams. Step inside at 1 East Sixty-fifth Street: the rose window, stained glass, mosaics, and marble podium are otherworldly.

script_body: The Frick Collection, at 1 East Seventieth Street, is the Indiana-limestone former home of art collector, coal magnate, and union buster Henry Clay Frick, designed by Carrère & Hastings, architects of the New York Public Library. Frick is infamous for helping instigate the 1892 crackdown on the Homestead strikers at the Carnegie Steel plant; he was also fearful that the Pittsburgh fumes would tarnish his prized works. John Russell Pope turned the building into a museum in the 1930s, and the central court with its fountain is one of the city's finest public spaces. The galleries hold Vermeers, Rembrandts, Titians, and Bellinis — and by the gallery's charter, nothing travels.

script_body: Directly opposite the Frick, between Seventieth and Seventy-first Streets, stands the Richard Morris Hunt Memorial, commemorating one of America's most influential architects. Hunt is known for the base of the Statue of Liberty, the Fifth Avenue facade of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and numerous mansions; he was also the first American trained at the École des Beaux Arts in Paris. Colleagues erected this monument in 1898, and Daniel Chester French, of Lincoln Memorial fame, sculpted the bronze bust and the two female figures — the left representing Art, the right Architecture. The figure on the right holds a replica of one of Hunt's buildings from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, the "White City."

script_body: On the northeast corner of Sixty-ninth Street and Park Avenue, at 701 Park, is the prestigious Union Club. Founded in 1836 by men from the top echelons of New York's upper crust, it is the city's oldest social club — and the very one that kept out J. P. Morgan's comrades. Many of the younger clubs in the city descend from it. One in particular, the Union League Club, was founded by Republicans who left the Union Club in 1863, incensed by its failure to expel Confederate sympathizers. Morgan, we now see, was not alone in his grievance.

script_body: The Asia Society, on the northeast corner of Park and Seventieth Street, was founded in 1956 by John D. Rockefeller III to foster understanding between Asians and Americans — and to house his massive Asian art collection. Asia House on East Sixty-fourth Street was its first home; in 1981 the Society moved here, into a building of red sandstone from Rajasthan, India and polished granite from Oklahoma, the combination of stones itself meant to illustrate the cooperation between Asia and America.

script_body: The radio- and television-broadcasting pioneer David Sarnoff lived in the six-story, thirty-room townhouse at 44 East Seventy-first Street until his death in 1971, having risen from a five-dollar-and-fifty-cent-a-week office boy to chairman of RCA and later NBC. On April 14, 1912, Sarnoff was working the Marconi station atop Wanamaker's department store on Eighth Street when he picked up a relayed message: "S.S. Titanic ran into iceberg, sinking fast." For the next seventy-two hours, the story goes, he stayed at his post, giving the world its first authentic news of the disaster.

script_body: The Gertrude Rhinelander House, now Polo Ralph Lauren, stands at 867 Madison on the corner of Seventy-second Street. The Rhinelanders made their fortune in colonial-era sugar; their Rhinelander Sugar House, behind the present Municipal Building downtown, became a brutal prison for American soldiers during the British occupation of 1776 to 1783. Gertrude herself never got to live here — her husband died while it was being built, and she couldn't afford to keep it.

script_body: Across Madison Avenue stands the imposing, perhaps out-of-place Whitney Museum of American Art, designed by Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer and built between 1963 and 1966. It houses the twentieth-century collection of Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, great-granddaughter of Cornelius "Commodore" Vanderbilt. A sculptor and patron, Whitney bought and exhibited John Sloan, Edward Hopper, and Stuart Davis early in their careers. By 1929 her collection ran to hundreds of master works, and she offered it to the Metropolitan Museum of Art — which declined. So she set up her own museum, placing primacy on latter-day artists.

By 1929 her collection contained hundreds of twentieth-century master works. At that time she approached the Metropolitan Museum of Art to see if they had interest in permanently exhibiting her collection; the Met declined her offer. script_body: In 1658, a group of Dutch farmers settled in northern Manhattan, in a landscape that reminded them of the Holland town of Haarlem. They christened their new settlement 'Nieuw Haarlem' — then a distant nine miles from New York City, which clustered around the southern tip of the island. The name was Anglicized after Dutch rule ceded to the British in 1664. During the eighteenth century, elite New Yorkers established country estates and working farms here; one such estate belonged to Alexander Hamilton, who gave his name to the neighborhood of Hamilton Heights, and whose home, Hamilton Grange, still stands as a monument to the area's colonial past.

Their new settlement, which they christened “Nieuw Haarlem,” was a distant nine miles away from New York City, which was then clustered around the southern tip of Manhattan Island. (The name was Anglicized after Dutch rule ceded to British in 1664.) One such estate was owned by Alexander Hamilton, who gave his name to the neighborhood Hamilton Heights, which was once his land. script_body: The extension of the subway up Lenox Avenue in 1904 set off a wave of speculative building in Harlem, especially above 130th Street. Real estate developers overbuilt — and simply could not fill their properties. That depressed market coincided with a major influx of African Americans to New York. Southern blacks, fleeing racial violence and seeking economic opportunity, migrated en masse to northern cities, while African Americans were being squeezed out of their neighborhoods on the west side of Midtown. For years, white developers, pressured by white Harlemites, had refused to rent or sell to blacks. But empty buildings and the urging of black entrepreneurs eventually convinced them to change their policies, and in the first decade of the twentieth century the Harlem housing market was opened to blacks. When efforts to stem the tide of black in-migration failed, most white Harlemites moved out. By the 1920s, Harlem above 125th Street was the undisputed capital of Afro-America — home to its political institutions, its legendary nightlife, and the outpouring of arts and letters known as the Harlem Renaissance.

At the same time, African Americans were being squeezed out of their neighborhoods on the west side of Midtown Manhattan. By the 1920s, Harlem, especially above 125th Street, was the undisputed capital of Afro-America, home to its political institutions and cultural life.

script_body: Listen to the street names around you. After the civil rights movement of the 1960s, many of Harlem's streets were renamed to honor prominent African Americans. Eighth Avenue became Frederick Douglass Boulevard; Seventh Avenue became Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard; and Sixth Avenue, originally named Lenox Avenue, became Malcolm X Boulevard — while 125th Street was renamed for Martin Luther King, Jr. The old names and the new names still coexist on signs and in conversation throughout the neighborhood.

script_body: The row of tenement houses at Nos. 107-145 on the north side of the street was built in 1905 for middle-class and ambitious working-class whites, but the early-century real estate depression left many apartments vacant, and the owner refused to rent to African Americans. When St. Philip's Episcopal Church, a black congregation from the Tenderloin, decided to move to Harlem in 1911, it bought these tenements. Its pastor, the Reverend Hutchens Bishop — a light-skinned man — was able to purchase the real estate because the developers who sold it to him thought he was white. With that transaction, the color line west of Lenox Avenue was broken, paving the way for the development of Black Harlem.

script_body: This intersection of 135th Street and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard was the institutional hub of Harlem during the 1920s and 1930s. Within a stone's throw, one could find the headquarters of the NAACP, the National Urban League, and Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association. Close by were the offices of the major black newspapers — the conservative Amsterdam News and the more militant New York Age — along with the New York Public Library and the YMCA. By 1920, Harlem had become New York's primary African American neighborhood, and most black political and social institutions had moved here.

script_body: The YMCA at 181 West 135th Street was founded in 1851 to give moral and spiritual guidance to young male migrants from rural areas — but its membership and outreach were restricted to white men until 1867. A 'colored men's branch' opened on West Fifty-third Street in 1900 to serve migrants from the South, and moved to this location in 1919. Demand was so great that an annex was built across the street in 1932. This branch also served as a hotel for black visitors denied access to the segregated hotels elsewhere in the city.

script_body: During the Harlem Renaissance, the literati met inside this YMCA to exchange ideas — among its guests were Ralph Ellison, Langston Hughes, and James Baldwin. The Y's Little Theater program launched the careers of actors such as Sidney Poitier, Eartha Kitt, Cicely Tyson, and Danny Glover. Other patrons who went on to prominence included Jackie Robinson, Richard Wright, Paul Robeson, Jesse Owens, Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson, and Willie Mays.

script_body: On the southwest corner of 135th Street, at 2294½ Adam Clayton Powell, Jr. Boulevard — now an empty building — stood Ed Small's Paradise, one of Harlem's most popular jazz clubs and restaurants from the 1920s to the 1940s. Those who could afford the prices at the 'Hottest Spot in Harlem' were treated to music, elaborate floor shows, and singing waiters. The dance floor got so crowded that each patron was said to have a dime's worth of floor space for dancing. A young Malcolm Little, after losing his job as a waiter here, began a downward spiral into criminality that eventually landed him in jail — where he converted to Islam and changed his name to Malcolm X. In the 1960s, basketball star Wilt Chamberlain reopened the restaurant as Big Wilt's Small's Paradise.

script_body: Across the street stood 220 West 135th Street, the former home of Florence Mills, one of the most popular singers and dancers of the 1920s. An international star, Mills performed on Broadway and abroad. Hoping that her success would make 'people think better of other colored folk,' she passed over an offer to perform in the Ziegfeld Follies in order to join an all-black revue, paving the way for entertainers like Josephine Baker. She died of appendicitis in 1927, at the age of thirty-one. Her funeral was the largest in Harlem's history: more than 5,000 mourners filled Harlem's Mother Zion AME Church, and more than 150,000 followed the funeral cortege through the streets. At the cemetery, a low-flying plane released a flock of blackbirds as a final goodbye.

script_body: Right next door, 224 West 135th Street — now Flo's Beauty Salon — was the former headquarters of the NAACP. Formed in 1909, the interracial organization fought through judicial and legislative channels for voting rights, integration, and equal opportunity. Its monthly publication, The Crisis, edited by W. E. B. Du Bois from 1909 to 1934, had a circulation of more than one hundred thousand by 1920. The NAACP's Legal Defense and Education Fund, established in 1939, would go on to try the landmark Brown v. Board of Education case of 1954: Legal Director Thurgood Marshall's argument before the Supreme Court led to nationwide school integration and sparked the legal phase of the civil rights movement. In 1965, Marshall became the first African American justice appointed to the United States Supreme Court.

Du Bois from 1909 to 1934, The Crisis was one of many important periodicals produced in Harlem in the early twentieth century. The NAACP’s Legal Defense and Education Fund, established in 1939, would go on to try the landmark Brown vs. Board of Education case of 1954. Legal Director Thurgood Marshall’s argument before the Supreme Court led to nationwide school integration and sparked the legal phase of the civil rights movement. In 1965, Marshall became the first African American justice to be appointed to the United States Supreme Court.

script_body: One of the most important literary sites on this block, 267 West 136th Street, is now a parking lot. During the 1920s, this boarding house was occupied entirely by the vanguard wing of the Harlem Renaissance: Zora Neale Hurston, Langston Hughes, painters Bruce Nugent and Aaron Douglas, and novelist Wallace Thurman — the de facto leader of the radical group — all called '267 House' home. Far more interested in bohemian themes than racial ones, Thurman resisted the idea that African American artists had to represent their race in their art, and mocked the Renaissance leaders who believed civil rights would be won through cultural production. Thurman and Hurston called such figures 'the Niggerati,' and the radical residents self-deprecatingly nicknamed their boarding home 'Niggerati Manor.'

script_body: The Harlem Renaissance was not a spontaneous burst of artistic expression — in many ways it was a political movement. Black intellectuals such as W. E. B. Du Bois, Charles Johnson, and Alain Locke promoted the notion that African Americans could gain equality and respect through arts and letters; when white Americans saw the cultural contributions of African Americans, they argued, they would naturally see blacks as their equals. The stakes were high in the 1920s, a nadir in American race relations: lynching was epidemic, and the summer of 1919 saw so many bloody anti-black riots across the country that it became known as the 'Red Summer.' Civil rights organizations joined black and white philanthropists in funding the work; The Crisis and Opportunity, the magazines of the NAACP and Urban League, sponsored literary contests. Yet while the writers and artists were black, the publishers and patrons were almost entirely white — a dichotomy that led many to argue the Renaissance catered to a 'white' view of black aesthetic forms.

The belief was cultural contribution would win equality and respect
The 1920s were a nadir; lynching epidemic; 1919's 'Red Summer' saw many anti-black riots
The Crisis and Opportunity sponsored literary contests; patrons were almost entirely white
source_passage: The Harlem Renaissance was not a spontaneous burst of artistic expression. In many ways it was a political movement. Black intellectuals such as W. E. B. Du Bois, Charles Johnson, and Alain Locke promoted the notion that African Americans could gain equality and respect through arts and letters. The stakes were particularly high in the 1920s, a nadir in American race relations. Lynching was epidemic; economic and educational opportunities remained closed to African Americans; and the summer of 1919 saw so many bloody race riots across the country that it became known as the “Red Summer.” The Crisis and Opportunity, the magazines of the NAACP and Urban League, sponsored literary contests. Yet, while the writers and artists were black, the publishers and patrons were almost entirely white. This dichotomy led many to argue that the Harlem Renaissance did not produce a “true” black form of expression.

script_body: For a brief period in the 1930s, 239 West 136th Street was the headquarters of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. At the time, virtually all railroad porters were black men, for whom these jobs were high-status positions leading to a middle-class lifestyle. Led by A. Philip Randolph, the Brotherhood was the nation's first African American labor union, and its most significant campaign was its struggle — won finally in 1937 — to gain official recognition from the Pullman Company.

script_body: The area bounded by 138th and 139th Streets and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., and Frederick Douglass Boulevards is the St. Nicholas Historic District. Originally the King Model Houses, these brownstones and apartment buildings were the project of developer David H. King, who in 1890 bought the large plot from the Equitable Life Assurance Company and commissioned three prominent architectural firms to design affordable, attractive homes for white middle-class New Yorkers. The result is some of the loveliest residential streets in the city — and the alleys running between and behind the buildings, where garbage and delivery vehicles are diverted, are a rarity in New York, leaving the streets relatively free of congestion, noise, and dirt.

script_body: Because of the economic depression of the 1890s, King managed to sell only nine of the 146 rowhouses and three apartment buildings before Equitable foreclosed in 1895 and took over. In the 1920s, after restricting them to whites for years, Equitable began selling the buildings to African Americans. Some black professionals bought homes here, but most owners were members of the black working class — laundresses, railroad porters, hairdressers, domestic servants, elevator operators — who converted many of the homes into rooming houses. During this period the streets became known as 'Strivers' Row,' reflecting the ambition of those who managed to reside here. As you walk, notice the signs on the gateposts still asking you to 'Walk Your Horses.'

script_body: You are standing at the eastern edge of Sugar Hill. If Strivers' Row was for those working hard to make it, Sugar Hill was for those who had succeeded. Its exquisite rowhouses and apartment buildings were originally occupied by white professionals, but as the boundaries of Black Harlem pushed outward, whites fled and wealthy blacks moved in. 'Sugar' was slang for money, found in abundance here, and it gave the neighborhood its nickname in the 1920s. Wealthy denizens included Lena Horne, socialite A'Lelia Walker Robinson, and NAACP officers W. E. B. Du Bois, Walter White, Thurgood Marshall, and Roy Wilkins. In the 1980s, the rap band the Sugarhill Gang made the neighborhood a household name with 'Rapper's Delight,' the first rap song to cross over to the pop charts. Sugar Hill is part of Hamilton Heights, once the country estate of Alexander Hamilton.

script_body: Looking west and up the hill from the corner, you'll notice an impressive Gothic building with white trim. This is Shepard Hall, the main building of the City College of New York, one of the nineteen colleges of the City University of New York system. Established in 1847 as the Free Academy, CCNY has historically provided educational opportunities for immigrant workers and their children; after World War I it gained a reputation for excellence and was known for a time as the 'People's Harvard.' When CCNY moved to this location in 1902, the city was building the subway system, and the Manhattan schist excavated for it — the bedrock of Manhattan Island — was used to construct Shepard Hall and other CCNY buildings.

script_body: On the southeast corner — formerly 2341-2359 Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard — stood the original Renaissance Theater, Ballroom, and Casino, known locally as 'the Renny.' From the 1920s to the 1950s it was one of Harlem's most popular nightclubs, and it was home to the Rennies, the nation's first all-black professional basketball team, founded in 1923. Professional basketball was segregated in the early twentieth century, but the Rennies were known during the 1930s as the best team in the world. When they stopped playing in 1940, they had an astounding record of 2,558 wins and only 592 losses.

script_body: At 136-142 West 138th Street stands Abyssinian Baptist Church, one of the oldest and largest Protestant churches in the United States. In 1808, a group of free blacks protesting segregated seating in the First Baptist Church of New York City formed Abyssinian together with a group of Ethiopian merchants. After homes on Worth Street, Waverly Place, and West Fortieth Street, the Reverend Adam Clayton Powell Sr., pastor from 1908, raised money to move the church to this location in 1920. By 1937, when Powell turned the pulpit over to his son Adam Clayton Powell Jr., the congregation had seven thousand members, making it the largest Protestant congregation in the country. Powell Jr. continued his father's civil rights tradition, serving as pastor while becoming the first African American congressman, representing Harlem in the U.S. House from 1944 to 1970.

script_body: In the 1920s, 120 West 138th Street was the site of Liberty Hall, the Harlem headquarters of Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association. A flamboyant and extremely popular figure who arrived from Jamaica in 1917, Garvey reminds us of the central role West Indian immigrants played in Harlem life. Initially influenced by Booker T. Washington's self-help doctrines, Garvey became a proponent of black pride and pan-Africanism. The UNIA appealed, unlike other civil rights organizations, to the Southern migrants and Caribbean immigrants who made up the black working class; its Harlem branch, the country's largest, had more than forty thousand members. Garvey's stance made him enemies among other black leaders, including A. Philip Randolph and W. E. B. Du Bois. Arrested on trumped-up charges of mail fraud in 1923 and convicted in 1927, he was deported to Jamaica — but he left a strong legacy that would influence the black nationalist movements of the 1960s and 1970s.

source_passage: In the 1920s, 120 West 138th Street was the site of Liberty Hall, the Harlem headquarters of Marcus Garvey’s Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA). Garvey was a flamboyant, charismatic, and extremely popular figure who arrived in New York from Jamaica in 1917. Initially influenced by the self-help doctrines and racial accommodationist stance of Booker T. Washington, Garvey became a proponent of black pride and pan-Africanism. The UNIA, an international organization, had a huge national membership, appealing, unlike other civil rights organizations, to the Southern migrants and Caribbean immigrants who made up the black working class. The Harlem branch of the UNIA, the country’s largest, had more than forty thousand members. Garvey’s political activities and stance made him enemies among other black leaders, including A. Philip Randolph, James Weldon Johnson, and W. E. B. Du Bois. Arrested on trumped-up charges of mail fraud in 1923, Garvey was convicted in 1927. His subsequent deportation to Jamaica effectively ended his activities in the United States. But Garvey left a strong legacy behind and would eventually prove a major influence on the black nationalist movements of the 1960s and 1970s.

script_body: Lenox Avenue was the site of all the major parades through Harlem in the early twentieth century. In July 1917, W. E. B. Du Bois, James Weldon Johnson, and other NAACP officers led ten thousand people down the avenue in a solemn protest march. Three weeks before, in East St. Louis, Illinois, nearly two hundred African Americans had died and six thousand had been burned out of their homes in the worst race riot in American history. The Harlem protesters walked in silence, bearing signs that read 'Thou Shalt Not Kill' and 'Mr. President, Why Not Make America Safe for Democracy?' The hypocrisy of a government fighting a war abroad in the name of liberty while refusing civil rights at home led many African Americans to question whether they should participate in World War I.

script_body: Black Americans did fight in World War I, and the 369th Regiment, an all-black unit from Harlem, became the most highly decorated American unit and the only one awarded the French croix de guerre. Known as the 'Harlem Hellfighters,' the 369th returned home triumphantly in February 1919 to a parade through Manhattan; when they crossed 110th Street and turned onto Lenox Avenue, the parade became a party as they were greeted by friends, family, and great cheers. Black soldiers had found better treatment abroad than at home, and many returned with a more militant stance — the 'New Negro' that Alain Locke would name in his 1925 essay.

script_body: The Countee Cullen Branch of the New York Public Library, at 104 West 136th, stands on the site of the former home of Madame C. J. Walker, the richest self-made woman in early twentieth-century America. Born in the South, Walker made her fortune developing and selling hair straighteners, skin lighteners, and other beauty products for African American women. In 1916, already wealthy, she moved to New York and built a home, beauty salon, and school here. She was active in politics and civil rights too, leading a delegation of women to see President Woodrow Wilson to protest segregation in the military, and giving significant sums to charities and civil rights organizations.

script_body: Walker's daughter, A'Lelia Walker Robinson, was famous for her lavish lifestyle and elaborate parties, hosting salons for literary figures of the Harlem Renaissance. At perhaps her most legendary party, she served African Americans caviar and champagne while whites, seated at a separate table, received chit'lins and bathtub gin. In 1927 she converted one floor of this home into the 'Dark Tower,' a coffeehouse where artists could gather — but it filled so quickly with wealthy and prominent New Yorkers that the bohemians it was meant for could barely fit, and the prices were out of their reach. Langston Hughes claimed that, more than any other event, her death in 1931 marked the end of the Harlem Renaissance.

source_passage: Her daughter A’Lelia Walker Robinson was known for her lavish lifestyle and elaborate parties. She hosted salons for literary figures of the Harlem Renaissance and fetes for diverse guests. Perhaps her most legendary party was when she served African Americans caviar and champagne while whites, seated at a separate table, received chit’lins and bathtub gin. In 1927 she converted one floor of this home into the “Dark Tower,” a coffeehouse where artists could gather around inexpensive refreshments and exchange ideas. But the bohemian types for whom the place was originally intended could barely fit in the room, so full was it of wealthy and prominent New Yorkers, and the prices were well out of reach for any but the latter. Langston Hughes claimed that, more than any other event, her death in 1931 marked the end of the Harlem Renaissance.

poi_name: Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture
script_body: On the northwest corner of 135th and Lenox stands the New York Public Library's Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, the premier research library for black history and culture. Arturo Schomburg, a Puerto Rican black, spent his life amassing a huge collection of books, pamphlets, manuscripts, and visual materials pertaining to the African and African American past. He began the endeavor in response to an elementary school teacher who claimed blacks had produced nothing worth studying — and proved him wrong. When the New York Public Library purchased Schomburg's collection in 1926, it held five thousand items; it now has over five million. Schomburg himself played a major role in the Harlem Renaissance, sponsoring readings and literary salons and serving as curator of his collection for the library.

script_body: You are standing on an important speakers' corner for soapbox orators of the early twentieth century. Legend has it that Marcus Garvey, on arriving in Harlem, stole the soapbox here from A. Philip Randolph; both men were frequently seen and heard at this corner, which was also the first view of Harlem for most Southern migrants — from Penn Station, they took the IRT to 135th and Lenox and exited the subway into another world. If they craved a reminder of home, they could stop at the stand of Pig Foot Mary on the southeast corner. Born Lillian Harris, she sold Southern-style comfort food like pig's feet and chit'lins; starting with three dollars and a folding table, Harris eventually made enough to become a major real estate investor and Harlem philanthropist.

trigger_address: 133rd Street between Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard and Lenox Avenue
script_body: The block of 133rd Street between Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard and Lenox Avenue was known in the 1920s, 1930s, and 1940s as 'Jungle Alley.' Here, downtown whites attracted to Harlem nightlife could live out exoticized fantasies of black culture — scantily clad women gyrating on stage to heavy percussion amid jungle decor. Many clubs, such as the Cotton Club and Connie's Inn, both since demolished, refused service to blacks, including the very entertainers who performed on their stages. But most clubs along Jungle Alley catered to a mixed clientele, and unlike the Cotton Club and Connie's, some were owned by black proprietors. Still, they all sold a white-inspired view of a primitive, exotic Black America that bore little resemblance to the reality at neighborhood joints like Small's Paradise and the Renny.

script_body: Williams Christian Methodist Church, at 2225 on the east side of Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard, is the former site of the Lafayette Theater. Opened in 1912, the Lafayette was one of the few integrated theaters in New York City and one of the few venues where blacks could perform in serious roles. During the 1930s it became the Harlem headquarters of the New Deal's Federal Theater Project, whose most notorious production was the 'Voodoo Macbeth' — directed by Orson Welles with an all-black cast, integrating African elements into the Shakespeare classic.

source_passage: Williams Christian Methodist Church, located at 2225 on the east side of Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard, is the former site of the Lafayette Theater. Opened in 1912, the Lafayette was one of the few integrated theaters in New York City. While the theater presented the same minstrel-style, all-black revues popular elsewhere, it did provide, in the early twentieth century, one of the few venues where blacks could perform in serious roles as well. During the 1930s, this was the Harlem headquarters of the Federal Theater Project of the New Deal’s Works Progress Administration. Its most notorious production was the “Voodoo Macbeth.” Directed by Orson Welles and featuring an all-black cast, this rendition integrated African elements into the Shakespeare classic.

trigger_address: Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard median near 132nd Street
script_body: Look south toward 125th Street: the sculpture on the median of Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard symbolizes the 'Tree of Hope.' The original tree, which stood in front of the Lafayette, was rumored to have magical powers, bringing employment to out-of-work actors who rubbed its bark. It became a real gathering place — casting agents looking for entertainers could find them in droves in front of the Lafayette — so the tree did, in a sense, fulfill its promise. The original oak was cut down in 1934, and this interpretive sculpture was erected in 1972. A piece of the original remains on the stage of the Apollo Theater, where amateur-night performers rub its bark for luck before going on.

script_body: You are in Harlem's central commercial district. In the early twentieth century, black-owned businesses clustered around 135th Street, but on 125th, all the stores were white-owned. The owners resisted Harlem's development as a black neighborhood and most refused to hire black workers through the 1930s, even though their clientele was almost entirely black. Even today, few of the businesses on 125th Street are owned by African Americans. In the 1960s, banks and insurance companies 'red-lined' the area, refusing to lend to anyone wanting to open a business in Harlem. Given that history, many community leaders welcomed the influx of major corporations to 125th Street in the 1990s — Pathmark, the first large supermarket to open in Harlem, along with Starbucks, Old Navy, and Harlem USA, a mall and movie multiplex backed by basketball star Magic Johnson. Some feared the impact of this corporate invasion; many welcomed the lower prices, jobs, and renewed confidence in the neighborhood's future.

script_body: The tall white building on the southwest corner of 125th Street and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard is the landmarked Hotel Theresa, now an office building. When it opened in 1913 it catered to a white-only clientele, but in 1937 a black entrepreneur bought it and overturned the segregationist policies. Because posh downtown hotels refused service to blacks, the Theresa became known as the 'Waldorf of Harlem.' In 1960, Fidel Castro, in town to visit the United Nations, stayed here to show solidarity with black Americans. The hotel also housed political organizations: A. Philip Randolph's 1941 March on Washington movement was coordinated here, pushing President Franklin Roosevelt to integrate defense industries during World War II, and in the 1960s, after his break from the Nation of Islam, Malcolm X established the Organization of Afro-American Unity at the Theresa — gathering crowds outside the building to hear him speak.

script_body: The old Blumstein's Department Store at 230 West 125th Street — now subdivided into smaller ground-level stores — once refused, like most stores on the block, to hire black workers in any but the most lowly positions, despite an almost entirely African American clientele. That was especially galling during the Great Depression, when Harlem's unemployment far exceeded the rest of the city's. In 1934, Adam Clayton Powell Jr. and other black leaders targeted Blumstein's in a boycott and picketing campaign under the slogan 'Don't buy where you can't work,' eventually forcing the largest department store in Harlem to hire black clerks. In time, Blumstein's would be the first department store to have a black Santa Claus.

script_body: Stop at the Apollo Theater at 253 West 125th Street. The burlesque house that opened here in 1914 initially refused admission to blacks, but in 1934 the former owners of the Lafayette Theater bought the Apollo and integrated it. It has since become the premier showcase of black talent in the United States — virtually every black American entertainer of note has performed on its stage. In the 1930s and 1940s audiences enjoyed dancer Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson; singers Bessie Smith, Billie Holiday, and Ethel Waters; and bandleaders such as Duke Ellington backed by costumed chorus girls. Wednesday amateur nights, an Apollo tradition since the 1930s and televised nationally since the early 1990s, have discovered greats like Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan, and James Brown. But the notoriously tough Apollo audience is no sure predictor: multiple-Grammy-winner Lauryn Hill was booed off the stage.

script_body: Before there was an English presence in New York, there was an African one: Dutch settlers brought African slaves to New Amsterdam as early as 1644. As late as 1760 the city had the highest number of blacks of any urban area in the colonies, and people of African descent made up at least 15 percent of the population before the Revolutionary War. As the center of population moved up Manhattan, African Americans were pushed to the periphery, forming one 'Little Africa' after another — in the Wall Street area, Greenwich Village, the Tenderloin in the West Thirties, and San Juan Hill in the West Fifties. The mechanization of Southern agriculture, antiblack violence, and roughly forty thousand West Indian immigrants in the 1920s swelled New York's black population from about 60,000 in 1900 to over 320,000 by 1930. Landlords' greed eventually trumped their racism: recognizing they could charge African Americans well above market value, they opened Harlem's empty buildings, and by 1920, 70 percent of New York City's blacks lived in Harlem.

People of African descent comprised at least 15 percent of the city’s population before the Revolutionary War. As the center of population moved up Manhattan Island, African Americans were pushed out of their neighborhoods and forced to the periphery, where one “Little Africa” after another was formed. Joining the Southern migrants, particularly during the 1920s, were forty thousand black immigrants from the West Indies. The black population of New York City, about 60,000 in 1900, had jumped to over 320,000 by 1930. By 1920, 70 percent of New York City’s blacks lived in Harlem.

script_body: When Green-Wood was chartered on April 18, 1838, Manhattan's churchyard cemeteries were filling fast and the island was running out of room, while newly incorporated Brooklyn had fewer than sixteen thousand residents and an abundance of unused land. The story begins with Henry Evelyn Pierrepont, scion of one of Brooklyn's most prominent families, who visited Cambridge, Massachusetts, to study the newly opened Mount Auburn Cemetery — the first planned, nondenominational, rural cemetery in America. He toured Europe looking for a model, and returned with an image of a sprawling garden cemetery for Manhattan. His idea was dismissed as a waste of valuable real estate. So he turned to Brooklyn, where he saw the chance to build a city like the great cities of Europe, with wide promenades, public squares, and a grand cemetery. When the City of Brooklyn began laying out its streets in 1835, it made no provision for a cemetery at all. Pierrepont gathered citizens who petitioned the state legislature for a charter, and the Hills of Gowanus, where you now stand, were selected as the site. Within a year the Green-Wood Corporation purchased nearly two hundred acres of grazing land at $750 per acre — a total of $134,650 — from the Wyckoff, Ibbotson, Dean, Sackett, Schermerhorn, Bennett, and Bergen families.

source_passage: When Green-Wood Cemetery was chartered on April 18, 1838, New York City was already the commercial and financial center of America and, with a population of more than three hundred thousand, its largest city. Manhattan churchyard cemeteries were rapidly filling and the island was quickly running out of available space. But newly incorporated Brooklyn had fewer than sixteen thousand residents and an abundance of unused land. Our story begins when Henry Evelyn Pierrepont (1808–1888), scion of one of Brooklyn's most prominent families, visited Cambridge, Massachusetts, to study the newly opened Mount Auburn Cemetery, the first planned, nondenominational, rural cemetery in America. He then toured Europe, looking for a cemetery model to bring to Manhattan. Pierrepont returned from Europe with an image of a sprawling garden cemetery for Manhattan. His idea was dismissed as a waste of valuable real estate. He turned to Brooklyn and saw the opportunity to create a city like the great cities of Europe—with wide promenades, public squares, and a grand cemetery. The Hills of Gowanus, where you now stand, were selected as the site. Within a year, the Green-Wood Corporation, organized by Pierrepont plus other prominent Brooklynites, purchased nearly two hundred acres of grazing land at $750 per acre, for a total of $134,650, from the Wyckoff, Ibbotson, Dean, Sackett, Schermerhorn, Bennett, and Bergen families.

script_body: To turn this grazing pasture into a cemetery, the corporation hired David Bates Douglass, who had served in the War of 1812 and taught mathematics and engineering at West Point, and had been chief engineer for the Croton Aqueduct System — he designed the High Bridge that still carries Croton's water across the Harlem River. One of his first tasks was to lay out 4.5 miles of road following the contours of the terrain. This route became known as "the Tour," designed to display Green-Wood's charms and to tempt potential lot buyers. The unexpected side effect: Green-Wood quickly became a major recreational and tourist destination for New Yorkers, who had almost no public parkland at all. Douglass even had songbirds imported from Europe to help set the ambiance.

source_passage: David Bates Douglass (1790–1849) was hired the next month to transform this grazing pasture into a cemetery. Douglass had served in the War of 1812 and had been a professor of mathematics and engineering at the United States Military Academy. Before working on Green-Wood, he had also been the chief engineer for the Croton Aqueduct System. Among other things he designed the High Bridge, which remains the oldest bridge still standing in the city, to transport Croton's water across the Harlem River to Manhattan. One of Douglass's first tasks was to lay out 4.5 miles of road that followed the contours of the terrain and demonstrated the beauty of the site. This route became known as "the Tour" and was designed and used not only to display Green-Wood's charms but also to serve as an incentive for potential lot buyers. One unexpected side effect of the Tour was that Green-Wood quickly became a major recreational and tourist destination for New Yorkers, who had access to almost no public parkland at all. Douglass even had songbirds imported from Europe to assist with the ambiance.
