script_body: The early years were lean: from the first interment on September 5, 1840, to the end of 1842, only 162 burials took place; by 1843 the total had crept to 352. Then 1844 brought a dramatic change — 354 people were buried in that single year and lot sales hit $20,000. Three things drove the boom: growing acceptance of nondenominational burial, an easing of the 1837 depression that left people more disposable income, and the relocation of former senator, governor, and mayor DeWitt Clinton's casket from Albany to Green-Wood, which signaled that the wealthy classes had embraced the place. By 1855, just fifteen years after the first burial, 45,576 people had been interred and over a hundred thousand visitors were coming annually.

This tremendous increase was caused by three factors: first, the growing acceptance of nondenominational burial...; second, an easing of the financial effect of the depression of 1837...; and third, the relocation of former senator, governor, and mayor DeWitt Clinton's casket from Albany to Green-Wood, which showed that the wealthy classes had accepted the place. By 1855, just fifteen years after the first interment, 45,576 persons had been buried here and over one hundred thousand local people and tourists were visiting annually.

script_body: Wary New Yorkers thought a distant cemetery seemed insecure, so Green-Wood enclosed itself with a two-mile fence. The current fence, some 21,120 feet long, went up beginning in 1860 at a cost of $40,000. Note its decorative cast-iron finials capping each post. In 2000 the cemetery launched a campaign to restore 280 missing finials — at a price near $50,000, more than the entire original fence cost.

script_body: The tour begins at the dramatic Gothic Revival gates designed by architect Richard Upjohn, built between 1861 and 1863, once Green-Wood was an established success and its trustees wanted an imposing entrance. Upjohn was one of America's most renowned nineteenth-century architects, working mainly in Greek and Gothic Revival and specializing in churches — his greatest surviving New York work is Trinity Church at Broadway and Wall Street. He later helped found the American Institute of Architects with Richard Morris Hunt. Gothic Revival was a perfect match for Green-Wood: it celebrated mystery, illusion, and the inherent irregularity of nature itself. The gates are a splendid example. The center tower stands 106 feet tall, flanked by two 90-foot peaks, the symmetry counterbalanced by office wings of differing shapes and sizes. They are built of red sandstone from Belleville, New Jersey — the same material Upjohn used for Trinity Church — and crowded with steep slate roofs, stone trefoils and quatrefoils, cast-iron bannerettes, open gables, and detailed finials. Embedded above the entranceways are four reliefs carved by John M. Moffitt in Nova Scotia yellow sandstone, symbolizing rebirth and resurrection: "Come Forth," "The Dead Shall Be Raised," "I Am the Resurrection and the Life," and "Weep Not." Higher up are smaller reliefs of Faith, Hope, Memory, and Love. In 1966 the main gates were designated a New York City landmark.

script_body: From the gates, walk toward the left, uphill onto Battle Avenue. Throughout the cemetery you'll spot small black iron street signs; with the map they help you navigate this most un-urban of settings. script_body: This tomb brings together two of the greatest artists of the late nineteenth century: it was designed by architect Stanford White, and the bronzes were created in 1883 by Augustus Saint-Gaudens. It holds Pennsylvania coal and steel magnate David Stewart, the father of Isabella Stewart Gardner, doyenne of Boston's art scene. The reliefs depict two robed angels — highly controversial at the time, because most depictions of death were gloomy and despairing, while White showed his angels as musicians, perhaps heralding the ascension to heaven. With little patience for the criticism, White wrote to Saint-Gaudens that "some people are such God damned asses they always think of death as a gloomy performance instead of a resurrection."

script_body: A few feet farther along Battle Avenue, on the other side of the road, a marble marker with a large cross carries the bronze emblem of the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. This is the grave of Louis Bonnard, a French émigré who developed and patented profitable inventions — a mechanical brick maker, a machine for molding cast iron — in the cellar workshop of his Mulberry Street tenement. As he lay near death, Bonnard became convinced he would be resurrected as an animal and could be abused. He sent for Henry Bergh, founder of the ASPCA, and promised his fortune to the newly established organization. Bergh arrived to find his benefactor living in abject poverty. Bonnard told him he was leaving everything to the ASPCA, then asked the skeptical Bergh to open a trunk in the room — and Bergh found it filled with money and jewels. Bonnard's family disputed the bequest, claiming the inventor was insane, but the courts upheld the donation, and the ASPCA became one of the best-endowed charities in New York.

script_body: This tall obelisk was erected by the City of Brooklyn to memorialize the 278 people who died in the Brooklyn Theater Fire on December 5, 1876; 103 of the victims are buried here. Theater was a main source of entertainment in nineteenth-century America, and that Tuesday evening more than a thousand patrons had gathered at the Brooklyn Theater downtown to watch star Kate Claxton in the popular Two Orphans. As the play was ending, around 11 p.m., someone told Claxton that a kerosene lamp had ignited a small fire in the scenery backstage. With the actors unsure what to do, Claxton supposedly whispered, "Go on, they will put it out, if we say anything there will be panic, go on." The fire couldn't be contained. As the audience realized, Claxton tried to reassure them — "We are between you and the flames" — but patrons fled in panic, clogging the few narrow exits. Within half an hour the roof collapsed and 278 lives were lost. The City of Brooklyn dug a seven-foot-deep, crescent-shaped common grave for the unidentified and the families who could not afford burial; 103 donated coffins were arranged with heads facing the center, and two thousand mourners attended with song, speeches, and flowers.

script_body: Kate Claxton was found the next morning, dazed and burned, wandering in Manhattan near City Hall. She claimed she could not recall how she had crossed the river — and this was years before the Brooklyn Bridge was finished. She was thereafter known as "Kate Claxton of the Big Brooklyn Fire." She kept acting until retiring in 1904, and is buried elsewhere in Green-Wood.

script_body: Across Battle Avenue from the theater-fire monument stand the graves of Henry Aaron Burr and his family. Henry Aaron Burr was the great-nephew of the infamous vice president Aaron Burr and a nephew of minister Jonathan Edwards — but he was famous in his own right as an innovator in the hat industry. After working as a bookkeeper for milliner Elisha Bloomer, Burr opened his own store across the street in 1835 and set out to perfect a machine for forming hats. After many failures he succeeded, patented it, and dramatically cut the cost of hat making; by 1856 millions of his machines were in use worldwide. The invention was so successful he was forced to sue for patent infringement fifty-six times, winning all but three. Burr was also a charter member of the Union Club and a director of the Mechanics' National Bank.

script_body: Along Syringa Path, to your left, lies the Uhl-Ottendorfer family plot. Anna and Jacob Uhl started the Staats-Zeitung — the City Paper — as a German weekly in New York in December 1834. When Jacob died in 1851, his widow Anna took over the paper, and in 1859 she married Oswald Ottendorfer, a German immigrant who had worked there over a decade. Under them the Staats-Zeitung became the preeminent German-language paper in New York, reaching a circulation of sixty-five thousand by 1880, and it ran as a daily until 1975. The Ottendorfers gave away much of their fortune to German American causes, including a free library whose building still stands on Second Avenue near Tenth Street in Manhattan. They are one of many newspaper families buried here — Henry Raymond of the Times, Horace Greeley of the Tribune, and J. Gordon Bennett of the Herald also rest in Green-Wood.

script_body: On a small grass island stands the imposing statue of DeWitt Clinton, his back to you as you approach. Clinton was a remarkable man — son of Revolutionary War general James Clinton, he chose government over the military, became personal secretary to his uncle Governor George Clinton around 1790, and within a decade was one of New York State's most powerful politicians. Appointed to the U.S. Senate in 1802, he returned the next year to serve as mayor of New York, holding that office, with two brief breaks, until 1815. As mayor he oversaw the creation of the New-York Historical Society and the Orphan Asylum, sanitation improvements, the 1811 street-grid system, and the fortification of the harbor before the War of 1812. He ran for president in 1812, losing to James Madison by a slim margin, and served three terms as governor. But he is best remembered as the "Father of the Erie Canal" for his tireless support of the project that assured New York's commercial dominance; he presided over its 1825 opening. His statue was cast by Henry Kirke Brown between 1850 and 1853, the base designed by Richard Upjohn, and was displayed in Manhattan's City Hall Park before being placed here. Two bronze reliefs on the base depict the building of the canal.

script_body: Sharing Clinton's small island of grass, a few feet to the south among the trees, is Nathaniel Currier — senior partner of the lithography firm Currier and Ives. In the second half of the nineteenth century the firm produced thousands of images for mass consumption; their work was excellent, but it was their unparalleled marketing that made them the nation's most successful lithographers. His partner, James Merritt Ives, is buried elsewhere in Green-Wood.

script_body: Opposite Clinton's tomb, a small white marble statue of a young man marks the grave of three-year-old Irwin Franklin, "Little Frankie." It was carved by the great American sculptor Daniel Chester French, best known for the seated Lincoln at the Lincoln Memorial. Frankie, who died in 1880, was the son of Rear Admiral Aaron Ward; father and son lie buried adjacent to each other. Such carving was often the "bread and butter" of master sculptors between large commissions.

script_body: Downhill off Fern Avenue stands the Greek Revival tomb of John Anderson, four columns in a style popular in antebellum America, built by Anderson himself in the early 1860s, twenty years before his death. Anderson owned a tobacco shop on Broadway across from City Hall Park, selling his "fine cut" Anderson's Solace Tobacco. In 1838 he hired an attractive young woman, Mary Cecilia Rogers, to draw young men to the shop, and she soon picked up the nickname "the Beautiful Seegar Girl." In July 1842, Mary disappeared; three days later she turned up floating in the Hudson River, and Anderson became the prime suspect. He was arrested, questioned, and immediately released, the details hushed up by influential friends in the Democratic Party — and his was the only statement among the questioned men not released to the press. The murder of Mary Rogers was one of the first crimes sensationalized by the New York papers, the Herald, Sun, and Tribune competing to spin a "real-life mystery." Rumors that she died from a botched abortion led the state senate to criminalize the practice, and the failure to solve the crime led to the Police Reform Act of 1845. Her story also became the basis for Edgar Allan Poe's The Mystery of Marie Roget. After her death Anderson gave away much of his fortune. The story outlived him: his daughter contested his will, claiming he was insane and believed Mary Rogers's ghost visited him regularly and that Garibaldi's ghost inhabited his house. A witness testified Anderson had said his house was haunted — "by people who want money." His daughter lost.

script_body: About ten feet behind the Mulberry Avenue street sign stands the grave of Colonel Abraham Vosburgh, its column carved with an eagle holding a sword — a reference to his military service — and broken, marking a life cut short. On April 22, 1861, Vosburgh marched at the head of the Seventy-first New York State National Guard toward Washington, answering Lincoln's plea to defend the capital. Without seeing any action, he died of consumption in Washington. After President Lincoln laid a wreath on his body, the colonel was returned to Brooklyn for burial. His regiment erected this monument, inscribed "Pro Patria" — For Country — originally ringed by a cast-iron fence with posts shaped like bayoneted rifles and a gate topped with a Union cap, belt, and sword. That fence has since disappeared. Vosburgh is far from the only officer here: from the Civil War alone Green-Wood holds nearly twenty generals from both sides and thirteen Medal of Honor recipients.

script_body: The Burnham burial site is a classic late nineteenth-century family plot, with a central monument crowned by an imposing statue, sculpted by John Moffitt, of a woman in classical dress holding a Bible, the whole ringed by a stone wall that replaced a decayed iron fence. Gordon W. Burnham earned his millions as president of the Waterbury Clock, Waterbury Watch, and American Pin companies. He is buried here with his first two wives. He died shortly before a third marriage: he caught a chill waiting in his unheated carriage for his fiancée Kate Sanborn's ferry, which ran an hour late; the chill became pneumonia, and he died three days before the wedding. A staunch Democrat, Burnham had delayed that wedding until after the March 4 inauguration of Grover Cleveland — so as not to be married under a Republican administration.

script_body: A short detour off Battle Avenue leads to the free-standing mausoleum of Marcus "Copper King" Daly — be sure to note the magnificent stained-glass windows at the rear. Born in Ireland, Daly came to America at fifteen with virtually no money. In 1880, after years of struggling, he scraped together enough to buy a small mine near Butte, Montana. Nominally a silver mine, in places its veins ran 55 percent copper — and Daly had hit the mother lode just as Thomas Edison was using copper to wire his new electric lights. His Anaconda Mining Company was soon joined by California financiers, and together they bought up neighboring claims until Daly's mines controlled nearly a quarter of the world's mined copper. About twenty-five miles from Butte he built the company town of Anaconda, diversified into coal and lumber, and became a millionaire several times over. Daly was deeply active in Montana Democratic politics and at constant war with his mining rival William A. Clark; the two fought with money and the press for control of the state. Clark's ambition was to become a U.S. senator; Daly's was simply to stop Clark. Clark spent $450,000 to keep the capital out of Daly's Anaconda — and he won that fight, and ultimately the Senate seat, but not until 1901, after Daly's death.

script_body: Up the steps marked "Battle Path" stands Green-Wood's Soldiers' Monument, erected in 1869 to honor the 148,000 New York men who fought "in aid of the war for the preservation of the Union and the Constitution." Built just four years after the war's end, it is far more realistic in its vision of battle than the nostalgic memorials of the 1880s and 1890s, when the blood and guts had faded from memory. Its four life-size soldiers — supposedly cast from the bronze of captured Confederate cannons — represent the Union Army. They originally held an ax, rifle, rammer, and sword, now all missing. In 1991 the four relief battle scenes on the central monument, which had been stolen, were refabricated and replaced.

source_passage: Erected in 1869, the Green-Wood Cemetery's Soldiers' Monument honors the 148,000 New York men who fought "in aid of the war for the preservation of the Union and the Constitution."... Built just four years after the end of the war, this monument is much more realistic in its vision of battle than the nostalgic memorials that were built in the 1880s and 1890s... The four life-size soldiers, supposedly cast from the bronze of captured Confederate cannons, represent the Union Army. The soldiers originally held objects (an ax, rifle, rammer, and sword) that are now missing. In 1991, the casts of the four battle scenes depicted in relief on the sides of the central monument, which had been stolen, were refabricated and replaced.

script_body: Near granite marker 18495 lies a low white gravestone whose only inscription is "Grandmother." This is the grave of Elizabeth Tilton. She had been married to Theodore Tilton and was a schoolteacher for the Reverend Henry Ward Beecher of Plymouth Church in Brooklyn Heights. She and Beecher had an affair, exposed by Victoria Woodhull; Theodore sued Beecher for "alienation of affection," and the story became national news. Beecher claimed victory with a hung jury, but the family was torn apart by the "trial of the century." Theodore left the United States in 1883 and spent his life in Paris; Elizabeth was ostracized by everyone but her daughter and a few religious friends, and died alone and blind in 1897. Her marker reads simply "Grandmother" in an attempt to keep tourists from invading her final resting place. Beecher stayed with his wife and lies in a prominent tomb elsewhere in Green-Wood.

script_body: Minerva and the Altar to Liberty, sculpted by Frederick Wellington Ruckstull, was unveiled on August 27, 1920 — the 144th anniversary of the Battle of Long Island, fought on this very spot in late August 1776. In Greek mythology Minerva, also known as Pallas Athena, whose temple is the Parthenon, sprang fully formed and armored from Zeus's head; she was the goddess of battle and protector of civilized life. The battle she marks was the first for the Continental army after the Declaration of Independence some seven weeks earlier. Two thousand American troops under Brigadier General William Alexander — called Lord Stirling by his men — fought Major General James Grant's British force three times larger. Much of the fighting swept across the ridge where you now stand, which is why it is called Battle Hill; it is said that atop this hill a group of American riflemen were surrounded, shot, and buried where they fell. The Greek Revival tomb directly behind Minerva is that of Charles M. Higgins, a Park Slope businessman and inventor of India ink, whose ambition was to build a memorial to the first battle for American freedom and who led the movement to erect the statue. This is the highest natural point in Brooklyn, 216 feet above sea level — and if you stand directly in front of Minerva, you'll see her left hand raised in salute to the Statue of Liberty, standing due west in New York harbor.

script_body: Along Liberty Path, among two evergreen shrubs to your right, are the unassuming graves of Leonard Bernstein, his wife, and his sister. Born in Lawrence, Massachusetts, Bernstein conducted the New York City Symphony Orchestra from 1945 to 1948 and was with the New York Philharmonic from 1957 until being named conductor laureate in 1969. He was the first conductor to use television successfully as a tool for music education, and a prolific composer — his best-known piece is the 1957 musical West Side Story. His grave is usually piled with small stones: it is a Jewish tradition to leave a stone when visiting, to honor the person buried, both to pay homage and to record your presence. Stones, related to the ground, last far longer than flowers.

script_body: Behind Higgins, hidden in a grove of trees, is the Edwin C. Litchfield plot. Litchfield was a prominent Brooklyn lawyer and businessman who, with his brother Electus, developed Brooklyn's street railways and the Gowanus Canal and acquired a large tract from the Cortelyou estate that they turned into Park Slope. He also played a prominent role in creating Prospect Park. In 1892, after his death, his family estate — Grace Hill — was converted into the Parks Department building inside the park and renamed Litchfield Villa in his honor. The rumor is that his grave is turned away from Park Slope, to protest the taking of his family home by the Parks Department.

script_body: At the intersection of Battle and Hemlock Avenues stands the imposing Howe family grave site, overseen by a bust of the patriarch, Elias Howe Jr. Born to a large, impoverished Massachusetts family, Howe went to work at six and never had a formal education. In 1846 he patented the first sewing machine. It was grossly inefficient, but it sewed 250 stitches a minute — five times faster than a skilled hand. Sewers and tailors fearing for their jobs met it with resistance, and manufacturers were reluctant to spend on machinery when cheap human labor was abundant. Realizing America wasn't ready, Howe went to England to market it, and returned two years later penniless — only to discover his invention had been stolen. After five years of litigation he won his patent suit, securing protection for the lockstitch formed by his eye-pointed needle and mechanical shuttle, and thereafter collected a royalty on every sewing machine made in America: his income rose from $300 a year to $200,000 — over $5 million today. Directly behind Howe is buried the family dog, Fannie, who died in 1881, her marble marker carved with a poem that begins, "Only a dog you say sir critic."

script_body: On the near right corner of the small Lake Path is the tombstone of William Kingsley, a Brooklyn contractor and one of the earliest proponents of building a bridge between Brooklyn and Manhattan. In 1865, at age thirty-two, he hired engineer Colonel Julius Walker Adams to draw up a design and cost estimates; Adams figured the bridge could be built for about $5 million. The Kingsley bridge was never built — in the end the Roebling bridge cost $15 million. Kingsley was a leader of Brooklyn's Democratic machine, and the Brooklyn Bridge project made him nearly a million dollars alone, perhaps thanks to his association with Manhattan "Boss" William M. Tweed. When the Tweed ring was broken in 1873, it emerged that Kingsley, a major stockholder and general superintendent of the project, was being paid 15 percent of total construction expenses — over $170,000 a year — a payment made, per the Bridge Company's records, at Tweed's suggestion. After Tweed's fall his salary was renegotiated to a flat $10,000; without that change he would have garnered roughly $1.75 million by the bridge's 1883 completion. Fittingly, his grave marker was cut from a granite stone taken from the Brooklyn Bridge itself, placed here by the bridge trustees to commemorate his role in making the Great Bridge a reality.

script_body: Set a few yards back from Mulberry Avenue, the white marble Culver marker depicts a shattered tree trunk hung with the trappings of youth — a stack of books, a uniform and rifle, a rope and ship's anchor. The shattered trunk symbolizes a young life abruptly ended; the books and globe, his life as a student; the Union uniform and rifle, perhaps a soldier's ambitions never realized.

script_body: Green-Wood's grave markers are a catalog of Victorian funerary art, illustrating Christian ideas of ascension, resurrection, and salvation. A few to look for: an intertwined alpha and omega — the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, from Revelation, "the beginning and the end." The phrase Fugit Hora — "the hours are fleeting," or "time flies." Animals recur: an eagle is a heavenly messenger or a sign of military service; a butterfly is Christian metamorphosis and resurrection; a lamb — purity and innocence — is the most common nineteenth-century symbol on children's graves. Among objects, the anchor is an early Christian symbol of salvation and hope, and also of death at sea; a broken column or tree trunk marks a young life shortened; an orb means resurrection; drapery over an urn signifies mourning.

script_body: On the near right corner where Green-Bough meets Fern stands the lavish white tomb of Charlotte Canda. She was the only daughter of Charles Canda, an officer in Napoleon's army who emigrated to America and ran a girls' finishing school in Manhattan. On a stormy night, February 3, 1845, a party celebrated Charlotte's seventeenth birthday. As it ended, she and her father escorted a friend home; not wanting the lady to walk alone, Charles saw her to the door, and when he returned the carriage was gone. The horse had bolted, crossed Broadway, and thrown Charlotte, who struck her head — she died just as her father reached her. The Candas were Catholic, and she was first interred in the old St. Patrick's Cathedral cemetery on Mott Street. This monument was essentially designed by Charlotte herself: she had been drawing a memorial for a recently deceased aunt, and her father found the sketch and embellished it with roses, flowers, birds, and wreaths, many repeated in the number seventeen — her age. The monument stands seventeen feet high and seventeen feet deep, incorporating her favorite things: books, musical instruments, drawing implements, and her parrot. Charlotte appears in the gown she wore the night she died, a star above her symbolizing immortal life, and a butterfly with wings extended for her liberated spirit. In the 1850s hers was the most popular grave in the cemetery, drawing thousands yearly. Just outside the consecrated ground to her right stands a monument with the coat of arms of Charles Albert Jarret de la Marie — her French fiancé, who committed suicide in the Canda residence a year after her death and could not be buried on consecrated ground, but lies as close as the church would allow.

script_body: Soon after Green-Wood opened, a local paper reported visitors "began to be attracted from the city in considerable numbers daily," predicting it would become "a popular and elegant place of resort." At first they came by carriage; by the 1860s, public horsecars from downtown Brooklyn or the Fulton ferries brought them, and the cemetery began selling picture postcards and stereo cards as souvenirs. These rural cemeteries became America's first urban parks. But after public parks spread the pastoral landscape without graves, the recreational popularity of the "rural" cemetery began to wane in the last quarter of the century. Frederick Law Olmsted, who criticized the idea of cemeteries becoming "the constant resort of mere pleasure seekers," at first refused to design one — though he recanted later and designed Mountain View Cemetery in California. The Civil War's immense casualties also drained the era's sentimentalism, and the rise of art museums made cemetery-visiting less desirable.

script_body: Up the hill above three small children's graves rises the mausoleum of Henry Evelyn Pierrepont, the man primarily responsible for Green-Wood. A city planner and businessman, the second son of Hezekiah B. Pierrepont, he is regarded as one of the first city planners in the United States and was active in planning Brooklyn's expansion after its 1834 incorporation; the next year he was appointed chair of a commission to lay out the new city's streets. He donated the cemetery's original fence and, in 1842, bought eight plots for himself and family. His monument, designed by Richard Upjohn, stands atop one of Green-Wood's few manmade hills. When he died, Pierrepont was the last survivor of the original trustees who created the cemetery.

script_body: Off Central Avenue, a smallish marble monument with a Masonic symbol and a carved steamship honors the engineers of the monitor Weehawken. The Weehawken followed the famous armored Monitor that fought the Merrimack to a draw in 1862. Beginning in January 1863 it helped blockade the Confederate port of Charleston as part of a flotilla led by the New Ironsides. When the ironclads attacked the harbor defenses in April, at least two thousand Confederate shots rained down; the Keokuk sank, and the New Ironsides sat for an hour directly atop a torpedo holding a ton of powder that the Confederates couldn't detonate because of a broken wire. In October 1863 the Weehawken ran aground attacking Fort Sumter, and the New Ironsides put itself between her and the batteries to draw fire while Union tugs pulled her out. She was rescued — but sank two months later. Her gravestone reads: "Sacred to the memory of the officers of the United States Navy who lost their lives by being drowned on the US Monitor Weehawken... when she foundered off Charleston, SC, December 6, 1863. The remains were exhumed from the engine room of the wrecked Monitor where they nobly fell at their post of duty."

The gravestone reads: Sacred to the memory of the officers of the United States Navy who lost their lives by being drowned on the US Monitor Weehawken... when she foundered off Charleston, SC, December 6, 1863. The remains were exhumed from the engine room of the wrecked Monitor where they nobly fell at their post of duty.

script_body: Up a steep hill where Vale Path meets Central Avenue, a cluster of very simple black marble monuments marks the Tiffany family. The large central stone is patriarch Charles Lewis Tiffany, surrounded by family including his most famous son, Louis Comfort Tiffany. The internationally renowned company was founded by Charles Tiffany and partner John B. Young in 1837, selling stationery and fancy goods from a shop at 237 Broadway; after Charles bought out his partners he renamed it Tiffany and Company. His son Louis was meant to take over the business, but his talents pulled him toward the decorative arts. He studied painting in New York and Paris and traveled the world, and his great gift emerged in glass: in the 1870s he and his rival John LaFarge — also buried here — revolutionized stained glass. In 1879 Louis opened his own firm and was soon granted a patent for Favrile glass, decorating the interiors of wealthy Manhattan mansions and clubs; in 1893 he built a factory in Corona, Queens, where his Tiffany Studios produced thousands of windows, lamps, and ceramics now in museums worldwide. He even designed stained-glass windows for vaults here in Green-Wood. More interested in art than status, his grave gives only his name and dates — though note his two wives, each calling herself "Wife of Louis Comfort Tiffany, N.A.," a nod to his membership in the National Academy of Design.

script_body: Along Valley Avenue, note the detailed blue-gray August Jacklitsch monument — one of the few "white bronze" memorials in Green-Wood. Only one firm, the Monumental Bronze Company of Bridgeport, Connecticut, made them, casting pure zinc from the mid-1870s to roughly World War I and selling through a catalog or a sales agent with an office near the cemetery. White bronze mimicked carved marble or granite but allowed far greater detail — families could even recreate the fashionable century plant, something impossible to carve in stone. There was one problem: the monuments were mass-produced, with only the nameplates individualized and then bolted on. That made them easy for vandals to dismantle — and a handy hiding place for bootleggers to stash liquor during Prohibition.

script_body: At Hillside Path stands the large monument to John "Soda Fountain King" Matthews — one of the guide's favorites. Crafted by Karl Muller in marble and terra-cotta in 1868, it was celebrated as the "Mortuary Monument of the Year." Matthews lies atop his tomb, gazing up at scenes from his life: a mix of animals, plants, the Four Evangelists, and carvings of his own children. Four corner gargoyles double as gutters, drawing rainwater off the roof. A life-size seated statue above him symbolizes grief and mourning; the center tower atop the roofline has been lost to decay. Walk around the tomb to see how weather has aged its southern and western sides while leaving the rest nearly intact. Matthews earned his title by pioneering a process that mixed marble chips with sulphuric acid to make carbonic acid gas, which, combined with water, carbonated a beverage — essentially what we now call seltzer. By 1870 he was supplying more than five hundred soda fountains. His slogan: "Youth as it sips its first glass, experiences sensations which, like the first sensations of love, cannot be forgotten but are cherished to the last."

script_body: Green-Wood had no chapel until the early twentieth century. When it solicited bids, Carrère & Hastings submitted a plan; rejected here, the firm modified it into what became the main branch of the New York Public Library at Forty-second Street and Fifth Avenue. The firm of Warren & Wetmore — best known for Grand Central Terminal, completed in 1913 — was chosen instead and built the chapel in 1912, a scaled-down version of Christopher Wren's Tom Tower at Christ Church, Oxford. After decades closed, the chapel reopened in April 2000; it is meant for individual contemplation but can be reserved for services. Alongside it stands the very large receiving tomb, its elaborate entrance echoing the cemetery's main gate. Capable of holding fifteen hundred bodies, it dates to the cemetery's earliest days: before modern digging equipment, those who died in winter, when the ground was frozen, were held here until the spring thaw. Its vast size is evident from the series of black metal vents along the hillside.

script_body: Perhaps the New York Times said it best in 1866: "It is the ambition of the New Yorker to live on Fifth Avenue, to take his airings in the Park, and to sleep with his fathers in Green-Wood." Returning to where we began, we can ponder the lives of those buried here and the shortness and unpredictability of life. Fugit hora — the hours are fleeting.

script_body: As the ferry crosses the harbor, step out onto the deck and look to your left for Governors Island — the 176-acre former U.S. Army and then Coast Guard base, closed in 1996. Almost half of it, eighty-five acres, is a National Historic Landmark, and five individual structures are landmarked as well. The three-story fort protecting the island on this side is Castle Williams, built between 1807 and 1811, one of three forts on the island.

script_body: Ferries have crossed this harbor since sailing vessels began running between the islands as early as 1713. The first steamer-ferry service between Staten Island and Manhattan was started by Daniel Tompkins, who launched the Nautilus in 1817; regular service has continued ever since. In 1905 municipal ferries began replacing the private companies, and the city has run the route ever since.

script_body: Built by architects Carrere & Hastings between 1904 and 1906, Staten Island Borough Hall is the main government building for the borough. It was designed to be immediately noticed by those arriving by ferry from Manhattan, standing as a symbol of Staten Island's equal membership in greater New York, and it is a New York City Landmark. Carrere & Hastings was one of the city's more prominent early-twentieth-century firms — and one wonders whether the fact that John Carrere was a Staten Island resident helped land this plum contract.

script_body: Built in 1904 in the collegiate Gothic style, Curtis High School was the first public high school on Staten Island and the first municipal building put up after the 1898 Consolidation of Greater New York. It is named for George William Curtis, a nineteenth-century writer and editor who kept a country estate on the island — an early advocate of women's suffrage and of professional civil service as a cure for political corruption. Locally he is remembered for sheltering Horace Greeley from pro-Confederate Staten Islanders during the Civil War. Curtis wrote for Harper's and The Nation and published Putnam's Monthly with his friend and fellow Staten Islander Frederick Law Olmsted.

script_body: Behind the iron fence and Greek Revival buildings stands Sailors' Snug Harbor, created in 1801 with a bequest from shipping merchant Robert R. Randall as an institution for the care of "aged, decrepit, and worn-out sailors." Snug Harbor bought this land in 1831 and built a campus for retired seamen; by 1900 it housed over a thousand people. As the number of American sailors dwindled, so did the institution — in 1975 it relocated to North Carolina, and a year later the complex became the Sailors' Snug Harbor Cultural Center.

script_body: Near the center of Staten Island, Historic Richmond Town is a great place to stop and walk around. This twenty-five-acre site holds twenty-seven historic buildings gathered from across the island — including the oldest extant schoolhouse in the nation, built in 1696. script_body: There have been fortifications on this site since 1663, and it was one of the last British positions to surrender after the American Revolution. The present fort was built in 1847 and dedicated in 1865 to Brigadier General James Wadsworth, following his death at the Civil War's Battle of the Wilderness. Since the early 1990s the installation has been part of the Gateway National Recreation Area, with a National Park Service visitor center, a short film on the history of New York's fortifications, and a scenic overlook on Tompkins Road.

script_body: When the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge was completed in 1964, designed by Swiss engineer Othmar Ammann, it was the world's longest suspension bridge, measuring 4,260 feet between its towers. It is no longer the longest, but it is still beautiful. Many Italian Americans in Bay Ridge, near the Brooklyn approach, did not want their homes destroyed for its approaches — and naming the bridge after Giovanni da Verrazano, who sailed into New York Harbor in 1524, was hardly enough to soothe their concerns. It took Robert Moses many years to beat back the opposition, but he eventually got his way: eight thousand Brooklynites lost their homes, and a good number more moved across the bridge to Staten Island. The Staten Island side is the starting point for the New York Marathon every November. Including its approaches the bridge runs 13,700 feet; it stands 228 feet above the water; each tower is 693 feet tall; and it costs seven dollars to cross — though the toll is collected only traveling from Brooklyn to Staten Island, so going this way you get a free ride.

script_body: Coney Island takes its name from an Anglicized version of the Dutch word for rabbit — the animals were abundant here in the 1600s. A vacation spot for New Yorkers since at least the mid-nineteenth century, it eventually held three of the most spectacular amusement parks in the nation: Steeplechase Park, Luna Park, and Dreamland. All are closed now; in their place stands Astroland, opened in 1954. From the boardwalk, look right to a large pier where residents fish and go crabbing, and where the Polar Bear Club swims every weekend through the winter — its New Year's Day plunge drawing news cameras and one-time swimmers from across the city.

source_passage: Coney Island is named for an Anglicized version of the Dutch word for rabbit; the animals were abundant here in the 1600s. It's been a vacation spot for New Yorkers from at least the mid-nineteenth century. Eventually, three of the most spectacular amusement parks in the nation were built here—Steeplechase Park, Luna Park, and Dreamland. They are all closed now. In their place stands Astroland, opened in 1954. ... From about where you're standing, the Polar Bear Club goes swimming every weekend during the winter. The New Year's Day swim brings out news cameras, tourists, and one-time swimmers from across the city.

script_body: The intersection of Gravesend Neck Road and McDonald Avenue was the town center of Gravesend, the only non-Dutch town among the original six settlements that made up seventeenth-century Brooklyn. Gravesend was founded in 1643 by Lady Deborah Moody, an Anabaptist who fled religious intolerance in Massachusetts — and here became the first woman to vote at a town meeting. The name comes either from the Dutch grafesande, read as both "end of the grove" and "count's beach," or from the British town of Gravesend.

script_body: Ocean Parkway, finished in 1876 before the automobile, stretches six miles from Coney Island to Prospect Park. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, who designed both Central Park in Manhattan and Prospect Park in Brooklyn, believed strongly in a network of scenic parkways throughout the city, and this is one of them. It originally had a central drive, greenery-filled malls — hence "parkway" — a bridle trail, and pedestrian walkways. The bridle trails are now service roads, but the beauty of the parkway remains.

script_body: Just off one of Brooklyn's busiest commercial streets, the small historic district of Prospect Park South hides large single-family houses ranging from Tudor to Queen Anne to neo-Japanese. The neighborhood was created by developer Dean Alvord, who bought forty acres here in 1899. To shape the place he wanted, Alvord required houses set back thirty-nine feet from the sidewalk, with eight feet between street and sidewalk left for greenery. Most of the houses were finished by 1905.

script_body: On Flatbush Avenue stands Erasmus Hall High School, whose famous graduates include Barbra Streisand, Neil Diamond, Barry Manilow, and Bobby Fischer. Through the gate at the center of the block you can see the original wooden 1786 Erasmus Hall inside the quad — the first secondary school chartered by New York State, set up by the Flatbush Reformed Dutch Church diagonally across the street. The present church building, finished in 1798, is the third on its site.

script_body: The 526-acre Prospect Park was designed by Calvert Vaux and Frederick Law Olmsted in 1866–1873, as soon as they finished Central Park. Like Central Park it gathers different landscapes — the long, hilly Long Meadow, a wooded ravine, a lake, several arches, and a number of buildings. And as in Manhattan, the city first backed a mediocre design by Egbert Viele before abandoning it for Vaux and Olmsted's. Many find Prospect Park as beautiful as Central Park, if not more so, thanks to the very high hills that crop up in several places.

script_body: Along Eastern Parkway sit the Brooklyn Public Library, the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, and the Brooklyn Museum. The library was founded in 1897 but not completed in this spot until 1941; the botanic garden opened in 1912. The museum, designed by Stanford White, was begun in 1897 and holds an excellent Egyptian art collection. All three remind us that Brooklyn was, until 1898, a separate city and not part of New York.

script_body: Set back from Bergen Street along what was Hunterfly Road, the Weeksville Houses are all that remain of two mid-nineteenth-century African American communities. Thirty years before the Civil War, William Thomas founded Carrville and James Weeks built the community that became Weeksville; both had their own schools, churches, and an orphanage. The beautiful Eastern Parkway and the streets built off it destroyed Carrville and Weeksville — much as the Cross Bronx Expressway would later destroy Bronx communities in the twentieth century.

script_body: Along the Jackie Robinson Parkway between Brooklyn and Queens, the route appears lined by one giant cemetery — and that is nearly true: eighteen different cemeteries crowd the road, holding a combined twenty thousand veterans and untold others. Adjacent Machpelah Cemetery holds the magician Harry Houdini, and nearby graves include Yiddish writer Sholom Aleichem, actor Edward G. Robinson, World Series fixer Arnold Rothstein, and jurist Benjamin Cardozo.

script_body: Flushing was established in 1645 under Dutch governor William Kieft, who assured the eighteen original freeholders the right to religious freedom — making the town one of the cornerstones of religious liberty in colonial America. Begun as a predominantly English community within a Dutch colony, Flushing was a haven for free blacks in the early nineteenth century and today may host more immigrants from different countries than anywhere else in New York City.

script_body: Built in 1694, the Friends Meeting House on Northern Boulevard is the oldest house of worship in New York City. It keeps the traditional Quaker spirit — without decoration or art, to allow undistracted worship — and during the Revolutionary War the British converted it into a prison and hospital. Step inside if you can: the second story rests on massive forty-foot hand-cut oak beams, and the original handmade ironwork is still in use. The Meeting House is on the National Register of Historic Places, and visitors are welcome.

script_body: Built in the colonial saltbox style in 1661 by John Bowne — an Englishman who reached Flushing by way of Boston — the Bowne House became a flashpoint for religious freedom. After converting to the Quaker faith, Bowne invited Quakers to meet in his kitchen, defying New Amsterdam governor Peter Stuyvesant, who had declared the Dutch Reformed Church the only acceptable order. When Stuyvesant moved against the Quakers, thirty townspeople signed the "Flushing Remonstrance," protesting that they could not "stretch our hands against them, to punish, banish or persecute them." Stuyvesant responded by arresting and fining the signers, and in 1662 he arrested Bowne himself, sentencing him to prison and banishment. After seven months in jail, Bowne sailed to the Netherlands and argued before the Dutch West India Company for religious tolerance; they freed him and rebuked Stuyvesant with a letter upholding the principle. Many historians regard this community resistance as a foundation of the First Amendment's freedom of religion. Nine generations of Bownes lived here, the last leaving in 1945; the house is now called "A National Shrine to Religious Freedom."

script_body: The modern red-brick house at 34-56 107th Street is the Louis Armstrong House, a National Historic Landmark and the home of jazz great Louis Armstrong for twenty-nine years, from 1942 until his death in 1971. Born in the Storyville neighborhood of New Orleans, Armstrong grew up amid the ragtime and blues that shaped his life; his musical career began in the marching band of the Colored Waifs' Home, where he was sent in 1912. His professional career got a boost when King Oliver made him second cornetist in 1922, bringing him to Chicago, and he reached New York as a trumpeter, joining Fats Waller and Edith Wilson's Broadway revue Hot Chocolate in 1929. He performed in numerous shows and films, returning to the stage in 1947; among his greatest hits are "Blueberry Hill" of 1949, "Mack the Knife" of 1955, and "Hello Dolly" of 1962.

script_body: Past the train tracks lies Forest Hills Gardens, a 142-acre community planned by Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. — son of the Central Park Olmsted — in the style of an English Tudor village. Construction began around 1910, but two world wars and the 1929 crash meant most houses weren't built until the 1940s and 1950s. Olmsted, with his colleague Grosvenor Atterbury, designed the railroad station, the greens, and nearby houses. The community was originally envisioned by Margaret Olivia Slocum Sage, wife of financier-philanthropist Russell Sage and founder of the Russell Sage Foundation.

script_body: Farmland in the early twentieth century, the Jackson Heights Historic District was ripe for speculative building just before the Queensboro Bridge opened in 1909. The Queensboro Realty Company bought up 350 acres and built the neighborhood over two decades. Its innovation lay in the blocks themselves — five- and six-story cooperative apartment houses with large rear gardens along the avenues, smaller attached single-family houses on the side streets. But in the 1920s the company tolerated "red-lining," an exclusionary policy directed against Jews, Catholics, and African Americans that blocked them from mortgages. Today Jackson Heights is a thriving, ethnically diverse community, home in the early 1990s to the largest Argentinean community in the city.

In the 1920s the company tolerated red-lining against Jews, Catholics, African Americans; later home to the largest Argentinean community in the city
source_passage: This area was farmland in the early twentieth century. Just prior to the Queensboro Bridge opening in 1909, this district had been ripe for speculative building. A group of investors called the Queensboro Realty Company bought up 350 acres and, over the next two decades, built this neighborhood. ... Along the avenues, builders created fiveand six-story cooperative apartment houses with large rear gardens. ... On the side streets they built smaller single-family attached houses. ... In the 1920s the Queensboro Realty Company tolerated the suburban practice of "red-lining," an exclusionary policy directed against unwanted buyers—here meaning Jews, Catholics, and African Americans ... In the early 1990s it was home to the largest Argentinean community in New York City.

script_body: The Triboro is actually three interconnected steel bridges linking the Bronx, Manhattan, and Queens. Its designers, Othmar Ammann and Aymar Embury II, had the misfortune to begin construction on October 25, 1929 — the same day the stock market collapsed. Work halted until 1933, and the bridge finally opened in July 1936.

script_body: Paralleling the Triboro to the right is the New York Connecting Railroad Bridge — the Hell Gate Bridge. When it was completed in 1917 it was the longest steel-arch bridge in the world, two and a half miles long with a 1,017-foot steel arch carrying four sets of rail lines. Gustav Lindenthal built it for the Pennsylvania Railroad to give direct train access between Manhattan, Queens, the Bronx, and points north.

source_passage: Paralleling the Triboro Bridge to the right is the New York Connecting Railroad Bridge, known to most New Yorkers as the Hell Gate Bridge. When this bridge was completed in 1917, it was the longest steel-arch bridge in the world. The bridge is two and a half miles in length and holds four sets of rail lines. The steel arch is a tremendous 1,017 feet. It was built for the Pennsylvania Railroad by Gustav Lindenthal (who also designed the Williamsburg and Queensboro Bridges) to provide direct train access between Manhattan, Queens, the Bronx, and points north.

script_body: The Bronx is New York's northernmost borough and the only one wholly on the mainland of the United States. It is named for Jonas Bronck, an early settler. Parts of the western Bronx were annexed by New York in 1875, and the eastern parts joined the city at the 1898 Consolidation. The borough became a destination for millions leaving Manhattan's tenements in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, who then moved on to the suburbs in the 1960s and 1970s. Over twenty percent of the Bronx is parkland.

script_body: The Grand Concourse stretches four and a half miles from the South Bronx northward and is 180 feet wide at its broadest. Completed south to 161st Street between 1902 and 1909 and extended later in the 1930s, the concourse became home to some of the Bronx's most elegant apartment buildings, especially in the 1920s and 1930s. At first only the service roads carried cars, with the larger center stretch reserved for horses and carriages; now everything is a car lane.

Park safely and look back the way you came: the "point" of the iron is what you see as you look south, and the building reads just like Manhattan's Flatiron from that angle.

script_body: Turn at 158th Street and Yankee Stadium — the "House That Ruth Built" — rises up ahead. The brewer Jacob Ruppert had the stadium built for his team in 1923, with opening day on April 18; it was redone in 1976. Over the years famous Yankees have included Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig, Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, Roger Maris, and Reggie Jackson. River Avenue, alongside, is lined with sporting-goods stores, most prominently the baseball shops owned by "Stan."

poi_name: Hall of Fame for Great Americans
script_body: Bronx Community College began in 1894 as the uptown campus of Greenwich Village's New York University; in 1973 NYU sold the grounds to the city, which turned them into BCC. The Hall of Fame Terrace, open to the public, was designed by McKim, Mead and White — a semicircular arcade with bronze busts of educators, lawyers, scientists, and others, giving a great westward view. Cleverly, the Hall of Fame was designed to hide the giant foundation walls of buildings Stanford White designed for the campus.

source_passage: Bronx Community College (BCC) was begun in 1894 as the uptown campus of Greenwich Village's New York University (NYU). In 1973, NYU sold the grounds to the city, which turned the buildings into BCC. ... The Hall of Fame (and much of the campus) was designed by McKim, Mead and White. It's a semicircular arcade with bronze busts of educators, lawyers, scientists, and others and gives visitors a great view westward. Although it isn't apparent from where you stand, the Hall of Fame was designed to hide the giant foundation walls of some of the buildings Stanford White designed for the campus.

script_body: On the corner stands Poe Cottage, built in 1816. The American author Edgar Allan Poe moved here in 1846, hoping the then-country air would cure his wife's tuberculosis. She died soon after they moved, but Poe stayed on until just before his own death in 1849, writing "Ulalume" and "The Bells" here. The cottage originally stood across the street and was moved to its current location in 1913.

script_body: Sedgwick Avenue runs along the western edge of the Jerome Park Reservoir, filled in 1905 and named for Leonard Jerome — Winston Churchill's grandfather — who had a racetrack named after him nearby. Jerome sponsored the American Jockey Club to lift horse racing's image in the United States toward the aristocratic status it held in England.

script_body: Wave Hill is a nonprofit, city-owned park in Riverdale, its beautiful grounds holding an excellent herb garden and a small greenhouse. Wave Hill House, on the grounds, was a country home built in 1843, and over the years it has sheltered Teddy Roosevelt in the summers of 1870 and 1871, Mark Twain from 1901 to 1903, and Arturo Toscanini from 1942 to 1945. Bashford Dean, zoologist and curator of arms and armor for the Metropolitan Museum, lived in Glyndor House, another building on the grounds.

poi_name: Ellis Island National Museum of Immigration
script_body: Further into the harbor, to your right, are Ellis Island and the Statue of Liberty. Ellis Island first opened as New York's immigration reception center in 1892, and its main building — now a museum — opened in 1900. Between its opening and 1924, some sixteen million immigrants entered America through this building. The island itself began as a 3.3-acre sandbar; to meet the demand for space, landfill grew it to its current 27.5 acres.

Between first opening and 1924, some 16 million immigrants entered America through this building. One interesting note about the island itself: Ellis Island began as a 3.3-acre sandbar. To accommodate the buildings and increased demand for space, landfill was added to grow the island to its current 27.5 acres.

script_body: The Statue of Liberty, one of the best-known landmarks in the world, was a gift from France, dedicated on October 28, 1886. Designed by sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi, its copper "skin" is supported by a metal structure built by Gustave Eiffel, and its stone base was designed by American architect Richard Morris Hunt.
